Gemini 3 models accept multimodal function responses (image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp, application/pdf, text/plain inline in the response part) and require each response to carry a matching call_id and name. Tool results consume the same 1,048,576-token input budget as everything else.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Parallel function calling is supported with no documented numeric cap on how many calls may be emitted in one turn. Gemini 3 returns a unique id per function call and requires exactly one response per call, matched by id and name -- results may return out of order but must be 1:1.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.unit: automatic function-calling remote calls per request (SDK default)
tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: CHANGED from null. SCOPE: SDK layer, not the model API. The google-genai SDK's automatic function calling loops with a default maximum of 10 remote calls per request; it is configurable and can be disabled, after which the caller drives the loop. The Gemini API itself documents no per-turn numeric cap on tool-call/result cycles -- there is no 'reached its tool-use limit' error analogous to Claude's, so the limits that actually bind a long agentic run are the 512-declaration aggregate ceiling (an observed API rejection, tier 4 -- see max_tools_hard) and the 1,048,576-token input window. The Interactions API does not support Python automatic function calling at all. Source re-pointed 2026-08-19 from the googleapis/python-genai GitHub repo to Google's published SDK documentation site, which states verbatim: 'by default the SDK will perform automatic function calling until the remote calls exceed the maximum remote call for automatic function calling (default to 10 times)'.

max_connected_servers.notes: No documented cap on simultaneous MCP server connections at the API layer, and the Interactions API reference documents no numeric cap on how many mcp_server tools an interaction may carry. The binding constraint is the 512 aggregate functionDeclarations (an observed API rejection, tier 4 -- see max_tools_hard). Client layer for contrast: Gemini CLI users report tools being 'silently dropped' past roughly 100 aggregate MCP tools (https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/21823, closed), and Gemini CLI's docs set a 600,000 ms (10 minute) default per-server request timeout.

max_total_tools.notes: TIER 4 / OBSERVED API ERROR, NOT PUBLISHED SPEC (re-graded 2026-08-19 from tier 2 -- a GitHub issue is tier 4 under methodology section 4 even when it quotes a real API rejection). The cited Gemini CLI issue (opened 2026-02-14, closed 'not planned') reports the verbatim API rejection 'At most 512 function declarations can be specified' when many MCP servers are enabled. UNCONFIRMED BY VENDOR DOCS: on 2026-08-19 I opened the Gemini API function-calling docs (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling -- no numeric cap, only the best practice 'Keep active set to 10-20 tools maximum'), the Interactions API overview (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/interactions-overview), the Live API tools page (https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/live-api/tools), the Vertex REST FunctionDeclaration reference and the Gemini Enterprise / Vertex function-calling reference; none of them publishes a maximum number of function declarations. The only tier-1 count Google publishes sits on a DIFFERENT surface: Firebase AI Logic states 'The maximum number of function declarations that you can provide with the request is 128' (https://firebase.google.com/docs/ai-logic/function-calling), presented there as a Firebase AI Logic SDK constraint. Planning guidance: 128 is the conservative documented number on that SDK; 512 is the observed hard rejection point on the raw API. SCOPE: aggregate client/API ceiling, identical in substance to max_tools_hard -- summed across every connected MCP server plus built-in tools in one request; there is no per-MCP-server cap.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Only a subset of the OpenAPI schema is accepted for function parameters (verbatim: 'Only a subset of the OpenAPI schema is supported'). Gemini 3-series and 2.5-series models accept type, nullable, required, format, description, properties, items, enum, anyOf, $ref, minItems, maxItems, minimum, maximum. Documented soft constraint, verbatim: 'For any mode, the API may reject very large or deeply nested schemas' -- Google publishes no numeric nesting-depth or property-count cap, so there is nothing analogous to OpenAI strict mode's 100-property / 5-level rules. Function names are validated by the API against 'Must start with a letter or an underscore. Must be alphanumeric (a-z, A-Z, 0-9), underscores (_), dots (.), colons (:), or dashes (-), with a maximum length of 64.' For MCP the function-calling page adds: 'MCP server names should not include the - character. Use snake_case server names instead.' Sources: https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/function-calling , https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode/issues/235
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: RATE LIMITS: Google no longer publishes per-model RPM/TPM/RPD tables -- the rate-limits page now says limits 'can be viewed in Google AI Studio' (only Batch API enqueued-token quotas remain tabulated), so the per-model rate numbers carried in the 2026-06-21 revision of this dataset are no longer sourceable and have been removed rather than restated. API CHANGES since 2026-06-21: the Interactions API went GA in June 2026 and is now the recommended surface for all new projects; the sampling parameters temperature / top_p / top_k were deprecated 2026-07-21; thinking_budget is replaced by thinking_level. The Interactions API does NOT support explicit context caching (implicit only, via previous_interaction_id), the Batch API, or Python automatic function calling. Tool configuration is interaction-scoped and must be re-sent on every interaction, so tool-definition tokens are re-paid per interaction unless implicit caching hits. Token accounting now exposes total_tool_use_tokens, total_thought_tokens and total_cached_tokens in the usage payload -- total_tool_use_tokens makes an MCP server's definition footprint directly measurable. MODEL-SPECIFIC AND THE BIGGEST COST TRAP IN THIS ROSTER: prompts over 200,000 tokens are billed at $2.50/1M input (vs $1.25) and $15.00/1M output (vs $10.00), and cached reads double from $0.125 to $0.25/1M. A 512-declaration MCP catalogue plus history can cross 200k on its own. Cache storage is $4.50/1M tokens/hour, 4.5x the Flash models. Minimum cacheable prompt 2,048 tokens (lower than the 4,096 of the Gemini 3.x Flash models). Computer Use is not supported on this model.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode. Gemini enforces its own looser OpenAPI-subset keyword rules plus an undocumented size/nesting rejection -- captured in tool_schema_limits_notes.

skills_supported.notes: CHANGED from false. Google now ships Agent Skills: a SKILL.md-based, model-invokable instruction bundle with an official library (github.com/google-gemini/gemini-skills, Apache-2.0), publicised 2026-03-25 and documented on ai.google.dev. IMPORTANT SCOPE: skills live at the AGENT/CLI layer (Gemini CLI, Antigravity, third-party coding assistants), not in the model API -- the Gemini docs state 'Most agents index skills only on startup' and the generateContent / Interactions endpoints neither accept nor process a skill object. For a raw API caller the only always-on instruction channel is still system_instruction, and Gems remain a consumer-product feature.

skills_loading_model.notes: Verbatim (Gemini CLI): 'At the start of a session, Gemini CLI scans the discovery tiers and injects the name and description of all enabled skills into the system prompt' and 'Only skill metadata (name and description) is loaded initially. Detailed instructions and resources are only disclosed when the model explicitly activates the skill, saving context tokens.' Activation is itself a tool call (activate_skill), after which 'The SKILL.md body and folder structure is added to the conversation history'.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Skills never enter a Gemini API request as a first-class object -- the agent host injects skill name+description into the system prompt at session start and appends the SKILL.md body only after activate_skill fires. The resident cost is therefore one metadata line per enabled skill and the burst cost is the skill body, both billed as ordinary input tokens. System instructions are billed as input on every request; caching can absorb a static instruction + tool-definition prefix once it clears the model's minimum cacheable size.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System instructions are counted as part of the input tokens; Google documents no fixed per-request overhead beyond the caller-supplied content. In the Interactions API tools and system instructions are interaction-scoped and must be re-specified on every interaction, so a large MCP tool block is re-billed each turn unless implicit caching hits.

prompt_caching.notes: Implicit caching is enabled by default for all Gemini 2.5 and newer models; cache hits reported in usage.total_cached_tokens. Minimum cacheable prompt for Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro: 2,048 tokens. Cached reads $0.125/1M for prompts <=200k and $0.25/1M above; cache storage $4.50/1M tokens/hour -- 4.5x the Gemini 3.x Flash models, so parking a large tool block in an explicit cache is materially more expensive here. Explicit caches are not supported in the Interactions API.

memory_feature.notes: No persistent cross-session memory product in the Gemini Developer API. The closest primitive is the Interactions API's server-side conversation state via previous_interaction_id, which is per-conversation session state (and a caching optimization), not a durable memory store.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-verified unchanged. Verbatim: '$1.25, prompts <= 200k tokens $2.50, prompts > 200k'. This long-context tier is unique to the Pro line in this roster -- the Flash models have no such break.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-verified unchanged. Verbatim: '$10.00, prompts <= 200k $15.00, prompts > 200k'. Includes thinking tokens.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-verified unchanged. Verbatim: '$0.125, prompts <= 200k $0.25, prompts > 200k'. Cache storage $4.50/1M tokens/hour.

batch_discount.value: 50% off standard price (Batch API: input $0.625/1M <=200K, $1.25/1M >200K; output $5.00/1M <=200K, $7.50/1M >200K)
batch_discount.notes: Re-verified unchanged.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Same tokenization rules as the Gemini 3.x models (image 258 tokens per <=384px image or 768x768 tile; audio 32 tokens/sec; video 263 tokens/sec). The >200k long-context price tier applies to the whole prompt regardless of modality. Cache storage $4.50/1M tokens/hour vs $1.00 (or $0.50 promotional) for the Flash models.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Thinking tokens billed at the output rate: $10.00/1M for prompts <=200k, $15.00/1M above.

release_date.notes: Re-verified: model-versions table lists release date 'June 17, 2025'; the model page still shows 'Latest update: June 2025'. Value unchanged.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Re-verified: the gemini-2.5-pro model page still carries 'Knowledge cutoff: January 2025' (the Gemini 3.x pages have dropped this row). Cross-checked against Oracle OCI's Gemini 2.5 Pro page, which also states 'January 2025'.

detail.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: still GA, no shutdown date, pricing unchanged. It remains the only Pro-class Gemini in this roster because Gemini 3.5 Pro has not shipped and gemini-3.1-pro-preview is still preview (released 2026-02-19, $2.00/$12.00 with the same >200k tier). For MCP-heavy sessions the 200k price break is the number that matters: a large aggregate tool catalogue plus conversation can cross it and double the input rate, and cache storage here is 4.5x the Flash models.

models.tokenizer_family: model-dependent (OpenAI GPT-5.x → o200k_base-family; Anthropic Claude → Anthropic tokenizer)

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (architecture page updated 2026-07-13). Microsoft still publishes no raw per-request context-window token number for Microsoft 365 Copilot, and the underlying model is now user-selectable (OpenAI GPT-5.x or Anthropic Claude), so a single number would be wrong anyway. What IS documented and binding for MCP work is the plugin scope: a 4,096-token limit that 'includes all context and response data', with guidance to 'Optimize for approximately 66% of the technical limit' (~2,730 tokens).

input_output_shared.notes: Still undocumented at the product layer as of 2026-08-19; would in any case vary with the selected underlying model.

max_input_tokens.notes: Not published. The product applies file/grounding limits (e.g. SharePoint list knowledge source capped at 20,000 items per the 2026-07-29 release notes) and the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget rather than a raw input-token cap.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not published by Microsoft for Microsoft 365 Copilot; inherited from the selected underlying model (OpenAI GPT-5.x or Anthropic Claude).

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not published. The documented output-side constraints are product-layer item counts: plugin response limit 25 items, grounding record limit 50 items, all inside the 4,096-token plugin budget.

extended_context.notes: No publicly documented extended-context mode for the Microsoft 365 Copilot product surface as of 2026-08-19.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Microsoft 365 Copilot is seat-licensed, so reasoning-token accounting is not exposed to customers. (Agent/Cowork consumption is separately metered in Copilot Credits, but not broken out per token class.)

tokenizer_family.value: model-dependent (OpenAI GPT-5.x → o200k_base-family; Anthropic Claude → Anthropic tokenizer)
tokenizer_family.notes: CHANGED from a flat 'o200k_base'. Microsoft 365 Copilot became a multi-vendor-model surface during the refresh window: release notes record 'Anthropic's Claude now available in Microsoft 365 Copilot' (2026-06-16) and 'Word: Choose Anthropic models when editing' (2026-08-11); Claude Opus 5 announced 2026-07-24. Microsoft publishes no tokenizer identity for either path, so the family is stated as model-dependent rather than asserted.

tokenizer_public.notes: Depends on the selected model: OpenAI-family counts are reproducible with the public tiktoken library; Anthropic's tokenizer is not public (API count endpoint only). Microsoft documents neither for the Copilot product layer.

tokenizer_access.value: model-dependent; use the upstream provider's tokenizer for the selected model (no Microsoft 365 Copilot count-tokens API)
tokenizer_access.notes: tiktoken (o200k_base / cl100k_base) is public and usable as a proxy for the OpenAI path; the Anthropic path needs Anthropic's count endpoint. Microsoft exposes no count-tokens API for Microsoft 365 Copilot.

count_tokens_method.value: approximate only — tiktoken o200k_base for the OpenAI path; no Microsoft 365 Copilot-native count API
count_tokens_method.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. There is still no Microsoft-provided token-count endpoint for Microsoft 365 Copilot, and the selected model may now be Anthropic rather than OpenAI, so local counts are an estimate.

image_token_rule.notes: Microsoft publishes no image-to-token conversion rule for Microsoft 365 Copilot; the underlying provider's rule applies but is not surfaced at the product layer.

audio_token_rule.notes: Meeting audio (Teams) is transcribed, but token accounting for audio is not published.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Standard ~4 chars/token rule of thumb for English text on o200k_base-family encodings; empirical, not a Microsoft-published figure.

function_calling.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (page updated 2026-08-05). Declarative agents call tools through plugins, which are either MCP servers or OpenAPI-described REST APIs.

native_mcp.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 (page updated 2026-08-11). A declarative agent plugin can point at a remote MCP server (`RemoteMCPServer` runtime, plugin manifest 2.4); the agent resolves the server's tools at runtime. MCP apps (tools returning UI widgets) render inline. Auth: none, API key, OAuth (static or dynamic client registration), or Microsoft Entra SSO. Separately, MCP-enabled agents reached Word/Excel/PowerPoint/Outlook on 2026-07-15 per the release notes.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: CHANGED from null to false. The architecture page (updated 2026-07-13) still states: 'Because Microsoft grounding and calls to external tools happen sequentially, you can't use chained operations with grounding data or looped operation plans.' Sequential-only processing is documented, so parallel tool calling is not available on this surface.

max_tools_hard.notes: No numeric per-request cap on the NUMBER of tools/functions is published for Microsoft 365 Copilot. The plugins page (re-opened 2026-08-19, updated 2026-08-05) explicitly declines to bound functions or MCP tools per plugin ('A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools'). The limits that DO bind, all AGGREGATE across the declarative agent rather than per MCP server: the manifest's 10-action/plugin-object ceiling per declarative agent (recorded under max_connected_servers, and derived there -- Microsoft never states it in MCP-server units), the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget that every injected tool definition competes for (a token budget, not a byte payload cap -- see max_request_size.notes, whose value is null for that reason), the documented quality cliff above 10 functions/tools, and the 5-plugin always-injected threshold beyond which semantic matching decides what is injected.

max_tools_practical.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19; wording now reads 'Due to token window limits, the quality of the responses might degrade if more than 10 functions or tools are included' (previous wording said 'functions'; MCP tools are now named explicitly). Scope: per plugin / per MCP server, not aggregate. Vendor-published but behavioural rather than enforced, hence recorded as the practical limit.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No dedicated tool-name length cap is published. Plugin manifest 2.4 (updated 2026-07-01) constrains function `name` by pattern only — must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$` (and `namespace` must match `^[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) — and applies the manifest-wide default of 4,000 characters to unqualified string properties. MCP tool names come from the server and are not separately bounded in Microsoft's docs.

max_tool_description_len.notes: CHANGED from null. Plugin manifest schema 2.4 (updated 2026-07-01) states that for `description_for_model`, 'Characters beyond 2048 MAY be ignored' — that is the model-facing tool/plugin description, i.e. exactly the field whose tokens land in the prompt. (Human-facing fields are tighter still: `name_for_human` beyond 20 chars and `description_for_human` beyond 100 chars MAY be ignored.) Confidence medium because the cap is expressed as MAY-be-ignored rather than a hard rejection, and because MCP tool descriptions arriving from the server are governed by the 4,096-token plugin budget rather than this manifest field.

max_request_size.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: was 4096 with unit "tokens"; now null. Across this dataset max_request_size is the BYTE ceiling on the request payload (Anthropic 32 MB, Gemini 100 MB, OpenAI 512 MB, Copilot Studio 5 MB connector payload), so a token budget stored in the same field made Microsoft 365 Copilot look ~5 orders of magnitude smaller than its peers and corrupted any cross-vendor min()/comparison. One field name, one meaning. Microsoft publishes NO byte/KB/MB request or response ceiling for the Microsoft 365 Copilot plugin/MCP path -- re-checked 2026-08-19 on this architecture page (its technical-limits table is expressed only in items, tokens and seconds), the plugins overview, the API plugin manifest 2.4 schema (character limits only, plus "Implementations are free to impose their own practical limits on manifest length") and the MCP-apps troubleshooting page (which only advises "Ensure responses aren't excessively large" with no number). WHAT THE 4,096 ACTUALLY IS, and where it now lives: a product-layer TOKEN budget for the plugin scope, verbatim "Token limit: 4,096* - Includes all context and response data", with the asterisk defined as "Limits include external overhead such as network latency and Microsoft service processing. Optimize for about 66% of the technical limit" (~2,730 tokens). Every injected tool definition, tool argument and tool result competes inside that one budget, and it is the ceiling that really binds this surface -- it is preserved in prose here, in tool_schema_limits_notes item (6), and in the max_tools_hard / max_total_tools notes, but it is NOT a byte ceiling and is not comparable to one. A 45-second timeout ("Timeout limit: 45 seconds* - Includes network latency and processing time") applies to the same scope.

max_tool_result_size.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: was 25 with unit "items"; now null. Across this dataset max_tool_result_size is a SIZE ceiling on a single tool RESULT (OpenAI 512 KB, Copilot Cowork 150 MiB per tool call); an item COUNT recorded in the same field is a different quantity and would corrupt any cross-vendor min()/comparison -- 25 would have read as the smallest result cap in the roster. Microsoft documents no byte or token ceiling on an individual plugin/MCP tool result for Microsoft 365 Copilot: the MCP-apps troubleshooting page only advises "Ensure responses aren't excessively large" (re-opened 2026-08-19), and no byte/KB/MB figure appears on the architecture page, the plugins overview or the API plugin manifest 2.4 schema. WHAT IS DOCUMENTED, and what actually binds a chatty tool here, verbatim from this page: "Plugin response limit: 25 items - Constrains external API response sizes" and "Grounding record limit: 50 items - Affects the amount of contextual data available" -- item counts, not sizes -- together with the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget, which truncates rather than rejects: "The token window for inputs to and outputs from a plugin truncates large content" (overview-plugins). Both item counts are also carried in tool_schema_limits_notes items (4) and (5); the token budget is described in max_request_size.notes and item (6).

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Recorded as 1 to represent the documented sequential-only model ('Microsoft grounding and calls to external tools happen sequentially'). Microsoft does not state a parallel-call count, so this encodes the constraint rather than a published integer.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No published cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. The binding documented constraint is the 45-second timeout for the plugin scope (including network latency and processing), reinforced by the sequential-processing model; the architecture page lists 'long-running processes' and 'complex decision trees requiring multiple conditional branches' as poor fits for declarative agents.

max_connected_servers.notes: DERIVED, and NOT a published MCP-server cap. Confidence lowered high -> medium on 2026-08-19 after re-opening the cited page. What the page actually says (re-read 2026-08-19): the `actions` property is 'A list of 1-10 objects that identify plugins that provide actions accessible to the declarative agent', and the Actions object section adds 'The array must contain at least one and no more than 10 objects.' The words MCP / Model Context Protocol do not appear on that page at all, so the unit here is action (plugin) OBJECTS, not MCP servers. The bridge to MCP is a different tier-1 page, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/extensibility/build-mcp-plugins (re-read 2026-08-19): an MCP server is attached to a declarative agent by adding an action ('Add an Action' -> 'Start with an MCP Server'), whose generated `ai-plugin.json` uses the RemoteMCPServer runtime and resolves the server's tools at runtime; that page publishes no numeric limit of its own. So an agent whose every action is an MCP server tops out at 10 MCP servers -- an inference across two tier-1 pages, not a sentence Microsoft has written. Related documented behaviour: at 5 or fewer plugins all are injected into the prompt; above 5, semantic matching selects which are injected per turn (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05).

max_total_tools.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19 from 10 to null. The previous 10 was the declarative-agent manifest's `actions` cap -- a count of plugin OBJECTS -- recorded on this dataset's TOOL-COUNT axis, which rendered Microsoft 365 Copilot as a 10-tool ceiling next to GitHub Copilot's 128 and Grok's 200. That is a unit conflation and a false cross-vendor comparison; the plugin-object ceiling now lives in max_connected_servers. Microsoft publishes NO aggregate cap on the number of individual tools: the plugins overview (tier 1, re-opened 2026-08-19) states verbatim 'A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools. All of a matched plugin's functions or tools are returned, even if only one is matched.' -- i.e. no per-request numeric tool-count cap is documented for this surface. The limits that DO bind, all aggregate across the declarative agent: (1) at most 10 action/plugin objects per agent (schema 1.8, 'A list of 1-10 objects that identify plugins') -- see max_connected_servers; (2) 5 or fewer plugins are always injected into the prompt, above that semantic matching decides which are injected per turn, and a matched plugin brings ALL of its tools with it; (3) the 4,096-token plugin I/O budget, inside which every injected tool definition, argument and result competes (documented in max_request_size.notes; that numeric field is null because it is this dataset's byte-payload ceiling and Microsoft publishes no byte figure for this surface); (4) the documented quality cliff -- 'Due to token window limits, the quality of the responses might degrade if more than 10 functions or tools are included' (max_tools_practical).

tool_definition_shape.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Plugin manifest 2.4 added the `RemoteMCPServer` runtime type, so a plugin is backed either by an MCP server (raw MCP tool schemas fetched from the server) or by an OpenAPI document (OpenAI-function-shaped operations declared in the `functions` array).

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. The 4,096-token plugin limit explicitly 'includes all context and response data', and plugins are injected into the prompt (all of them when there are 5 or fewer). Tool definitions therefore consume the budget before any tool is called.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Confidence raised medium→high and re-sourced. Two documented deferral mechanisms now exist: (1) semantic matching — with more than 5 plugins on an agent, only matched plugins are injected per turn (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05); (2) dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (page updated 2026-07-16) — with `"functions": []` and `run_for_functions: ["*"]` on a `RemoteMCPServer` runtime, the agent resolves the server's tool list at runtime per session from the MCP server instead of pinning a static list at publish time. Microsoft publishes no token-saving figure for either.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: PRODUCT-LAYER LIMITS (Microsoft 365 Copilot declarative agents), re-verified 2026-08-19. (1) Actions (plugin OBJECTS; an MCP server is attached as one action, per build-mcp-plugins) per agent: 1-10 — declarative agent schema 1.8, GA, which caps `actions` without ever mentioning MCP; the MCP-server reading is derived. (2) Always-injected plugins: 5 or fewer; above that, semantic matching selects which are injected. (3) Functions / MCP tools per plugin: no numeric cap is published — 'A plugin can include an unlimited number of functions or MCP tools' (overview-plugins, 2026-08-05) — but Microsoft documents that response quality might degrade above 10 functions or tools. (4) Plugin response: 25 items. (5) Grounding records: 50 items. (6) Plugin I/O token budget: 4,096 TOKENS covering context AND response; optimize to ~66% (~2,730 tokens). This is a token budget, not a byte payload ceiling -- Microsoft publishes no byte/KB/MB request or response limit for this surface, so max_request_size (this dataset's byte field) is null. (7) Turn timeout for the plugin scope: 45 seconds including network latency. (8) Sequential tool/grounding processing only. (9) Manifest strings: 4,000-character default; instructions 8,000; name 100; description 1,000; disclaimer.text 500. (10) Model-facing plugin/function description (`description_for_model`): characters beyond 2,048 MAY be ignored; `name_for_human` beyond 20 and `description_for_human` beyond 100 MAY be ignored (plugin manifest 2.4). (11) Function names must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$`; namespaces `^[A-Za-z0-9]+$`. (12) Conversation starters: 12. (13) Capability caps in 1.8: WebSearch sites 4; TeamsMessages urls 5; Meetings items_by_id 5; Email group_mailboxes 25; EmbeddedKnowledge 10 files at 1 MB each; editorial_answers 300. (14) MCP plugin auth: none, API key, OAuth (static or dynamic registration), Microsoft Entra SSO.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: NEW SINCE 2026-06-21. (a) Declarative agent manifest 1.8 shipped July 2026, adding EmailActions and MeetingActions write capabilities, a `file` property on worker agents, and `embedded_resource_snapshot_id` on embedded knowledge; no change to the 10-action cap. (b) MCP-enabled agents became available inside Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Catalyst (2026-07-15 release notes). (c) Federated Copilot connectors — MCP-based, read-only, user-identity, non-indexing data connectors surfaced in Copilot Chat, Copilot in Excel and the Researcher agent — became manageable in the Microsoft 365 admin center (2026-07-15); Microsoft-published connectors are enabled by default, partner connectors need admin approval with a 7-day review window; the gallery lists 12 categories and 50+ sources. Microsoft publishes no numeric result/tool/timeout limit for federated connectors. (d) Dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (2026-07-16). (d2) The Microsoft 365 Copilot extensibility overview (updated 2026-08-05) now lists FOUR extensibility paths — agents, Copilot connectors (synced into Microsoft Graph, or federated with real-time retrieval over MCP), the Microsoft Work IQ API (which exposes Microsoft 365 data to external agents over both Agent-to-Agent and Model Context Protocol), and the Microsoft 365 Copilot APIs (Retrieval, Search, Chat, Interaction Export, Meeting Insights). Microsoft publishes no numeric tool, token or payload limit for the Work IQ MCP path. (e) SharePoint list knowledge source capped at 20,000 items (2026-07-29). (f) Agent submission to the Agent Store from Agent Builder (2026-07-15), admin-reviewed. (g) Multi-vendor model choice: Anthropic Claude selectable in Copilot Chat from 2026-06-16, Claude Opus 5 from 2026-07-24, Anthropic models in Word from 2026-08-11. Governance unchanged: tenant admins control plugin/agent availability per user and group; distribution via the Microsoft 365 app catalog or AppSource; one declarative agent definition per app package. Adjacent Microsoft surfaces now have their own entries in this file: Copilot Cowork (`microsoft-copilot-cowork`) and Copilot Studio (`microsoft-copilot-studio`).

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf enforcement) is documented for Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins. Plugin manifest 2.4 constrains parameter names by regex and requires `required` values to match declared `properties`, but publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling.

skills_supported.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Declarative agents remain the Microsoft 365 Copilot skills analog: instructions + plugins (tools) + knowledge sources, authored in Agent Builder, the Microsoft 365 Agents Toolkit, or Copilot Studio.

skills_loading_model.notes: Agent instructions are always injected. Plugins: all injected when there are 5 or fewer; above 5, semantic matching selects per turn. MCP plugins may additionally resolve their tool list at runtime (dynamic tool discovery), which is partial progressive disclosure. Recorded as always_on because the default small-agent case injects everything.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Declarative agent instructions (up to 8,000 characters) are injected as system-prompt context every turn. Plugin/tool definitions are injected into the 4,096-token plugin budget that also has to hold tool arguments and tool results — Microsoft's own guidance is to plan for ~66% of it (~2,730 tokens). All functions of a matched plugin are injected even when only one function matched, and Microsoft documents quality degradation above 10 functions/tools per plugin. Dynamic tool discovery (2026-07-16) resolves MCP tool lists at runtime rather than pinning them at publish time, but Microsoft publishes no token saving for it.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Agent instructions plus Microsoft 365 Copilot's own grounding scaffolding are injected per turn. Microsoft publishes no token count for the base system prompt overhead; the only published number in this area remains the 4,096-token plugin scope.

prompt_caching.notes: Changed false→null: Microsoft neither documents nor denies prompt caching at the Microsoft 365 Copilot product layer, and the product is seat-licensed so no cache discount is surfaced to customers. Recording the absence of documentation rather than asserting the feature is off. (Contrast: GitHub Copilot now publishes explicit cached-input rates.)

memory_feature.notes: Microsoft Graph grounding (mail, calendar, files, meetings) plus Work IQ supply per-turn enterprise context that consumes the window. Re-sourced to the Microsoft 365 Copilot release notes, which track the connector/grounding surface continuously; Microsoft publishes no token accounting for it.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token input price exists for Microsoft 365 Copilot: it is sold as a per-user-per-month add-on licence. Token-metered billing in the Microsoft Copilot family appears only in Copilot Studio and Copilot Cowork (Copilot Credits) and in GitHub Copilot (AI Credits) — see those entries.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token output price is published or charged for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input rate is published for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-processing discount concept is published for the seat-licensed Microsoft 365 Copilot product.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: No per-unit token charge is surfaced for images, documents or meeting audio — they are covered by the seat licence. Consumption-metered work (Copilot Cowork tasks, Copilot Studio agents) is billed in Copilot Credits instead, at $0.01 per credit on pay-as-you-go.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: No per-token billing exists on the seat-licensed surface, so reasoning tokens are not separately priced or reported to customers.

CHANGED CONTEXT 2026: Microsoft 365 Copilot is no longer a single-vendor-model product — Anthropic Claude became selectable in Copilot Chat on 2026-06-16, Claude Opus 5 shipped 2026-07-24, and Anthropic model choice reached Word on 2026-08-11 (Microsoft 365 Copilot release notes). Treat this entry as a product layer over a user/tenant-selectable OpenAI GPT-5.x or Anthropic Claude model.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: Microsoft still publishes no knowledge cutoff for the Microsoft 365 Copilot product layer. It would now be ambiguous in any case, since the underlying model is user/tenant-selectable between OpenAI GPT-5.x and Anthropic Claude. Graph and web grounding make the effective recency of answers a retrieval property rather than a training-cutoff property.

detail.notes: PRODUCT-LAYER ENTRY, refreshed 2026-08-19. Microsoft 365 Copilot is a product layer over a user/tenant-SELECTABLE frontier model — no longer OpenAI-only: Anthropic Claude arrived in Copilot Chat 2026-06-16, Claude Opus 5 on 2026-07-24, and Anthropic models in Word on 2026-08-11. All the numbers here are product-level, not raw model-API limits. Binding MCP limits: 1-10 actions (plugins / MCP servers) per declarative agent (schema 1.8, GA); 5-or-fewer plugins are always injected and above that semantic matching selects per turn; no numeric cap on functions/tools per plugin is published but quality is documented to degrade above 10; the plugin scope has a 4,096-token budget covering context AND response (optimize to ~2,730) and a 45-second timeout; plugin responses cap at 25 items and grounding at 50; tool/grounding calls are sequential, not parallel. New in this window: dynamic tool discovery for MCP plugins (runtime `tools/list` instead of a pinned manifest list), MCP agents inside Word/Excel/PowerPoint/Outlook, MCP-based federated Copilot connectors, and manifest 1.8's EmailActions/MeetingActions. The model-facing `description_for_model` field is now recorded as a 2,048-character soft cap. Cost remains per seat; the price of the Business add-on dropped to a promotional $18/user/month.

context_window_tokens.notes: CHANGED 200000 → null. Under this dataset's tiered-evidence rule a context window needs Tier-1 vendor documentation; Microsoft publishes none for consumer Copilot, so the value is null. What is documented: Smart mode uses 'GPT-5's real-time router to choose the best response approach' and Think Deeper uses 'advanced reasoning models by OpenAI', with 'usage limits [that] may apply to certain features and differ for free and Microsoft 365 Premium users'.

native_mcp.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 and broadened. Documented surfaces: VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, Xcode, Eclipse, Cursor and Windsurf; Copilot CLI (local and remote servers); the GitHub Copilot app (repository-configured and user-added servers); and the cloud agent plus code review (repository-level config with the GitHub and Playwright servers pre-configured). The GitHub MCP Registry is called out as 'currently in public preview and subject to change'; the MCP capability itself is production-documented.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Neither GitHub nor the VS Code docs state whether agent mode emits parallel tool calls; it would in any case depend on the selected model. Recorded as undocumented rather than assumed.

max_tools_hard.notes: SOURCE UPGRADED tier 2 → tier 1. The VS Code documentation now states the cap directly: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time', with the error 'Cannot have more than 128 tools per request.' (Field reports show the runtime variant 'Tool limit exceeded (132/128). Click Configure Tools in the chat input to disable 4 tools and retry'.) SCOPE: AGGREGATE — every enabled tool in the request counts, across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools; there is no per-MCP-server cap. LAYER: client/host (VS Code + Copilot Chat), not the model API. Mitigation: the `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` setting groups tools behind virtual stubs so large catalogs stay under 128.

max_tools_practical.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 by opening the GitHub engineering blog (published 2025-11-19): GitHub 'trimmed the default 40 built-in tools down to 13 core ones', improving SWE-Lancer and SWEbench-Verified 'success rates by 2-5 percentage points' and cutting latency by 'an average of 400 milliseconds'. Remaining built-ins are grouped into four virtual categories (Jupyter Notebook Tools, Web Interaction Tools, VS Code Workspace Tools, Testing Tools) via embedding-guided routing and adaptive clustering. EMPIRICAL, not a spec: this is the vendor's recommended working-set size, not an enforced cap — MCP servers can push the total far higher, up to the 128 hard cap, with quality falling off.

max_tool_name_len.notes: Still not published by GitHub or the VS Code docs for the Copilot MCP surface. The selected model's own naming constraints apply downstream (e.g. OpenAI-family 64-character function names), and VS Code namespaces MCP tool names, which consumes part of any such budget — but no Copilot-layer number is documented.

max_tool_description_len.notes: Not published for the Copilot MCP surface. MCP tool descriptions are passed through to the selected model, so that model's limits apply; GitHub documents no Copilot-layer cap. The binding pressure is token consumption in the context window, which GitHub addresses qualitatively: 'Disabling unused toolsets also frees up tokens in the AI's context window.'

max_request_size.notes: No request payload size cap is published for the Copilot surface. The binding constraints are the selected model's context window (up to 1M tokens in VS Code and Copilot CLI on supported models) and the 128-tool aggregate cap. Note the billing consequence: input tokens — including every injected tool definition — are metered per model, and crossing the long-context threshold (e.g. > 272K input tokens on GPT-5.5) moves the request into a higher-priced tier.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No separate tool-result size cap is published for GitHub Copilot. Results return as input tokens against the selected model's window and are billed as such.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No parallel tool-call count is published for the Copilot surface; it would be a property of the selected model in any case.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published for GitHub Copilot. The model context window and the AI-credit budget bound long agent runs indirectly.

max_connected_servers.notes: A limit on the NUMBER of connected MCP servers is not documented in the VS Code or GitHub docs. The binding constraint is aggregate: total enabled tools across every server plus built-ins must stay at or below 128 per request, with `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` grouping surplus tools behind virtual stubs. Practically, a handful of chatty servers reaches 128 quickly — six 30-tool servers already exceed it.

max_total_tools.unit: tools per request (aggregate across all connected MCP servers and built-in tools)
max_total_tools.notes: SOURCE UPGRADED tier 2 → tier 1 (VS Code documentation). Identical number and scope to max_tools_hard: 128 is the AGGREGATE ceiling on tools enabled in one chat request across all connected MCP servers, built-in tools and extension-contributed tools. Tool sets (`#name` groupings) help curate the working set; virtual tools keep large catalogs addressable without exceeding the cap.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Copilot speaks MCP directly; tool definitions are MCP tool schema objects, which the host re-serializes into the selected model's native tool format before the request.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 and now vendor-stated rather than inferred: 'Fewer tools means better tool selection accuracy and fewer errors. Disabling unused toolsets also frees up tokens in the AI's context window.' Under AI Credits billing those input tokens are directly chargeable.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Source upgraded to the Tier-1 VS Code docs, which document `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` as the setting that automatically manages large tool collections to avoid hitting the 128-tool ceiling. Mechanism detail from GitHub's engineering blog: embedding-guided tool routing and adaptive clustering group functionally related tools into virtual categories the model expands on demand. Tool sets are a complementary manual grouping referenced with `#`.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: CLIENT-LAYER LIMITS (GitHub Copilot / VS Code), re-verified 2026-08-19 against Tier-1 VS Code docs. (1) Hard aggregate tool cap: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time' — across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools. Errors: 'Cannot have more than 128 tools per request.' / 'Tool limit exceeded (132/128).' (2) Default built-in toolset trimmed from 40 to 13 core tools (2025-11-19), the rest grouped into four virtual categories. (3) `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` groups surplus tools behind virtual stubs so a large catalog stays under 128. (4) Tool sets let a user reference a curated group with `#name`. (5) Tool definitions consume input tokens against the selected model's window and are billed as input under AI Credits. (6) No Copilot-layer tool-name or tool-description length cap is published; the selected model's constraints apply downstream. (7) Extended capability: a 1M-token context window on supported models, available in VS Code and Copilot CLI only, which raises the practical tool budget but increases AI-credit consumption.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Refreshed 2026-08-19. Multi-vendor picker (~34 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft MAI, xAI, Moonshot, Alibaba). Tool limits sit at the VS Code/Copilot client layer (128 aggregate); the selected model's own API limits also apply and the more restrictive binds. New since 2026-06-21: (a) 1M-token context windows and configurable reasoning levels shipped 2026-06-04 for VS Code, Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, with GitHub warning that 'Choosing a larger context window or higher reasoning level will consume more AI credits per interaction'; (b) MAI-Code-1.1-Flash (Microsoft's own coding model) reached GA in Copilot on 2026-08-11 at $0.20/$1.20 per 1M input/output tokens — see the `mai-code-1-1-flash` entry; (c) the billing table now exposes cached-input and cache-write columns per model, and long-context pricing tiers keyed to input-token thresholds (e.g. GPT-5.5 '≤ 272K' vs '> 272K'). MCP servers: local (stdio) and remote (HTTP) both supported; the GitHub MCP Server is hosted by GitHub; the GitHub MCP Registry is in public preview. Minimum IDE versions vary per model (VS Code v1.104.1-v1.131 depending on the model).

strict_function_schema.notes: GitHub Copilot publishes no OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode of its own; whatever the selected model enforces applies downstream (e.g. OpenAI strict mode's 100-property / 5-level ceiling when an OpenAI model is chosen).

skills_supported.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. MCP servers are the skills/extensibility mechanism across IDEs, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app and cloud agents; the GitHub MCP Server plus registry servers supply the tool catalog.

skills_loading_model.notes: Enabled tools from all connected servers are presented per request (subject to the 128 cap), so the default is always-on. Virtual tools (`github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold`) convert large catalogs into deferred stubs — partial progressive disclosure — and tool sets let a user curate the working set manually.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: MCP tool definitions are injected as input tokens on every agent-mode turn and are billed as input under AI Credits, so tool-definition bloat has a direct, per-interaction dollar cost as well as a context cost. GitHub states plainly that 'Disabling unused toolsets also frees up tokens in the AI's context window.' The 40→13 default-toolset trim improved benchmark success rates by 2-5 points and cut ~400 ms of latency, which is the clearest vendor evidence that fewer tool definitions is better on both axes. Virtual tools reduce the injected surface by clustering; a 1M-token window (VS Code / Copilot CLI, supported models) raises the ceiling but pushes the request toward higher-priced long-context tiers.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Copilot injects IDE context (open files, selection, recent edits), repository context and the enabled tool definitions each turn. GitHub publishes no token breakdown for this overhead; the ~40% reserved-output-headroom figure circulating in community reports is unverified.

prompt_caching.notes: CHANGED null → true. GitHub's models-and-pricing table now exposes prompt caching directly in the billing columns: 'Model | Release status | Category | Tier | Threshold (input tokens) | Input | Cached input | Cache write | Output', and states that users pay for 'input tokens (what's sent to the model), output tokens (what the model generates), and cached tokens (context the model reuses or stores).' Examples: GPT-5.5 $5.00 input vs $0.50 cached input; MAI-Code-1.1-Flash $0.20 input vs $0.02 cached input. 'GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, and GPT-5.6 Luna include a cache write cost in addition to cached input. Earlier OpenAI models have no cache write cost.' GitHub does not document which prefix segments (tool definitions, system prompt, repo context) are cached or how to control it.

memory_feature.notes: No persistent cross-session memory feature is documented for the Copilot IDE/CLI surface; context is per session, with repository-level configuration supplying the durable part.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Deliberately null because GitHub Copilot is a multi-model surface with a per-model rate table rather than one price. Verified examples per 1M input tokens (2026-08-19): MAI-Code-1.1-Flash $0.20; GPT-5 mini $0.25; Gemini 3.6/3.7 Flash $0.75 (promotional); Claude Haiku 4.5 $1.00; Gemini 3.5 Flash $1.50; GPT-5.4 $2.50; Claude Opus 4.5 $5.00; GPT-5.5 $5.00 (standard tier, '≤ 272K' input tokens; a higher long-context tier applies above that).

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Model-dependent, same reasoning as input. Verified examples per 1M output tokens (2026-08-19): MAI-Code-1.1-Flash $1.20; GPT-5 mini $2.00; Gemini 3.6/3.7 Flash $3.75 (promotional); Claude Haiku 4.5 $5.00; Gemini 3.5 Flash $9.00; GPT-5.4 $15.00; Claude Opus 4.5 $25.00; GPT-5.5 $30.00.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Model-dependent; the pricing table now has explicit 'Cached input' and 'Cache write' columns. Verified examples per 1M cached-input tokens (2026-08-19): GPT-5.5 $0.50 (vs $5.00 uncached, a 90% discount); MAI-Code-1.1-Flash $0.02 (vs $0.20). Cache write is charged only on GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna; earlier OpenAI models have no cache-write cost.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-processing discount is published for GitHub Copilot; the cost levers exposed are cached input, model choice, context-window size and reasoning level.

billing_unit.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: '1 AI credit = $0.01 USD', with token consumption (input, cached input, cache write, output) converted to credits at per-model rates. Plans verified on the plans page: Copilot Free ($0), Copilot Student (free, verified), Copilot Pro $10/month, Copilot Pro+ $39/month, Copilot Max $100/month, Copilot Business $19 per granted seat/month, Copilot Enterprise $39 per granted seat/month; 'each plan comes with an allowance of GitHub AI Credits' — the per-plan credit allowances are not stated on the plans page itself, so the specific 1,900/3,900-credit figures previously recorded here are no longer asserted. Larger context windows and higher reasoning levels consume more credits per interaction.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Image input is supported in Copilot Chat and metered as tokens at the selected model's rate; GitHub publishes no separate image-token rate for the Copilot surface.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: GitHub's rate table has no reasoning-token column, so it does not state whether thinking tokens bill at the output rate. What is documented is directional: raising the reasoning level increases AI-credit consumption per interaction.

release_date.notes: GitHub Copilot GA June 2022; multi-model picker added 2023-2024; MCP support GA across IDEs, Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app and cloud agents. Usage-based AI Credits billing went live 2026-06-01. New since the last refresh: 1M-token context windows and configurable reasoning levels shipped 2026-06-04.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not a single-model surface, so no single cutoff applies. The picker spans ~34 models across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft MAI, xAI, Moonshot and Alibaba, each with its own cutoff; GitHub publishes cutoffs for none of them on the Copilot reference pages. (The one Microsoft first-party datapoint: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash has a December 2025 pretraining cutoff per its model card — see the `mai-code-1-1-flash` entry.)

detail.notes: MULTI-MODEL PRODUCT ENTRY, refreshed 2026-08-19. GitHub Copilot is the most MCP-relevant Microsoft Copilot surface: MCP is documented across IDEs (VS Code, JetBrains, Xcode, Eclipse, Cursor, Windsurf), Copilot CLI, the GitHub Copilot app, and cloud agents/code review. KEY LIMIT, now Tier-1 sourced: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time' (VS Code docs) — an AGGREGATE, client-layer cap across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools, mitigated by `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` (virtual-tool clustering) and tool sets. GitHub's own guidance puts the practical working set far lower: the default built-in toolset was cut from 40 to 13 tools, worth 2-5 benchmark points and ~400 ms. New since 2026-06-21: 1M-token context windows and configurable reasoning levels (2026-06-04, VS Code + Copilot CLI + Copilot app), MAI-Code-1.1-Flash GA (2026-08-11), and an AI-Credits rate table that now exposes cached-input and cache-write pricing plus long-context tiers keyed to input-token thresholds — so prompt caching is confirmed present on this surface (changed from null to true). Tool definitions are input tokens and are therefore directly billable: trimming an MCP catalog cuts both context and cost.

models.tokenizer_family: model-dependent (OpenAI GPT-5.5 / GPT-5.6 variants, or Anthropic Claude Opus / Sonnet / Fable 5)

context_window_tokens.notes: Microsoft publishes no context-window token number for Copilot Cowork, and the underlying model is user-selectable, so a single value would be wrong. The documented input-side ceiling is expressed in characters instead: 'Maximum prompt/message length: 250,000 characters' (roughly 60k-65k tokens at ~4 chars/token, but Microsoft does not publish that conversion).

input_output_shared.notes: Not documented for the Cowork surface.

max_input_tokens.notes: Not published in tokens. The documented equivalents are a 250,000-character maximum prompt/message and attached files of less than 200 MB.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not published; inherited from the selected model.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not published; inherited from the selected model.

extended_context.notes: No numeric extended-context mode is published for Copilot Cowork.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Not broken out. Cowork exposes an 'effort level' control that defaults to Medium and 'balances quality, speed, and cost', and billing is in Copilot Credits determined by 'model use, context retrieval, tool calls, and runtime' — so reasoning effort is priced, but not as a named token class.

tokenizer_family.value: model-dependent (OpenAI GPT-5.5 / GPT-5.6 variants, or Anthropic Claude Opus / Sonnet / Fable 5)
tokenizer_family.notes: The Cowork FAQ lists the selectable models as GPT 5.5 and GPT 5.6 variants, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet and Claude Fable 5 (Preview). Microsoft publishes no tokenizer identity for either family on this surface. At GA the blog stated Cowork ran on 'Anthropic models, including Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 4.6', with a first-party 'Cowork 1' model announced as forthcoming.

tokenizer_public.notes: Depends on the selected model; Microsoft documents none for this surface.

tokenizer_access.notes: No Cowork-native count-tokens API exists. tiktoken is usable as a rough proxy only if one assumes an OpenAI-family model for the turn.

count_tokens_method.notes: No native token-count method. The one published budgeting number developers can design against is the SKILL.md body target of under 5,000 tokens.

image_token_rule.notes: Image preview and input are supported (PDF, Office documents, CSV, Markdown, code, images, HTML, email); no image-to-token rule is published.

audio_token_rule.notes: No audio token accounting is published for Copilot Cowork.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Generic ~4 chars/token rule of thumb; useful because Cowork's own input cap is expressed in characters (250,000).

function_calling.notes: Cowork connectors are invoked through MCP `tools/call`; the plugin development guide documents JSON-RPC 2.0 messaging with `tools/list` for discovery and `tools/call` for invocation.

native_mcp.notes: Copilot Cowork supports MCP natively through `remoteMcpServer` connectors declared in the M365 app package manifest. Requirements: streamable HTTP over HTTPS with TLS 1.2+, `tools/list` support for dynamic discovery, `tools/call` for invocation, a tool-call response in under 30 seconds, and a recommended 99.9% uptime SLA for store-published apps. Core MCP operations documented as supported: initialize, tools/list, tools/call, notifications/initialized. Auth: none (anonymous), OAuthPluginVault, ApiKeyPluginVault.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Not documented. Cowork is positioned around 'complex, long-running, multi-tool tasks', but Microsoft does not state whether tool calls are issued in parallel.

max_tools_hard.notes: No numeric per-request cap on the NUMBER of tools is published for Copilot Cowork. The limits that DO bind are packaging- and account-scoped: 10 MCP connectors per app package, 20 skills per app package, and up to 50 custom skills and plugins per user drawn from the Microsoft 365 App Store. Beyond those, the selected model's context window and the 250,000-character prompt ceiling bound how much tool surface fits.

max_tools_practical.notes: No empirical tool-count cliff has been published or measured for Copilot Cowork specifically. Microsoft's only qualitative guidance in this family is the Microsoft 365 Copilot plugins note that quality can degrade above 10 functions/tools per plugin, and the GitHub Copilot 40→13 built-in trim; neither has been validated on Cowork.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No tool-name length cap is published. The adjacent documented naming rule is for skills: skill names are 1-64 characters in kebab-case, and folder paths run up to 256 characters.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No tool-description length cap is published for Cowork connectors. The comparable published budget is the SKILL.md body target of under 5,000 tokens (1,500-2,000 words ideal).

max_request_size.notes: No byte-size request cap is published. The documented input ceilings are a 250,000-character maximum prompt/message and attached files under 200 MB; on the tool path, a single tool call may carry up to 8 workspace files at 150 MiB each with a 150 MiB total per call.

max_tool_result_size.unit: MiB per tool call (file payloads, max 8 workspace files)
max_tool_result_size.notes: Per the Cowork plugin development guide: a tool call may involve up to 8 workspace files, with a per-file limit of 150 MiB and a total of 150 MiB per call. Scope: per tool call. This is a byte cap on file payloads, not a token cap — the token cost of whatever is injected still lands in the selected model's context window.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Not documented for Copilot Cowork.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published. The documented per-call constraint is a response time of under 30 seconds; long-running work is the product's stated purpose, so runtime is metered in Copilot Credits rather than capped by a published cycle count.

max_connected_servers.unit: MCP connectors per M365 app package
max_connected_servers.notes: The Cowork plugin development guide caps connectors at 10 per app package (alongside 20 skills per package). Scope: per M365 app package. AGGREGATE across packages, the account-level ceiling is the documented 'up to 50 custom skills and plugins' a user can add from the Microsoft 365 App Store.

max_total_tools.notes: No aggregate cap on individual tools is published. The aggregate ceilings Microsoft does publish are on containers, not tools: 10 connectors and 20 skills per app package, and up to 50 custom skills and plugins per user. A single connector may expose many tools, so the real ceiling is the selected model's context window.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Connectors are remote MCP servers (`remoteMcpServer` in the app package manifest, manifest schema v1.28, strict with `additionalProperties: false`); tool definitions are MCP tool schema objects fetched via `tools/list`.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Confidence medium — inferred rather than stated outright. Microsoft does not say 'tool definitions are input tokens' for Cowork, but it budgets the adjacent skill text in tokens (SKILL.md body target under 5,000 tokens, 1,500-2,000 words ideal), which only makes sense if that text is injected into the model context. The same must hold for connector tool schemas resolved via `tools/list`.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Not documented. Cowork requires `tools/list` support for 'dynamic discovery', but Microsoft does not say whether the resolved tools are injected eagerly for every turn or deferred/selected per task, so no deferral claim is made here.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: PRODUCT-LAYER LIMITS (Copilot Cowork app packages), as of 2026-08-19. (1) Connectors (remote MCP servers) per package: 10. (2) Skills per package: 20. (3) Custom skills and plugins per user, from the Microsoft 365 App Store: up to 50. (4) SKILL.md body target: under 5,000 tokens (1,500-2,000 words ideal). (5) Companion files per skill: 20, at 5 MB each, 10 MB total per skill; companion download timeout 15 seconds. (6) Files per tool call: up to 8 workspace files; 150 MiB per file and 150 MiB total per call. (7) Tool-call response time: under 30 seconds. (8) Skill name: 1-64 characters, kebab-case; folder path up to 256 characters. (9) Prompt/message: 250,000 characters; attached file: under 200 MB. (10) Transport: streamable HTTP over HTTPS, TLS 1.2+; JSON-RPC 2.0; initialize / tools/list / tools/call / notifications/initialized. (11) Auth: none (anonymous), OAuthPluginVault, ApiKeyPluginVault. (12) Manifest v1.28 is strict (`additionalProperties: false`). (13) Store-published apps: 99.9% uptime SLA recommended.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Copilot Cowork requires a Microsoft 365 Copilot User Subscription Licence and bills consumption in Copilot Credits on top of it. Built-in skills at GA: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, Email, Scheduling, Calendar Management, Meetings, Daily Briefing, Enterprise Search, Communications, Deep Research, Adaptive Cards. Custom skills live in the user's OneDrive at /Documents/Cowork/skills/. Generally available for work and school accounts; preview for personal accounts. Available in browser, desktop (Windows/Mac) and mobile (iOS/Android). Regional availability is limited to Anthropic-supported countries/regions. Microsoft Purview Information Barriers are not supported for plugin/skill management and sharing, and in IB-enabled tenants embedded knowledge file uploads are blocked tenant-wide. Effort level defaults to Medium.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf) is documented for Cowork connectors. The app package manifest itself is strict (`additionalProperties: false`, schema v1.28), but that constrains the manifest, not the MCP tool input schemas.

skills_supported.notes: Copilot Cowork has the most explicit 'skill' primitive Microsoft ships: prompt-based `SKILL.md` workflow packages that 'teach Cowork new domain expertise (financial analysis, legal research, HR workflows...)', distributed in M365 app packages alongside MCP connectors, or stored per user in OneDrive.

skills_loading_model.notes: Microsoft does not state whether skill bodies are always injected or progressively disclosed. The documented SKILL.md body target of under 5,000 tokens, plus separate companion files with their own 15-second download timeout, is consistent with a body-plus-on-demand-companions model, but that is an inference and is recorded as undocumented rather than asserted.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: The only vendor-published token budget on any Microsoft Copilot surface: a SKILL.md body should stay under 5,000 tokens (1,500-2,000 words ideal). With up to 20 skills per package and up to 50 custom skills and plugins per user, a fully loaded account could nominally carry 250k tokens of skill text if everything were injected at once — which is why the loading model matters and why Microsoft's silence on it is the most important gap in this entry. Companion files (20 per skill, 5 MB each, 10 MB per skill, 15-second download timeout) are fetched separately and are the natural place for detail that should not sit in the always-on budget.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Not published. Cowork injects built-in skill scaffolding (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, Email, Scheduling, Calendar, Meetings, Daily Briefing, Enterprise Search, Communications, Deep Research, Adaptive Cards) plus workspace and Microsoft Graph context; Microsoft gives no token count for any of it.

prompt_caching.notes: Not documented. Billing is in Copilot Credits determined by 'model use, context retrieval, tool calls, and runtime', with no cache line item exposed, so any caching that happens is invisible to the customer.

memory_feature.notes: Not documented as a named feature. Cowork works over the user's Microsoft 365 content and a per-user OneDrive skills folder, which provides durable context, but Microsoft publishes no cross-session memory primitive or its token accounting.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Cowork is not priced per token. It bills in Copilot Credits, at $0.01 per credit on pay-as-you-go (or via P3 commitment discounts), with cost determined by 'model use, context retrieval, tool calls, and runtime'. Microsoft publishes no token-to-credit conversion, so a $/1M-token figure cannot be derived.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token output rate is published; consumption is metered in Copilot Credits.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input rate is published for Copilot Cowork.

batch_discount.notes: No batch discount is published; the documented discount lever is a P3 commitment on Copilot Credits versus the $0.01/credit pay-as-you-go rate.

billing_unit.notes: Requires a Microsoft 365 Copilot User Subscription Licence, then usage-based billing in Copilot Credits: '$0.01 per credit' pay-as-you-go, or P3 commitment discounts. Cost is driven by model use, context retrieval, tool calls and runtime. Administrators can set consumption limits per user or group; billing is charged per organization. Microsoft's GA post claims 30-40% cost savings versus Claude Cowork with a Microsoft 365 connector.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Document, image and PDF handling are part of task execution and are absorbed into the Copilot Credit cost of the task rather than priced per unit. File previews are supported for PDF, Microsoft 365 documents, CSV, Markdown, code files, images, HTML and email.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Not exposed as a token class. The user-facing analogue is the 'effort level' control (default Medium) which 'balances quality, speed, and cost' — so more reasoning costs more credits, but Microsoft publishes no token-level accounting.

release_date.notes: NEW ENTRY. Copilot Cowork reached worldwide general availability on 2026-06-16 per the Microsoft 365 Blog — five days before this dataset's previous as_of date, which is why it was missing. It 'executes complex, long-running, multi-tool tasks' and returns finished work rather than drafts.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not published for the Cowork surface; it would belong to whichever underlying model the user selects (GPT-5.5/5.6 variants, Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet, or Claude Fable 5 in preview).

detail.notes: NEW ENTRY (added 2026-08-19). Copilot Cowork is the Microsoft Copilot surface that most resembles an agentic coding/work harness, and it is MCP-native: connectors are remote MCP servers declared in an M365 app package (`remoteMcpServer`, manifest v1.28), speaking JSON-RPC 2.0 over streamable HTTP with `tools/list` + `tools/call`. It GA'd worldwide on 2026-06-16 — five days before the previous refresh's as_of date, which is why it was absent. Its limits are packaged rather than per-request: 10 connectors and 20 skills per app package, up to 50 custom skills and plugins per user, up to 8 workspace files and 150 MiB per tool call, tool calls under 30 seconds, prompt up to 250,000 characters, attachments under 200 MB. Microsoft publishes NO numeric cap on tools per request and NO context-window token figure, so the binding constraint is the selected model's window (GPT-5.5/5.6 or Claude Opus/Sonnet/Fable 5). Most valuable finding for this dataset: the SKILL.md body target of under 5,000 tokens is the only vendor-published context budget for a skill anywhere in the Microsoft Copilot family. Billing is usage-based in Copilot Credits at $0.01/credit on top of a Microsoft 365 Copilot seat.

models.tool_definition_shape: raw_mcp (surfaced through a Power Platform custom connector)

context_window_tokens.notes: Microsoft publishes no context-window token number for Copilot Studio agents. The quota page (updated 2026-07-08) expresses limits in characters, items and payload bytes instead: agent instructions 8,000 characters; knowledge sources 500 per agent; connector payload 5 MB (public cloud) or 450 KB (GCC).

input_output_shared.notes: Not documented at the Copilot Studio platform layer.

max_input_tokens.notes: Not published in tokens. Character- and byte-scoped equivalents: instructions 8,000 characters; connector payload 5 MB public cloud / 450 KB GCC; file upload 512 MB with up to 500 files.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not published for Copilot Studio agents.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not published for Copilot Studio agents.

extended_context.notes: No numeric extended-context mode is published for Copilot Studio.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Not exposed. Copilot Credits 'measure complexity of tasks' including information retrieval, prompt responses, and actions and custom skills execution — a task-complexity metric rather than a token class breakdown.

tokenizer_family.notes: Microsoft publishes no tokenizer identity for Copilot Studio agents. Models are Microsoft-hosted and selectable, and the platform bills in Copilot Credits rather than tokens, so no tokenizer is surfaced to makers.

tokenizer_public.notes: Unknown; no tokenizer is documented for this platform.

tokenizer_access.notes: No Copilot Studio tokenizer or count-tokens endpoint is published.

count_tokens_method.notes: No token-count method exists for Copilot Studio. Consumption is reported in Copilot Credits, and the documented design budgets are in characters, items and payload bytes.

image_token_rule.notes: No image-to-token rule is published for Copilot Studio.

audio_token_rule.notes: Voice experiences exist in Copilot Studio, but no audio token accounting is published.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Generic ~4 chars/token rule of thumb, useful because Copilot Studio's own budgets (8,000-character instructions) are expressed in characters.

function_calling.notes: Copilot Studio agents call tools through an orchestrator: 'The agent orchestrator evaluates each user message and decides whether a tool is needed. The tool's name and description are critical. Well-described tools are invoked more accurately.'

native_mcp.notes: MCP is GA in Microsoft Copilot Studio (page updated 2026-08-03; GA announced on the Microsoft Copilot Blog). MCP servers are attached as Power Platform custom connectors: Tools page → Add a tool → Model Context Protocol → select connector and authorize; individual tools can then be toggled on or off ('Allow all' is on by default). Tools are listed and configurable per server; MCP resources are surfaced only when the server owner configures them as outputs of MCP tools; prompts are not documented. Generative orchestration must be enabled to use MCP. Streamable HTTP is the supported transport — SSE transport is deprecated and remains in public preview only.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Not documented. The tools overview describes orchestrator-driven selection but does not state whether calls are issued in parallel.

max_tools_hard.notes: No numeric per-request cap on the NUMBER of tools is published for Copilot Studio. What the docs state qualitatively is that 'Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers count against the total number of tools an agent can host' and that concurrent MCP server instances in one conversation are capped — without publishing the number — with the guidance to 'keep the count of attached servers small and remove servers you no longer use.' The published hard ceilings elsewhere in the platform are the 5 MB connector payload, 500 knowledge sources per agent, 100 skills per agent and 1,000 topics per agent.

max_tools_practical.notes: No empirical tool-count cliff has been published or measured for Copilot Studio. The documentation explicitly 'does not describe degraded performance or specific behavior changes when many tools are present', instead advising that tool names and descriptions drive selection accuracy and that attached-server counts should be kept small.

max_tool_name_len.notes: Not published. Tool names come from the MCP server via the custom connector; Copilot Studio documents no length constraint of its own.

max_tool_description_len.notes: Not published, despite the docs stressing that 'The tool's name and description are critical.' No character cap is stated for either field.

max_request_size.unit: MB (connector payload, public cloud; 450 KB in GCC)
max_request_size.notes: Connector payload limit: 5 MB in the public cloud, 450 KB in GCC (quota page updated 2026-07-08). This is a byte cap on the connector transport that carries MCP traffic, so it bounds both tool arguments and tool results, and it is the single hardest numeric limit on the Copilot Studio MCP path.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No separate tool-result cap is published; results traverse the same connector and are therefore bounded by the 5 MB public-cloud / 450 KB GCC connector payload limit. Files created during a turn are separately capped at 10 MB per file.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Not published. The docs note that concurrent MCP server instances in one conversation are capped but do not give the number.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published. The binding throughput constraints are rate limits: 8,000 requests per minute for messages to an agent per Dataverse environment on a paid plan, and 100 RPM / 2,000 RPH of generative AI messages for Microsoft 365 Copilot licensed users (10 RPM / 200 RPH in trial and developer environments).

max_connected_servers.notes: No numeric cap on attached MCP servers is published. The docs state that concurrent MCP server instances in one conversation are capped without giving the figure, and advise keeping the attached-server count small. Recorded as undocumented rather than unbounded.

max_total_tools.notes: No aggregate tool-count cap is published. The adjacent published per-agent aggregates are 100 skills per agent, 500 knowledge sources per agent (all types) and 1,000 topics per agent (Dataverse environments) — none of which is a tool count, so none can be substituted for one.

tool_definition_shape.value: raw_mcp (surfaced through a Power Platform custom connector)
tool_definition_shape.notes: MCP servers are wrapped in a Power Platform custom connector; the agent then lists and toggles the server's MCP tools individually. Tool definitions originate as MCP tool schemas.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Confidence medium — inferred. Microsoft does not state that tool definitions consume context on this surface, but it emphasises that tool names and descriptions drive selection accuracy, warns that MCP servers 'count against the total number of tools an agent can host', and bills Copilot Credits partly on 'prompt responses', all of which imply the definitions are injected into the prompt.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Not documented. Makers can manually toggle individual MCP tools on or off per agent (a static curation control), but no automatic deferral, clustering or tool-search mechanism is described.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: PLATFORM-LAYER LIMITS (Microsoft Copilot Studio), quota page updated 2026-07-08. (1) Connector payload: 5 MB public cloud, 450 KB GCC — the hard cap on MCP traffic. (2) Instructions: 8,000 characters. (3) Knowledge sources per agent: 500 (all types). (4) Skills per agent: 100 (web app and Teams app). (5) Topics per agent: 1,000 in Dataverse environments (250 in Dataverse for Teams). (6) Trigger phrases per topic: 200. (7) File upload: 512 MB, up to 500 files. (8) Files created during a turn: 10 MB each. (9) Agents per team (Teams app): 50. (10) SharePoint knowledge: 25 sites per agent with generative orchestration, 1,000 files per source, 50 folders, 10 subfolder levels, 512 MB per file (7 MB without a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence). (11) Generative orchestration must be enabled for MCP. (12) Streamable HTTP transport; SSE deprecated. (13) No numeric cap on tools per request or MCP servers per agent is published.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Rate limits (Dataverse environment scope): 8,000 RPM for messages to an agent on a paid plan. Generative AI messages: 50 RPM / 1,000 RPH for 1-10 prepaid packs; 80 RPM / 1,600 RPH for 11-50 packs; 100 RPM / 2,000 RPH for 51-150 packs, plus 1 RPM / 20 RPH per additional 10 packs above 150; 10 RPM / 200 RPH in trial and developer environments; 100 RPM / 2,000 RPH for pay-as-you-go environments and for Microsoft 365 Copilot licensed users. Power Platform requests per 24 hours: 250,000 standard, 6,000 for the Teams (Microsoft 365) tier. Access to MCP servers is governed by Power Platform connector policies and data loss prevention rules. A Microsoft MCP server certification programme is in preview.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf) is documented for Copilot Studio MCP tools. Schema validity is governed by the Power Platform custom connector definition and the MCP server itself.

skills_supported.notes: Copilot Studio agents are the skills analog: instructions plus tools (MCP servers, connectors, Power Automate flows, prompts) plus knowledge sources, orchestrated by generative orchestration. Note the platform also has a distinct legacy 'skills' primitive (Bot Framework skills) capped at 100 per agent, which is not the same thing as a tool.

skills_loading_model.notes: Not documented. Makers toggle individual tools on or off per agent, and the orchestrator decides per message whether a tool is needed, but Microsoft does not state whether all enabled tool definitions are injected each turn or selected first.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Agent instructions (up to 8,000 characters) plus every enabled tool's name and description are what the orchestrator reasons over, and Microsoft stresses that 'Well-described tools are invoked more accurately' — so description quality is traded directly against context cost. Knowledge sources (up to 500 per agent) are retrieved rather than always injected. Because billing is in Copilot Credits by task complexity rather than tokens, makers get no per-turn token feedback to optimize against, which makes this the least measurable Microsoft Copilot surface for footprint work.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Not published. Generative orchestration injects its own scaffolding plus the agent's instructions and enabled tool descriptions; Microsoft gives no token count.
