prompt_caching.notes: Not documented. Copilot Credits are metered by task complexity, with no cache line item exposed to makers.

memory_feature.notes: Not documented as a named token-consuming memory primitive at the platform layer; conversation state and knowledge-source retrieval provide the durable context instead.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Copilot Studio is not priced per token. Since 2025-09-01 'the common currency for agents changed from messages to Copilot Credits', consumed via prepaid packs, a prepaid subscription of Copilot Credit Commit Units (CCCUs), or pay-as-you-go billed to an Azure subscription. Microsoft publishes credit billing rates per task type, not per token, so no $/1M-token figure can be derived.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: No per-token output rate is published; consumption is metered in Copilot Credits.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input rate is published for Copilot Studio.

batch_discount.notes: No batch discount is published. The documented discount levers are prepaid packs and one-year prepaid CCCU commitments versus pay-as-you-go.

billing_unit.notes: Copilot Credits, effective 2025-09-01 (previously 'messages'; no change in quantity per prepaid pack or in the pay-as-you-go rate). Three purchase paths: Copilot Studio prepaid subscription (CCCU pool via the Azure portal), pay-as-you-go (month-end billing, requires an Azure billing policy on the environment), and a tenant-level Copilot Credits prepaid pack. Credits measure task complexity — information retrieval, prompt responses, and actions and custom skills execution. Microsoft 365 Copilot licensed users get zero-rated usage for classic answers, generative answers and Microsoft Graph tenant grounding in Copilot Chat, Teams and SharePoint.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: File uploads (512 MB, up to 500 files) and knowledge ingestion are covered by the credit model rather than per-unit media pricing; the connector payload cap of 5 MB (450 KB GCC) is the practical constraint on what a tool call can move.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Not exposed as a token class; credits reflect task complexity rather than a token breakdown.

release_date.notes: NEW ENTRY. The date recorded is the Model Context Protocol GA announcement in Microsoft Copilot Studio (the capability this dataset tracks), per the Microsoft Copilot Blog. The Copilot Studio product itself is older (Power Virtual Agents lineage) and Microsoft publishes no single product launch date, hence medium confidence on the date's meaning rather than its accuracy.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not published; Copilot Studio agents run on selectable Microsoft-hosted models whose cutoffs Microsoft does not surface at the platform layer.

detail.notes: NEW ENTRY (added 2026-08-19). Copilot Studio is the maker-facing Microsoft Copilot surface where MCP is GA, and it was previously represented in this file only as a footnote inside other entries' other_limits_notes — a gap worth closing because its limit profile is genuinely different from Microsoft 365 Copilot's. MCP servers attach as Power Platform custom connectors; generative orchestration must be enabled; streamable HTTP is the supported transport and SSE is deprecated. Resources appear only when the server owner exposes them as tool outputs, and prompts are not documented. CRITICALLY, Microsoft publishes NO numeric cap on tools per request or MCP servers per agent here — the docs say only that MCP servers 'count against the total number of tools an agent can host', that concurrent MCP server instances per conversation are capped without giving the number, and that makers should 'keep the count of attached servers small'. The hardest published number on the MCP path is the 5 MB connector payload (450 KB in GCC). Other binding aggregates are per agent, not per request: 100 skills, 500 knowledge sources, 1,000 topics, 8,000-character instructions. Billing moved from messages to Copilot Credits on 2025-09-01, metered by task complexity, so makers get no token-level feedback.

models.tool_definition_shape: raw_mcp (as presented by the GitHub Copilot host)

context_window_tokens.notes: Model card: 'Context length 256K tokens'. This is a genuine Tier-1 vendor figure — notably the only published context-window number anywhere in the Microsoft Copilot family, since every Copilot product surface declines to publish one. Note it sits below the 1M-token extended context GitHub Copilot offers on some third-party models, so MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is not on the 1M list in GitHub's supported-models reference.

input_output_shared.notes: The model card gives a single 256K context length without splitting input and output pools, and does not state whether they share the window.

max_input_tokens.notes: Not stated separately on the model card; bounded by the 256K context length.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not specified on the model card.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not specified on the model card.

extended_context.notes: No extended-context mode is published for this model. GitHub's supported-models reference lists the 1M-token context window as an extended capability of specific Claude, GPT-5.x and Kimi K3 models; MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is not among them.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Not documented. GitHub's Copilot rate table meters input, cached input, cache write and output for this model but names no reasoning-token class.

tokenizer_family.notes: The Microsoft AI model card does not name a tokenizer. Under this dataset's tiered-evidence rule, tokenizer identity requires Tier-1 vendor documentation, and none exists — so this is null rather than assumed from the architecture ('transformer architecture with self-attention using sparse Mixture-of-Experts layers').

tokenizer_public.notes: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is a closed-weight, Microsoft-hosted model with no published tokenizer artifact, no Hugging Face model card and no downloadable weights; the model card is a PDF describing behaviour, not a config. Recorded as not public rather than unknown because no distribution channel for a tokenizer exists.

tokenizer_access.notes: No tokenizer or count-tokens endpoint is published for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. Token counts are only observable after the fact, through GitHub Copilot's AI-credit usage reporting.

count_tokens_method.notes: No native or third-party count method exists. GitHub bills this model per token (input $0.20, cached input $0.02, output $1.20 per 1M) but exposes no pre-flight counting API, and no public tokenizer allows a local estimate.

image_token_rule.notes: The model card lists 'Inputs Text, Image' but publishes no image-to-token conversion rule.

audio_token_rule.notes: Audio is not a listed modality: the model card gives 'Inputs Text, Image' and 'Outputs Text'.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Generic ~4 chars/token rule of thumb, applied for want of a published tokenizer. Treat with extra caution here: Microsoft claims MAI-Code-1.1-Flash needs '25% fewer tokens to complete a task' than version 1.0, implying tokenizer or behaviour changes that a generic ratio will not capture.

function_calling.notes: The model card describes the model as built for 'agentic tool use' and 'tool-using developer scenarios', and it ships as an agent-mode model in GitHub Copilot, where tool calling is the operating mode.

native_mcp.notes: MCP support here is a property of the HOST, not the model: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is 'Available in GitHub Copilot for all clients' per the model card, and GitHub Copilot speaks MCP natively across IDEs, Copilot CLI, the Copilot app and cloud agents. Microsoft publishes no standalone MCP-capable API endpoint for this model, so its MCP behaviour is whatever the Copilot host provides. Confidence medium for that indirection.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Not documented on the model card or in GitHub's Copilot documentation.

max_tools_hard.notes: No model-layer cap on the number of tools per request is published for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. The limit that binds in practice is imposed by the host: VS Code enforces 128 enabled tools per chat request (see max_total_tools). Beyond that, the 256K context window is the ceiling — at a typical ~500-800 tokens per MCP tool definition that is a few hundred tool definitions before the window is consumed by tools alone, which is why the host cap bites first.

max_tools_practical.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19: the previous citation (docs.github.com models-and-pricing) was re-opened and contains no tool count at all. The 13 comes from GitHub's engineering blog (2025-11-19, tier 4), re-opened 2026-08-19, which states 'we're rolling out a reduced toolset that trims the default 40 built-in tools down to 13 core ones' and 'we identified a core toolset of 13 essential tools'. NOTE WHAT THAT NUMBER IS: a product decision about the size of the DEFAULT BUILT-IN toolset in VS Code, not a measured degradation threshold, and not measured on MAI-Code-1.1-Flash -- the same post notes 'GitHub Copilot Chat can access hundreds of tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP).' EMPIRICAL and inherited from the host surface; no published benchmark isolates this model's tool-selection degradation curve. Confidence low for both reasons; the hard host-layer cap that actually binds is the 128 tools/request in max_total_tools.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No tool-name length constraint is published for this model.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No tool-description length constraint is published for this model.

max_request_size.notes: No request payload size cap is published. The binding constraint is the 256K-token context length; GitHub's Copilot pricing for this model carries no long-context tier, unlike GPT-5.5's '> 272K' tier.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No tool-result size cap is published; results consume the 256K context window as input tokens and are billed at the input rate.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Not documented for this model.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No per-turn tool-call cycle cap is published for this model; the host's agent loop and the AI-credit budget bound long runs instead.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model-layer property. In the VS Code host a limit on the number of connected MCP servers is not documented; the aggregate 128-tool-per-request cap is what binds.

max_total_tools.unit: tools per request (host-layer cap in VS Code, aggregate across all servers)
max_total_tools.notes: HOST-LAYER limit inherited from the surface this model runs on: 'A chat request can have a maximum of 128 tools enabled at a time' (VS Code documentation). Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in and extension tools. This is not a MAI-Code-1.1-Flash constraint — Microsoft publishes none — but it is the number that actually gates an MCP catalog when this model is selected in Copilot.

tool_definition_shape.value: raw_mcp (as presented by the GitHub Copilot host)
tool_definition_shape.notes: The Copilot host speaks MCP and re-serializes tool definitions into the selected model's native tool format before the request; Microsoft does not publish MAI-Code-1.1-Flash's native tool-definition schema.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tool definitions are injected into the prompt and billed as input tokens on this surface — GitHub prices MAI-Code-1.1-Flash at $0.20 per 1M input tokens and $0.02 per 1M cached-input tokens, and states that disabling unused toolsets 'frees up tokens in the AI's context window'.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Available through the host, not the model: VS Code's `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` setting groups surplus tools behind virtual stubs so a large catalog stays under the 128-tool cap. Nothing model-specific is published.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: MODEL-LAYER: Microsoft publishes no tool-count, tool-name, tool-description, schema-depth or request-size limits for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. The model card documents only the 256K context length, a December 2025 pretraining cutoff, text+image input / text output, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer architecture, and support for agentic tool use. HOST-LAYER (GitHub Copilot / VS Code, which is where this model is reachable): 128 enabled tools per chat request, aggregate across all MCP servers and built-in tools; `github.copilot.chat.virtualTools.threshold` for virtual-tool clustering; tool sets for manual curation. When both layers apply, the host cap binds first.
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Distribution: 'Available in GitHub Copilot for all clients' per the model card, with use inside GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code called out and Copilot CLI support noted as planned for later rollout; GitHub's own reference lists it among supported models but NOT among those offering the 1M-token extended context or configurable reasoning levels. Vendor performance claims versus MAI-Code-1.0: 25% greater token efficiency, tokens stream 25% faster, 25% fewer tokens to complete a task, 22% improvement on Terminal-Bench 2.1, 15% improvement on .NET tasks, code survival up 4%, return visits up 9%, at roughly a quarter of the cost. These are vendor benchmarks, not independent measurements. Closed weights; no Hugging Face card, no self-hosting path.

strict_function_schema.notes: No strict function-schema mode is documented for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash. Recorded as false for absence of any published enforcement, not as a positive statement that arbitrary schemas are accepted.

skills_supported.notes: Via the host rather than the model: when MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is selected in GitHub Copilot, MCP servers supply the tool/skill catalog exactly as they do for any other model in the picker. Microsoft publishes no model-native skills primitive.

skills_loading_model.notes: Inherited from the GitHub Copilot host: enabled tools are presented per request, subject to the 128-tool cap, with virtual tools deferring surplus tools behind stubs.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: MCP tool definitions consume the model's 256K context window as input tokens and are billed at $0.20 per 1M ($0.02 cached). This is the cheapest per-token model in GitHub's Copilot rate table, so an oversized MCP catalog costs less here than on GPT-5.5 ($5.00 input) or Claude Opus 4.5 ($5.00 input) — but it also has the smallest window among the flagship options, since it is excluded from the 1M-token extended-context list. Tool-definition bloat therefore bites on capacity before it bites on cost.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Not published. Overhead is whatever the GitHub Copilot host injects (IDE context, repository context, enabled tool definitions); Microsoft publishes no model-side system-prompt token accounting.

prompt_caching.notes: GitHub's Copilot rate table lists a cached-input price of $0.02 per 1M tokens for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash against $0.20 uncached — a 90% discount — which confirms prompt caching is active for this model on the Copilot surface. No cache-write cost is listed (that applies only to GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra and Luna). Microsoft publishes no cache TTL, minimum cacheable prefix or breakpoint control.

memory_feature.notes: No model-native persistent memory is documented; session context is supplied by the host.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is listed as GA in the Lightweight category at $0.20 per 1M input tokens. Billed as AI Credits at 1 credit = $0.01 USD. Microsoft publishes no independent API price for this model outside the Copilot surface.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: $1.20 per 1M output tokens — a 6x input-to-output ratio, and the cheapest output rate in GitHub's table (compare GPT-5.5 at $30.00 and Claude Opus 4.5 at $25.00).

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: GitHub Copilot models-and-pricing table, verified 2026-08-19: $0.02 per 1M cached-input tokens, a 90% discount on the $0.20 uncached input rate. No cache-write cost applies to this model.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-processing discount is published; the exposed cost levers on the Copilot surface are cached input and model choice.

billing_unit.notes: Billed through GitHub Copilot's AI Credits system (1 AI credit = $0.01 USD) at the per-model token rates above. There is no separate Microsoft-hosted pay-per-token endpoint for MAI-Code-1.1-Flash documented at Tier 1 as of 2026-08-19.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Image input is a listed modality on the model card, but GitHub's rate table publishes only text-token rates for this model and no separate image-token price.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Not documented. This model is not on GitHub's configurable-reasoning-levels list, and the rate table has no reasoning-token column.

release_date.notes: NEW ENTRY. The official Microsoft AI model card gives a release date of August 11, 2026, matched by the Microsoft AI news post 'MAI-Code-1.1-Flash: Better, faster, at a quarter of the cost' (August 11, 2026), which states the model is 'now in production in GitHub Copilot'. It supersedes MAI-Code-1-Flash (released 2026-06-02).

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Model card: 'Pretraining cut-off date: December 2025'. Recorded as year-month because the card gives no day.

detail.notes: NEW ENTRY (added 2026-08-19). MAI-Code-1.1-Flash is Microsoft's own first-party agentic coding model, released 2026-08-11 and in production in GitHub Copilot. It is included here because it is a Microsoft model shipped inside a Microsoft Copilot surface, and because it is the ONLY entity in this vendor's file with a Tier-1 published context window: 'Context length 256K tokens' per the official Microsoft AI model card. Also published: December 2025 pretraining cutoff, text+image input / text output, sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer, agentic tool use. It supersedes MAI-Code-1-Flash (2026-06-02) — that predecessor has no entry in this file and is not added, since only the current-generation model belongs in the roster. MCP and tool limits are HOST-supplied, not model-supplied: reachable only through GitHub Copilot, where VS Code's aggregate 128-tools-per-request cap binds. No tokenizer is published, so token counts on this model cannot be reproduced locally — a real gap given Microsoft's claim of '25% fewer tokens to complete a task'. Pricing is Tier-1 and concrete: $0.20 input / $0.02 cached input / $1.20 output per 1M tokens, the cheapest in GitHub's Copilot rate table.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: the Known Limitations context-window table still lists this model at 256k tokens; the official HF model card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B) repeats '256k context'.

input_output_shared.notes: Known Limitations, re-read 2026-08-19: both input and output tokens are included in the context calculation — 'Plan your max_tokens accordingly.'

max_input_tokens.notes: No separate input ceiling is published. The chat endpoint reference states only that 'The token count of your prompt plus max_tokens cannot exceed the model's context length', so the effective input ceiling is 256k minus the requested max_tokens. Not recorded as a number because it is request-dependent, not a documented constant.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default value for max_tokens is documented on the chat endpoint reference (re-read 2026-08-19); the parameter is described without a stated default or maximum.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: No per-completion output ceiling is published. The only documented bound is 'prompt + max_tokens cannot exceed the model's context length' (256k). This is a genuine documentation gap, not an absence of constraint — the shared 256k window is what binds.

extended_context.notes: No extended/beta context tier beyond 256k appears in the Known Limitations table (re-read 2026-08-19).

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: CHANGED sourcing: this model IS a reasoning model. The Reasoning page lists mistral-medium-3-5 as supporting the per-request reasoning_effort parameter ('high' emits a ThinkChunk before the TextChunk; 'none' omits it); the HF model card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B) repeats 'configurable reasoning effort per request'. Mistral does NOT document how thinking tokens are counted or billed, and there is no thinking-budget parameter — so the value stays null rather than assuming they bill as output.

tokenizer_family.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Mistral's tokenization deep-dive still documents V1/V2/V3 with V3-Tekken as the tiktoken-based variant used by recent models; the official HF card for this model (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B) names Tekken and pins a minimum mistral-common version. Exact Tekken sub-version per model is not published.

tokenizer_public.notes: mistral-common remains open source; tokenizer files are downloadable from the HF Hub.

tokenizer_access.value: pip install mistral-common; MistralTokenizer.from_hf_hub("<hf-model-id>") pulls the Tekken tokenizer from the HF Hub
tokenizer_access.notes: Refreshed 2026-08-19 to the current documented loading path. Extras: pip install "mistral-common[image]" / "mistral-common[audio,hf-hub]".

count_tokens_method.value: from mistral_common.tokens.tokenizers.mistral import MistralTokenizer; tok = MistralTokenizer.from_hf_hub("<hf-model-id>"); n = len(tok.encode_chat_completion(ChatCompletionRequest(messages=[...])).tokens)
count_tokens_method.notes: CHANGED: the previously recorded MistralTokenizer.v3() call is superseded by the documented from_hf_hub + encode_chat_completion flow. Caveat verified 2026-08-19: the mistral-common usage docs show no worked example of putting `tools` into the ChatCompletionRequest, so tool-definition token counts obtained this way are reconstructions, not a vendor-blessed recipe. Mistral exposes no server-side count-tokens endpoint.

image_token_rule.notes: Still undocumented, and now confirmed as a deliberate gap: the Vision capability page carries the FAQ heading 'How many tokens correspond to an image and/or what is the maximum resolution?' with no answer beneath it (checked 2026-08-19). The only published image constraint is a 20 MB per-image cap in Known Limitations (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations).

audio_token_rule.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19: the model card does not list audio as a capability for this model, and the official HF card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B) gives the modalities as text+image in / text out. Audio is handled by the separate Voxtral models and endpoints, so no audio token rule applies here. (The 2026-06-21 entry's 'audio transcription listed as a feature' claim did not hold up on re-read.)

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: CHANGED to null: the previous 4.0 was an unsourced industry rule of thumb. Searched Mistral's tokenization deep-dive, the mistral-common docs and the Tekken tokenizer card (https://huggingface.co/toksuite/mistralai-tekken, vocab 130,000, tier 3) on 2026-08-19 — no chars-per-token or bytes-per-token figure is published for Tekken. The only quantitative claim Mistral makes is relative: Tekken is '~30% more efficient at compressing source code, Chinese, Italian, French, German, Spanish, and Russian' and 2x/3x on Korean/Arabic versus the Llama 3 tokenizer. Use mistral-common for exact counts.

function_calling.notes: Function Calling is listed in the model card's feature list (re-verified 2026-08-19) and the model appears in the function-calling guide's supported-model list (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling).

native_mcp.notes: Platform-level: any function-calling model can be pointed at registered Connectors (MCP servers), whose tools the model 'discovers automatically and calls ... based on the user's request'. Still Public Preview as of 2026-08-19; the API interface can change. Vibe Code additionally speaks MCP directly over stdio, HTTP and streamable HTTP (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers).

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Re-verified on the chat endpoint reference 2026-08-19: parallel_tool_calls — 'Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use, when enabled the model can call multiple tools in parallel.' Default Value: true.

max_tools_hard.notes: Unchanged and re-verified 2026-08-19: Known Limitations still states 'Maximum number of tools per request: 128.' SCOPE = AGGREGATE — it counts every tool in the request's `tools` array together: your own functions, every tool pulled in from each connected Connector (MCP server), and Mistral's built-in tools (web search, code interpreter, image generation, document library), which are passed in the same array (https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat). It is not a per-MCP-server cap; no per-server tool cap is documented anywhere.

max_tools_practical.notes: CHANGED 20 → null (2026-08-19 final audit): no empirical source has measured a Mistral model's tool-count degradation, so no practical tool ceiling can be asserted for Mistral Medium 3.5. The previously cited leaderboard (https://presenc.ai/research/ai-agent-tool-calling-accuracy-benchmarks-2026, tier 4, re-opened 2026-08-19) measures only Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Qwen 3 235B, Llama 4 405B, Qwen 3 32B, Llama 4 70B and DeepSeek V4 — NO Mistral model appears in it, so its "accuracy degrades to 85-91 percent at 5 tools, then to 65-78 percent at 20+ tools" band (exemplified on Claude Opus 4.7: 96% at 1 tool → 91% at 5 → 76% at 20+) is evidence about those models only. The practitioner write-up previously quoted alongside it (https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-19-over-tooled-agent-problem, "safe zone ... at roughly 10-20 tools per reasoning context") likewise names no Mistral model. Mistral itself publishes no tool-count guidance: the function-calling docs (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling/, tier 1, checked 2026-08-19) list Mistral Medium 3.5 among the function-calling models but state no maximum or recommended number of tools and no degradation threshold. Binding limits that DO apply: the documented 128-tool hard cap per request (see max_tools_hard, https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations, tier 1) and the 256,000-token shared input+output context window that every tool definition is billed into. Any cross-vendor 10-20-tool rule of thumb applied to Mistral is an unmeasured extrapolation, not a Mistral measurement.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: {"type": "function", "function": {name, description, parameters}} with a JSON-Schema `parameters` object — identical in shape to OpenAI function calling. tool_choice accepts auto (default) | any/required | none | a named tool.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: Known Limitations states that tool descriptions consume tokens from the available context. Tool definitions are therefore billed as input tokens and eat the same 256k window as the messages — the premise of the footprint measurement.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Still no automatic/lazy tool loading: nothing in the API defers tool schemas or lets the model search a catalog. What exists as of 2026-08-19 is manual, human-side pruning — admins can 'turn individual tools on or off for a whole org or one workspace' inside a Connector, Vibe Code offers a `/connectors` picker to choose which tools to enable, and the Vibe CLI supports enabled_tools/disabled_tools glob or regex filters (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers). Those shrink what is sent, but every surviving tool is still serialized into every request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character ceiling or pattern for function/tool names is published: the API reference documents the `tools` parameter but not a Function object schema with maxLength/pattern (checked 2026-08-19). Two adjacent caps that DO bind: Connector (MCP server registry) names are 'up to 64 characters, alphanumeric with underscores and dashes only' (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management), and the Vibe CLI namespaces MCP tools as {server_name}_{tool_name} (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers), so a long server alias eats into whatever name budget the model-side parser has.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No character or token ceiling for a tool description is published (re-checked 2026-08-19). The binding constraint is budgetary, not syntactic: Known Limitations says descriptions consume tokens from the available context, so long descriptions across 128 tools are charged against the shared 256k window.

max_request_size.notes: No byte/MB payload ceiling is documented for POST /v1/chat/completions (the chat endpoint reference documents no array or payload size limits, checked 2026-08-19). Adjacent caps that are documented and that DO bind on neighbouring paths: 512 MB per uploaded file, 512 MB per batch file with up to 100,000 requests, 20 MB per image, 500 MB / 60 minutes per audio file. For chat itself the binding ceilings are the 256k token window and the 128-tool aggregate cap.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No numeric size ceiling for an individual tool result is documented (checked 2026-08-19). A tool result is an ordinary `tool`-role message, so it is charged against the shared 256k input+output window — that window, not a size rule, is what a chatty MCP tool blows.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: parallel_tool_calls is a boolean (default true) — no numeric ceiling on how many tool calls the model may emit in one turn is published (re-checked on the chat endpoint reference 2026-08-19). The 128-tool aggregate cap limits what is offered, not how many are invoked at once.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No numeric ceiling on tool-call/result cycles per turn or per agentic loop is published; the function calling guide's worked example loops back to the model until it produces a final answer without stating a cycle ceiling (re-checked 2026-08-19). Cost and the 256k window are what bound a long agentic run.

max_connected_servers.notes: No numeric ceiling on the number of Connectors (MCP servers) per workspace, org, agent or conversation is published (Connectors API reference and management docs re-checked 2026-08-19); listing uses keyset pagination with a page_size shown as high as 1000, which implies large counts are expected. Mistral advertises 'more than 60 integrations' plus custom MCP connectors (https://mistral.ai/news/more-control-over-connectors/). The limit that actually binds when you attach many servers is the aggregate 128-tool per-request cap.

max_total_tools.notes: No separate aggregate catalog ceiling exists above the per-request cap: on Mistral the aggregate cap IS max_tools_hard = 128 tools per request, summed across your own functions, every connected Connector's tools and the built-in tools. GET /v1/connectors/{id}/tools paginates (default page_size 100) with no documented maximum tool count per connector (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management).

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19. Connector (MCP server registry) names: 'up to 64 characters, alphanumeric with underscores and dashes only', unique within a workspace (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management / https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/beta/connectors). Tool function name cap: not published — the API reference documents the `tools` parameter but no Function object maxLength/pattern (https://docs.mistral.ai/api). No documented limit on JSON-Schema nesting depth, property count, enum size, or on unsupported keywords such as oneOf/anyOf/$ref — Mistral publishes no schema-shape rules at all, so the only reliable ceiling is the token budget: tool descriptions and schemas are charged as input against the shared 256k window (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Vibe CLI namespaces MCP tools as {server_name}_{tool_name} (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers).
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19 — rate limits are set at the ORGANIZATION level and apply across all workspaces (the 2026-06-21 entry said 'per API key', which the tier docs contradict); three independent limits are enforced: requests per second, tokens per minute and tokens per month, with tier upgrades driven by cumulative billed amount and the actual numbers only visible in Admin > Limits (https://docs.mistral.ai/deployment/ai-studio/tier). Batch processing is 50% cheaper and does not compete with real-time limits; max batch file 512 MB / 100,000 requests, results retained 24h; streaming connections drop after 10 minutes of inactivity (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Prompt caching is now documented and is EXPLICIT, not automatic: pass prompt_cache_key, cache blocks are 64 tokens so cached_tokens is always a multiple of 64 and prompts under 64 tokens never hit, and cached prompt tokens bill at 10% of the standard input price (https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/conversations/advanced/prompt-caching). Connectors remain Public Preview; connector tool schemas are serialized into the request, so a large MCP server consumes a real share of the 256k window and of the 128-tool aggregate cap. Regional endpoints (EU/US) are GA and a Priority Tier with custom rate limits and an uptime SLA is in public preview (https://mistral.ai/news/regional-inference-open-models-new-compute/).

strict_function_schema.notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: Mistral documents no OpenAI-style `strict` flag and no structural schema restrictions (no 100-property / 5-level-depth / no-oneOf rules). The function calling guide exposes only name/description/parameters plus tool_choice and parallel_tool_calls. Structured Outputs is a separate response-format feature, not a tool schema mode.

skills_supported.notes: Upgraded sourcing 2026-08-19: Mistral now has a literal Skills primitive (Studio and Vibe), announced 2026-07-09, in addition to Agents. A Skill packages 'a reusable method, checklist, or procedure that an AI assistant can apply when a task matches', with a trigger description, instructions and optional attached files, and Studio versions it immutably with rollback.

skills_loading_model.notes: CHANGED always_on -> progressive_disclosure. Vibe documents a three-stage load: at session start 'Work loads only each Skill's name and description (~100 tokens each)'; when a task matches the description the full SKILL.md loads into context; referenced supporting files load only as needed. Studio says the same in prose — 'the description field ... determines when the assistant loads the Skill' (https://docs.mistral.ai/getting-started/quickstarts/studio/create-skill). NOTE the asymmetry that matters for footprinting: Skills are progressively disclosed, but MCP/Connector TOOL definitions are not — those are serialized into every request.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Re-measured against the docs 2026-08-19. Skills: ~100 tokens per enabled Skill at discovery (name + description only), then the full SKILL.md on activation, then referenced files on demand (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/skills); Mistral publishes no size ceiling for SKILL.md and only an unquantified 'supporting files are subject to a file-count limit'. Agents: the agent's `instructions` and its tool list are fixed at creation and injected into the conversation, billed as input tokens. Connector (MCP) tool schemas are NOT progressively disclosed — every tool left enabled is serialized into every request and charged as input (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Prompt caching can recover 90% of the cost of that repeated prefix if a stable prompt_cache_key is supplied (https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/conversations/advanced/prompt-caching).
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: No fixed platform-injected system prompt is documented (checked 2026-08-19). Overhead is developer-controlled through the agent's `instructions` field (https://docs.mistral.ai/studio/agents/introduction) plus whichever Skills are enabled (~100 tokens each until activated) and whichever tool definitions are attached, all of which are billed as input against the shared 256k window.

prompt_caching.notes: CHANGED false -> true. Prompt caching is documented as of 2026-08-19 and is explicit: set prompt_cache_key to 'a stable application-level identifier, such as a conversation ID, session ID, or workflow ID'. Cache blocks are 64 tokens, so cached_tokens is always a multiple of 64 and 'prompts with fewer than 64 prompt tokens do not have cache hits'; supplying the key 'doesn't guarantee' a hit. Cached prompt tokens bill at 10% of the standard input price. TTL is not published, nor is whether tool definitions specifically are cacheable — only that a compatible cached PREFIX is matched, which a stable tools array at the head of the request should satisfy.

memory_feature.notes: Agents documentation describes 'persistent state across conversations' and agent-to-agent handoffs (re-checked 2026-08-19). Server-side conversation history is replayed as input tokens on each continuation, so a long session's context — and cost — grows turn over turn. The exact `store` parameter semantics are no longer spelled out on the current Agents introduction page.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-verified against the API pricing table and the model card 2026-08-19; unchanged.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-verified against the API pricing table and the model card 2026-08-19; unchanged.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: CHANGED null -> 0.15. DERIVED: prompt caching now exists and 'cached prompt tokens are billed at 10% of the standard input token price', so this is 10% of the 1.5 USD/1M input rate. Mistral does not print a per-model cached rate on the pricing page (the marketing page phrases it as 'cached input tokens reduce input cost by up to 90%', https://mistral.ai/pricing), hence confidence medium rather than high.

batch_discount.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: 'Batch processing, for high-volume work, reduces the price by 50%'. Batch does not compete with real-time rate limits; max batch file 512 MB / 100,000 requests (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations).

billing_unit.notes: Priced per million input and output tokens, counted separately.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Checked 2026-08-19: no per-image or per-tile token rule and no per-image surcharge is published — the Vision page leaves 'How many tokens correspond to an image' as an unanswered FAQ heading (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/vision); images are simply capped at 20 MB each (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Audio is not a capability of this model; transcription/TTS run on the separate Voxtral models and endpoints and are priced separately (https://mistral.ai/pricing/api).

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Left null deliberately. The model does emit thinking content when reasoning_effort='high' (a ThinkChunk precedes the TextChunk), and Mistral warns it means 'increased token usage', but no page states which meter those tokens land on or exposes a separate reasoning-token price or budget. Assume output-priced for planning, but that is not documented.

release_date.notes: Re-verified on the model card 2026-08-19; unchanged.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Still not published. Checked the Mistral model card (https://docs.mistral.ai/models/model-cards/mistral-medium-3-5-26-04) and the official Hugging Face model card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B) on 2026-08-19 — neither states a training-data cutoff date.

detail.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19; still Mistral's flagship general-purpose model and unchanged since the 2026-06-21 capture (no successor shipped — the only model releases between 2026-06-21 and today were OCR 4.0 on 2026-06-23, Leanstral 1.5 on 2026-06-30 and OCR 4.1 on 2026-07-16, none of them generalist). API string mistral-medium-3-5-26-04 (alias mistral-medium-latest); v26.04, released 2026-04-28, Modified MIT open weights. The official HF card corrects two things in the previous entry: it is a DENSE 128B model (not MoE), it takes text+image in and emits text only (no audio), and it exposes a per-request reasoning_effort of 'none' or 'high'. 256k context, 128-tool aggregate cap, $1.5/$7.5 per 1M in/out — all unchanged.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: the Known Limitations context-window table still lists this model at 256k tokens; the official HF model card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603) repeats '256k context'.

input_output_shared.notes: Known Limitations, re-read 2026-08-19: both input and output tokens are included in the context calculation — 'Plan your max_tokens accordingly.'

max_input_tokens.notes: No separate input ceiling is published. The chat endpoint reference states only that 'The token count of your prompt plus max_tokens cannot exceed the model's context length', so the effective input ceiling is 256k minus the requested max_tokens. Not recorded as a number because it is request-dependent, not a documented constant.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default value for max_tokens is documented on the chat endpoint reference (re-read 2026-08-19); the parameter is described without a stated default or maximum.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: No per-completion output ceiling is published. The only documented bound is 'prompt + max_tokens cannot exceed the model's context length' (256k). This is a genuine documentation gap, not an absence of constraint — the shared 256k window is what binds.

extended_context.notes: No extended/beta context tier beyond 256k appears in the Known Limitations table (re-read 2026-08-19).

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: CHANGED sourcing: this model IS a reasoning model. The Reasoning page lists mistral-small-latest as supporting the per-request reasoning_effort parameter ('high' emits a ThinkChunk before the TextChunk; 'none' omits it); the HF model card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603) repeats 'configurable reasoning effort per request'. Mistral does NOT document how thinking tokens are counted or billed, and there is no thinking-budget parameter — so the value stays null rather than assuming they bill as output.

tokenizer_family.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Mistral's tokenization deep-dive still documents V1/V2/V3 with V3-Tekken as the tiktoken-based variant used by recent models; the official HF card for this model (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603) names Tekken and pins a minimum mistral-common version. Exact Tekken sub-version per model is not published.

tokenizer_public.notes: mistral-common remains open source; tokenizer files are downloadable from the HF Hub.

tokenizer_access.value: pip install mistral-common; MistralTokenizer.from_hf_hub("<hf-model-id>") pulls the Tekken tokenizer from the HF Hub
tokenizer_access.notes: Refreshed 2026-08-19 to the current documented loading path. Extras: pip install "mistral-common[image]" / "mistral-common[audio,hf-hub]".

count_tokens_method.value: from mistral_common.tokens.tokenizers.mistral import MistralTokenizer; tok = MistralTokenizer.from_hf_hub("<hf-model-id>"); n = len(tok.encode_chat_completion(ChatCompletionRequest(messages=[...])).tokens)
count_tokens_method.notes: CHANGED: the previously recorded MistralTokenizer.v3() call is superseded by the documented from_hf_hub + encode_chat_completion flow. Caveat verified 2026-08-19: the mistral-common usage docs show no worked example of putting `tools` into the ChatCompletionRequest, so tool-definition token counts obtained this way are reconstructions, not a vendor-blessed recipe. Mistral exposes no server-side count-tokens endpoint.

image_token_rule.notes: Still undocumented, and now confirmed as a deliberate gap: the Vision capability page carries the FAQ heading 'How many tokens correspond to an image and/or what is the maximum resolution?' with no answer beneath it (checked 2026-08-19). The only published image constraint is a 20 MB per-image cap in Known Limitations (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations).

audio_token_rule.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19: the model card does not list audio as a capability for this model, and the official HF card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Small-4-119B-2603) gives the modalities as text+image in / text out. Audio is handled by the separate Voxtral models and endpoints, so no audio token rule applies here. (The 2026-06-21 entry's 'audio transcription listed as a feature' claim did not hold up on re-read.)

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: CHANGED to null: the previous 4.0 was an unsourced industry rule of thumb. Searched Mistral's tokenization deep-dive, the mistral-common docs and the Tekken tokenizer card (https://huggingface.co/toksuite/mistralai-tekken, vocab 130,000, tier 3) on 2026-08-19 — no chars-per-token or bytes-per-token figure is published for Tekken. The only quantitative claim Mistral makes is relative: Tekken is '~30% more efficient at compressing source code, Chinese, Italian, French, German, Spanish, and Russian' and 2x/3x on Korean/Arabic versus the Llama 3 tokenizer. Use mistral-common for exact counts.

function_calling.notes: Function Calling is listed in the model card's feature list (re-verified 2026-08-19) and the model appears in the function-calling guide's supported-model list (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling).

native_mcp.notes: Platform-level: any function-calling model can be pointed at registered Connectors (MCP servers), whose tools the model 'discovers automatically and calls ... based on the user's request'. Still Public Preview as of 2026-08-19; the API interface can change. Vibe Code additionally speaks MCP directly over stdio, HTTP and streamable HTTP (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers).

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Re-verified on the chat endpoint reference 2026-08-19: parallel_tool_calls — 'Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use, when enabled the model can call multiple tools in parallel.' Default Value: true.

max_tools_hard.notes: Unchanged and re-verified 2026-08-19: Known Limitations still states 'Maximum number of tools per request: 128.' SCOPE = AGGREGATE — it counts every tool in the request's `tools` array together: your own functions, every tool pulled in from each connected Connector (MCP server), and Mistral's built-in tools (web search, code interpreter, image generation, document library), which are passed in the same array (https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat). It is not a per-MCP-server cap; no per-server tool cap is documented anywhere.

max_tools_practical.notes: CHANGED 20 → null (2026-08-19 final audit): no empirical source has measured a Mistral model's tool-count degradation, so no practical tool ceiling can be asserted for Mistral Small 4. The previously cited leaderboard (https://presenc.ai/research/ai-agent-tool-calling-accuracy-benchmarks-2026, tier 4, re-opened 2026-08-19) measures only Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Qwen 3 235B, Llama 4 405B, Qwen 3 32B, Llama 4 70B and DeepSeek V4 — NO Mistral model appears in it, so its "accuracy degrades to 85-91 percent at 5 tools, then to 65-78 percent at 20+ tools" band (exemplified on Claude Opus 4.7: 96% at 1 tool → 91% at 5 → 76% at 20+) is evidence about those models only. Skills: ~100 tokens per enabled Skill at discovery (name + description only), then the full SKILL.md on activation, then referenced files on demand (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/work/skills); Mistral publishes no size ceiling for SKILL.md and only an unquantified 'supporting files are subject to a file-count limit'. Agents: the agent's `instructions` and its tool list are fixed at creation and injected into the conversation, billed as input tokens. Connector (MCP) tool schemas are NOT progressively disclosed — every tool left enabled is serialized into every request and charged as input (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Prompt caching can recover 90% of the cost of that repeated prefix if a stable prompt_cache_key is supplied (https://docs.mistral.ai/studio-api/conversations/advanced/prompt-caching).

prompt_caching.notes: CHANGED false -> true. Prompt caching is documented as of 2026-08-19 and is explicit: set prompt_cache_key to 'a stable application-level identifier, such as a conversation ID, session ID, or workflow ID'. Cache blocks are 64 tokens, so cached_tokens is always a multiple of 64 and 'prompts with fewer than 64 prompt tokens do not have cache hits'; supplying the key 'doesn't guarantee' a hit. Cached prompt tokens bill at 10% of the standard input price. TTL is not published, nor is whether tool definitions specifically are cacheable — only that a compatible cached PREFIX is matched, which a stable tools array at the head of the request should satisfy.

memory_feature.notes: Agents documentation describes 'persistent state across conversations' and agent-to-agent handoffs (re-checked 2026-08-19). Server-side conversation history is replayed as input tokens on each continuation, so a long session's context — and cost — grows turn over turn. The exact `store` parameter semantics are no longer spelled out on the current Agents introduction page.

input_output_shared.notes: Known Limitations, re-read 2026-08-19: both input and output tokens are included in the context calculation — 'Plan your max_tokens accordingly.'

Not recorded as a number because it is request-dependent, not a documented constant.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: No per-completion output ceiling is published. The only documented bound is 'prompt + max_tokens cannot exceed the model's context length' (256k). This is a genuine documentation gap, not an absence of constraint — the shared 256k window is what binds.

extended_context.notes: No extended/beta context tier beyond 256k appears in the Known Limitations table (re-read 2026-08-19).

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Mistral Large 3 is not listed among the models that accept reasoning_effort on the Reasoning page (only mistral-small-latest and mistral-medium-3-5 are, checked 2026-08-19), so no reasoning-token accounting applies.

tokenizer_family.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. tokenizer_access.notes: Refreshed 2026-08-19 to the current documented loading path. Extras: pip install "mistral-common[image]" / "mistral-common[audio,hf-hub]".

image_token_rule.notes: Still undocumented, and now confirmed as a deliberate gap: the Vision capability page carries the FAQ heading 'How many tokens correspond to an image and/or what is the maximum resolution?' with no answer beneath it (checked 2026-08-19). audio_token_rule.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19: the model card does not list audio as a capability for this model, and the official HF card (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-3) gives the modalities as text+image in / text out. Audio is handled by the separate Voxtral models and endpoints, so no audio token rule applies here. (The 2026-06-21 entry's 'audio transcription listed as a feature' claim did not hold up on re-read.)

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: CHANGED to null: the previous 4.0 was an unsourced industry rule of thumb. Searched Mistral's tokenization deep-dive, the mistral-common docs and the Tekken tokenizer card (https://huggingface.co/toksuite/mistralai-tekken, vocab 130,000, tier 3) on 2026-08-19 — no chars-per-token or bytes-per-token figure is published for Tekken. The only quantitative claim Mistral makes is relative: Tekken is '~30% more efficient at compressing source code, Chinese, Italian, French, German, Spanish, and Russian' and 2x/3x on Korean/Arabic versus the Llama 3 tokenizer. Use mistral-common for exact counts.

function_calling.notes: Function Calling is listed in the model card's feature list (re-verified 2026-08-19) and the model appears in the function-calling guide's supported-model list (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling).

native_mcp.notes: Platform-level: any function-calling model can be pointed at registered Connectors (MCP servers), whose tools the model 'discovers automatically and calls ... based on the user's request'. Still Public Preview as of 2026-08-19; the API interface can change. Vibe Code additionally speaks MCP directly over stdio, HTTP and streamable HTTP (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers).

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Re-verified on the chat endpoint reference 2026-08-19: parallel_tool_calls — 'Whether to enable parallel function calling during tool use, when enabled the model can call multiple tools in parallel.' Default Value: true.

max_tools_hard.notes: Unchanged and re-verified 2026-08-19: Known Limitations still states 'Maximum number of tools per request: 128.' SCOPE = AGGREGATE — it counts every tool in the request's `tools` array together: your own functions, every tool pulled in from each connected Connector (MCP server), and Mistral's built-in tools (web search, code interpreter, image generation, document library), which are passed in the same array (https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/chat). It is not a per-MCP-server cap; no per-server tool cap is documented anywhere.

max_tools_practical.notes: CHANGED 20 → null (2026-08-19 final audit): no empirical source has measured a Mistral model's tool-count degradation, so no practical tool ceiling can be asserted for Mistral Large 3. The previously cited leaderboard (https://presenc.ai/research/ai-agent-tool-calling-accuracy-benchmarks-2026, tier 4, re-opened 2026-08-19) measures only Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Qwen 3 235B, Llama 4 405B, Qwen 3 32B, Llama 4 70B and DeepSeek V4 — NO Mistral model appears in it, so its "accuracy degrades to 85-91 percent at 5 tools, then to 65-78 percent at 20+ tools" band (exemplified on Claude Opus 4.7: 96% at 1 tool → 91% at 5 → 76% at 20+) is evidence about those models only. The practitioner write-up previously quoted alongside it (https://tianpan.co/blog/2026-04-19-over-tooled-agent-problem, "safe zone ... at roughly 10-20 tools per reasoning context") likewise names no Mistral model. Mistral itself publishes no tool-count guidance: the function-calling docs (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/function_calling/, tier 1, checked 2026-08-19) list Mistral Large 3 among the function-calling models but state no maximum or recommended number of tools and no degradation threshold. Binding limits that DO apply: the documented 128-tool hard cap per request (see max_tools_hard, https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations, tier 1) and the 256,000-token shared input+output context window that every tool definition is billed into. Any cross-vendor 10-20-tool rule of thumb applied to Mistral is an unmeasured extrapolation, not a Mistral measurement.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: {"type": "function", "function": {name, description, parameters}} with a JSON-Schema `parameters` object — identical in shape to OpenAI function calling. tool_choice accepts auto (default) | any/required | none | a named tool.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: Known Limitations states that tool descriptions consume tokens from the available context. Tool definitions are therefore billed as input tokens and eat the same 256k window as the messages — the premise of the footprint measurement.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Still no automatic/lazy tool loading: nothing in the API defers tool schemas or lets the model search a catalog. What exists as of 2026-08-19 is manual, human-side pruning — admins can 'turn individual tools on or off for a whole org or one workspace' inside a Connector, Vibe Code offers a `/connectors` picker to choose which tools to enable, and the Vibe CLI supports enabled_tools/disabled_tools glob or regex filters (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers). Those shrink what is sent, but every surviving tool is still serialized into every request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character ceiling or pattern for function/tool names is published: the API reference documents the `tools` parameter but not a Function object schema with maxLength/pattern (checked 2026-08-19). Two adjacent caps that DO bind: Connector (MCP server registry) names are 'up to 64 characters, alphanumeric with underscores and dashes only' (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management), and the Vibe CLI namespaces MCP tools as {server_name}_{tool_name} (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers), so a long server alias eats into whatever name budget the model-side parser has.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No character or token ceiling for a tool description is published (re-checked 2026-08-19). The binding constraint is budgetary, not syntactic: Known Limitations says descriptions consume tokens from the available context, so long descriptions across 128 tools are charged against the shared 256k window.

max_request_size.notes: No byte/MB payload ceiling is documented for POST /v1/chat/completions (the chat endpoint reference documents no array or payload size limits, checked 2026-08-19). Adjacent caps that are documented and that DO bind on neighbouring paths: 512 MB per uploaded file, 512 MB per batch file with up to 100,000 requests, 20 MB per image, 500 MB / 60 minutes per audio file. For chat itself the binding ceilings are the 256k token window and the 128-tool aggregate cap.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No numeric size ceiling for an individual tool result is documented (checked 2026-08-19). A tool result is an ordinary `tool`-role message, so it is charged against the shared 256k input+output window — that window, not a size rule, is what a chatty MCP tool blows.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: parallel_tool_calls is a boolean (default true) — no numeric ceiling on how many tool calls the model may emit in one turn is published (re-checked on the chat endpoint reference 2026-08-19). The 128-tool aggregate cap limits what is offered, not how many are invoked at once.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No numeric ceiling on tool-call/result cycles per turn or per agentic loop is published; the function calling guide's worked example loops back to the model until it produces a final answer without stating a cycle ceiling (re-checked 2026-08-19). Cost and the 256k window are what bound a long agentic run.

max_connected_servers.notes: No numeric ceiling on the number of Connectors (MCP servers) per workspace, org, agent or conversation is published (Connectors API reference and management docs re-checked 2026-08-19); listing uses keyset pagination with a page_size shown as high as 1000, which implies large counts are expected. Mistral advertises 'more than 60 integrations' plus custom MCP connectors (https://mistral.ai/news/more-control-over-connectors/). The limit that actually binds when you attach many servers is the aggregate 128-tool per-request cap.

max_total_tools.notes: No separate aggregate catalog ceiling exists above the per-request cap: on Mistral the aggregate cap IS max_tools_hard = 128 tools per request, summed across your own functions, every connected Connector's tools and the built-in tools. GET /v1/connectors/{id}/tools paginates (default page_size 100) with no documented maximum tool count per connector (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management).

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19. Connector (MCP server registry) names: 'up to 64 characters, alphanumeric with underscores and dashes only', unique within a workspace (https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/connectors/management / https://docs.mistral.ai/api/endpoint/beta/connectors). Tool function name cap: not published — the API reference documents the `tools` parameter but no Function object maxLength/pattern (https://docs.mistral.ai/api). No documented limit on JSON-Schema nesting depth, property count, enum size, or on unsupported keywords such as oneOf/anyOf/$ref — Mistral publishes no schema-shape rules at all, so the only reliable ceiling is the token budget: tool descriptions and schemas are charged as input against the shared 256k window (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Vibe CLI namespaces MCP tools as {server_name}_{tool_name} (https://docs.mistral.ai/vibe/code/cli/mcp-servers).
tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19 — rate limits are set at the ORGANIZATION level and apply across all workspaces (the 2026-06-21 entry said 'per API key', which the tier docs contradict); three independent limits are enforced: requests per second, tokens per minute and tokens per month, with tier upgrades driven by cumulative billed amount and the actual numbers only visible in Admin > Limits (https://docs.mistral.ai/deployment/ai-studio/tier). Batch processing is 50% cheaper and does not compete with real-time limits; max batch file 512 MB / 100,000 requests, results retained 24h; streaming connections drop after 10 minutes of inactivity (https://docs.mistral.ai/resources/known-limitations). Connectors remain Public Preview; connector tool schemas are serialized into the request, so a large MCP server consumes a real share of the 256k window and of the 128-tool aggregate cap. Regional endpoints (EU/US) are GA and a Priority Tier with custom rate limits and an uptime SLA is in public preview (https://mistral.ai/news/regional-inference-open-models-new-compute/).

strict_function_schema.notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: Mistral documents no OpenAI-style `strict` flag and no structural schema restrictions (no 100-property / 5-level-depth / no-oneOf rules). skills_supported.notes: Upgraded sourcing 2026-08-19: Mistral now has a literal Skills primitive (Studio and Vibe), announced 2026-07-09, in addition to Agents. context_window_tokens.notes: 1,050,000 tokens, unchanged from gpt-5.5/gpt-5.4. Prompts over 272K input tokens are billed at 2x input / 1.5x output for the whole request.

input_output_shared.notes: Single 1,050,000-token pool shared by input and output.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived: 1,050,000 - 128,000 = 922,000. Not published as a separate figure.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default max_output published; the model page states only the 128,000 maximum.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: 128,000, inclusive of reasoning tokens.
