tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model-level cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Qwen Code (the vendor's own CLI host) documents a per-tool-call `timeout` defaulting to 10 minutes and a `discoveryTimeoutMs` handshake timeout (30s stdio / 5s remote) but no cycle cap; agentic loops are bounded by the host and by context.

max_connected_servers.notes: Tier-1 and NEW since the 2026-06-21 pass: the Model Studio MCP reference states 'Maximum 10 MCP servers.' Scope: AGGREGATE per request, enforced at the hosted-API layer on the Responses API path ('Available through the Responses API only'; 'Supports MCP servers using the SSE protocol'). It bounds the number of servers, not the number of tools. Self-hosted deployments and the Qwen-Agent / Qwen Code hosts are outside its scope and publish no equivalent server-count constraint of their own.

max_total_tools.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from a vLLM recipe page named for Qwen3.5 to this model's own vLLM recipe. Tier 4: a serving-framework doc, not a vendor spec. It documents serving this model at '--max-model-len 262144' with '--enable-auto-tool-choice' and '--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder' and documents no numeric ceiling on the number of tools. No aggregate tool-count cap is published at the model layer; the effective aggregate ceiling is derived - (262,144 - reasoning and answer headroom) / average tool-definition tokens - and is set by the operator's --max-model-len. Host layers cap lower in practice (Cursor ~40 tools, Claude Desktop ~100), and the hosted Model Studio Responses API - which does cover this id - caps connected MCP servers at 10.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open-weight: the model API layer publishes no tool count/size cap. Binding limits, in the order they usually bite: (1) hosted Model Studio Responses API - 'Maximum 10 MCP servers' per request, SSE transport only, MCP available through the Responses API only; (2) hosted rate limits - 600 RPM and 1,000,000-5,000,000 TPM per open-source model id (Singapore/Beijing); (3) the 262,144-token context window shared by tool definitions + prompt + reasoning + output; (4) the serving stack - vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens and KV cache, plus a matching --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder (without it tool calls are emitted as plain text); (5) the agent host - Qwen Code applies includeTools/excludeTools and mcp.allowed/mcp.excluded filters and a 10-minute default tool-call timeout, and third-party hosts cap lower (Cursor ~40 tools, Claude Desktop ~100).

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style `strict` structured-function mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf enforcement) is documented for Qwen. Schemas are passed through as ordinary JSON Schema.

skills_supported.notes: No packaged, model-invokable 'skill' format analogous to Anthropic Agent Skills. The vendor's agent stack is Qwen-Agent (pip install -U "qwen-agent[gui,rag,code_interpreter,mcp]"), which exposes a function_list of tools/plugins and mcpServers configs, and Qwen Code, which loads MCP servers from settings.json. Both are tool wiring, not a progressive-disclosure skill bundle: everything configured is injected up front.

skills_loading_model.notes: No skill system, so no loading model. Tools/plugins registered in Qwen-Agent's function_list or Qwen Code's mcpServers are always-on for the session and injected in full at request time.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: No skills system to cost. The context cost that matters is the tool surface: MCP tool schemas are translated to OpenAI-shaped function definitions, rendered into the chat template's <tools> block, and counted as input tokens on every request in the conversation - they are re-sent each turn, so the footprint is multiplied by turn count unless a prefix cache absorbs it.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompt is billed as input tokens. Tool definitions are folded into the system message for cache-prefix purposes (Model Studio context-cache reference), so system prompt + tool JSON form one contiguous prefix. No fixed platform-injected overhead is documented for self-hosted deployments.

prompt_caching.notes: Scope split, corrected at the 2026-08-19 refresh. (a) Self-host: vLLM's own Qwen recipe serves this generation with --enable-prefix-caching, so a stable system-prompt + tool-definition prefix is reused across turns - this is the value recorded here (tier 2). (b) Hosted Model Studio: the previous entry claimed DashScope context caching applied. It does not for the open-source model ids - the Model Studio context-cache reference lists only the commercial qwen3.7-max/plus, qwen3.6-max-preview/plus/flash and qwen3.5-plus/flash tiers for both explicit (10% of input price) and implicit (20%) caching; qwen3.6-27b, qwen3.6-35b-a3b and qwen3.5-35b-a3b appear in none of those lists. Where caching does apply, tool definitions ride in the cached system-message prefix but 'cannot be cached independently'.

memory_feature.notes: No built-in cross-session memory in the model or in the open-source serving path. Qwen-Agent ships RAG/memory helper modules that an application can wire up, but they are application state injected as ordinary input tokens, not a model feature.

detail.notes: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is the sparse (35B total / 3B activated) member of the Qwen3.6 generation, April 2026. SUPERSEDED as the open-weight lead by the Qwen3.8 generation (August 2026) but still GA: published on HuggingFace under Apache-2.0, priced on Alibaba's Model Studio open-source table ($0.375/$2.25 per M), and absent from Model Studio's decommissioning list. context_window_tokens.notes: Model card: 262,144 tokens natively, extensible to 1,010,000 with YaRN. config.json confirms max_position_embeddings = 262144. Shared input+output pool.

input_output_shared.notes: Single position budget (max_position_embeddings 262144) shared by prompt, tool definitions, <think> trace and answer.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived: 262,144 native window minus the card's 81,920-token complex-problem output allocation. No vendor max-input cap is published; the serving stack sets it (--max-model-len).

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Card, Best Practices: 'We recommend using an output length of 32,768 tokens for most queries.'

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Card: 'For benchmarking on highly complex problems, such as those found in math and programming competitions, we suggest setting the max output length to 81,920 tokens.' A recommendation, not an API-enforced cap.

extended_context.notes: Card: extensible up to 1,010,000 tokens via YaRN (rope_type yarn, factor 4.0). config.json ships rope_type 'default', so YaRN is an explicit operator override (VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1, --max-model-len 1010000). Static YaRN can degrade short-context quality.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: The model emits <think>...</think> before the answer (--reasoning-parser qwen3 splits it out); reasoning tokens are generated tokens that consume the output budget and bill at the output rate.

tokenizer_family.notes: CORRECTED at the 2026-08-19 refresh. The previous entry said '~151,643 tokens' - that figure comes from the Qwen1-era tokenization note (github.com/QwenLM/Qwen), which describes Qwen-7B ('151,643 regular tokens and 208 control tokens'), a different and much smaller vocabulary. The Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 generation ships a new tokenizer: config.json reports vocab_size 248320, tokenizer_config.json reports tokenizer_class Qwen2Tokenizer with 33 added special tokens at ids 248,044-248,076 (<|endoftext|>, <|im_start|>/<|im_end|>, vision/video/audio pads, <think>/</think>). The model cards state 'Token Embedding: 248,320 (Padded)'. Still tiktoken-style byte-level BPE.

tokenizer_public.notes: tokenizer.json / tokenizer_config.json are published in the public HuggingFace repo under the model's license; counts are locally reproducible.

tokenizer_access.notes: tokenizer_config.json: tokenizer_class = Qwen2Tokenizer, model_max_length = 262144. Loadable with transformers AutoTokenizer; the chat template (which is what actually renders tool definitions into the prompt) ships in the same file, so apply_chat_template(tools=...) is the accurate way to count an MCP tool surface.

count_tokens_method.value: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B'); len(tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=tools, tokenize=True))
count_tokens_method.notes: Use apply_chat_template with the tools argument rather than encoding the raw JSON: the template wraps tool definitions in a <tools> block plus format instructions, so raw-JSON counts understate the real footprint.

image_token_rule.value: Variable: the vision encoder patches an image into a resolution-dependent number of visual tokens; no closed-form per-image formula is published
image_token_rule.notes: Alibaba's vision reference states only that 'the total token count for all images and text must not exceed the model's maximum input' and that the number of images per request is 'determined by the model's total token limit' - it publishes no pixels-per-token constant or per-image cap. The model card gives no formula either. Count multimodal input with the model's AutoProcessor rather than estimating.

audio_token_rule.notes: The model card scopes this model to text, image and video input; audio is handled by the separate Qwen3-Omni / Qwen3.5-Omni line. Note that the shared tokenizer nevertheless reserves <|audio_start|>, <|audio_end|> and <|audio_pad|> ids in the 248,044-248,076 special-token block (it is one vocabulary across the generation), so the presence of those ids is not evidence of audio support in this checkpoint.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Set to null at the 2026-08-19 refresh. The previous value (3.5) was attributed to the Qwen1 tokenization note, which documents a 151,643-token vocabulary - a different tokenizer from the 248,320-vocab one this generation ships, so the ratio does not carry over. No vendor-published characters-per-token figure exists for the Qwen3.5/3.6/3.8 tokenizer; measure with the published AutoTokenizer instead of estimating.

function_calling.notes: Tier-1: the Model Studio function-calling reference lists the Qwen3.6 / Qwen3.5 / Qwen3 open-source series among the models that support function calling, using the OpenAI-shaped `tools` array. Independently confirmed at the weights level: the model's tokenizer_config.json chat template renders a <tools> block and requires 'Function calls MUST follow the specified format' inside <tool_call></tool_call> tags.

native_mcp.notes: MCP is supported both through the vendor's agent stack and, new since the 2026-06-21 pass, as a first-class hosted-API feature. Tier-1: the Model Studio MCP reference lets you 'add MCP server information in the tools parameter when using the Responses API', with 'Maximum 10 MCP servers', SSE transport, and 'Available through the Responses API only'; its supported list explicitly includes the 'Qwen3.6 open-source series (except qwen3.6-27b)' and the 'Qwen3.5 open-source series'. Self-hosted, the same surface is reached through Qwen-Agent (mcpServers in function_list) or Qwen Code (settings.json mcpServers over stdio/HTTP/SSE). MCP tool schemas are converted to OpenAI-shaped function definitions and injected as input tokens.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Tier-1: Model Studio documents a `parallel_tool_calls` request parameter - 'set the parallel_tool_calls request parameter to true' - so all tool calls are returned simultaneously. The Qwen function-calling guide adds that 'the current default tool calling template natively supports Parallel Function Calls'.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric cap on the number of tools is documented for Qwen at the model-API layer: the Model Studio function-calling reference describes the OpenAI-style `tools` array without stating a maximum, and self-hosted vLLM/SGLang enforce no tool count. Scope note: the limits that DO bind are (1) an AGGREGATE cap of 'Maximum 10 MCP servers' per request on the Model Studio Responses API MCP path, (2) the empirical ~30-50-tool selection cliff (see max_tools_practical), and (3) the 262,144-token context window shared by tool definitions, prompt and output. There is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap.

max_tools_practical.notes: Empirical, not spec. No Qwen-specific published degradation point exists. Anchors: 'Scaling Enterprise Agent Routing' (arXiv 2606.17519, 2026-06-16) measured routing F1 dropping 16-23 percentage points across three frontier models as a catalog scaled from 10 agents to 110 agents / 584 tools; MCP-Atlas (arXiv 2602.00933) exposes only 10-25 tools per task by design. 40 is a conservative mid-point of the community ~30-50 range for a capable model. Aggregate scope (all connected servers + built-ins combined).

tool_definition_shape.notes: Tier-1: tools are supplied as {"type":"function","function":{"name","description","parameters"}} with JSON-Schema parameters, over the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions endpoint that both Model Studio and self-hosted vLLM/SGLang expose. The Qwen function-calling guide notes the chat template 'has already included support for the Hermes-style tool use'; vLLM ships both `hermes` and `qwen3_coder` parsers, and the Qwen recipes use --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder for this generation.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tier-1 confirmation: the Model Studio context-cache reference states that 'for function calling, if a request includes the `tools` parameter, the tool definition is included in the system message for cache calculation' and that 'tool definitions cannot be cached independently'. Tool JSON is therefore serialized into the prompt and billed as input tokens; on a self-hosted deployment it is rendered into the chat template and consumes context.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No runtime tool-search / deferred-definition-loading mechanism (the Claude ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / defer_loading equivalent) is documented for Qwen. The nearest facility is static filtering in Qwen Code - per-server includeTools/excludeTools allow/deny lists and global mcp.allowed / mcp.excluded globs - which shrinks the catalog before the request, not lazily during it. Qwen Code does discover servers progressively: 'sending a prompt before MCP finishes simply means the model sees the tools that are ready at that moment'.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character-count or character-class cap on tool names is published. Model Studio only recommends: 'The name field is a custom tool function name. We recommend using the same name as the function, such as get_current_weather or get_current_time.' Long client-namespaced MCP names therefore cost tokens rather than being rejected.

The Model Studio function-calling reference only recommends that the `name` field match the implementing function (e.g. get_current_weather); no length or character-class rule is published. The practical constraint is the input token budget. The chat template renders tools into a <tools> block and requires calls inside <tool_call></tool_call> tags. vLLM's Qwen3.5 recipe enables tool calling on the multimodal serving path with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder and runs with --enable-prefix-caching, which is the practical mitigation for a large static tool-definition prefix.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No vendor cap on description length; the description is serialized into the <tools> block and counts against the shared 262,144-token window.

serving_frameworks.value: vLLM, SGLang, HuggingFace Transformers, Ollama (quantized GGUF)
serving_frameworks.notes: vLLM ships a maintained Qwen3.5 recipe with text-only (--language-model-only), multimodal-with-tool-calling and latency-optimised variants, all using --reasoning-parser qwen3 and --enable-prefix-caching.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: vLLM's Qwen3.5 recipe gives the canonical tool-calling command: '--reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-prefix-caching --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder'. Prefix caching matters here: the tool-definition block sits at the head of every request, so caching it is what keeps a multi-turn MCP session affordable. MCP arrives via Qwen-Agent, Qwen Code, or Alibaba's hosted Responses API (the 'Qwen3.5 open-source series' is on its supported list; max 10 MCP servers, SSE only).

detail.notes: Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is the sparse member of the Qwen3.5 generation, open-sourced 2026-02-16 - the generation that introduced this tokenizer (248,320 vocab) and the 262,144-token native window that Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 inherit. TWO GENERATIONS SUPERSEDED (by Qwen3.6, April 2026, and Qwen3.8, August 2026) but still GA: Apache-2.0 weights remain published, the id is still priced on Alibaba's Model Studio open-source table ($0.25/$2.0 per M - the cheapest entry in this file), and it does not appear on Model Studio's decommissioning list (which does schedule a large batch of Qwen3-era ids for retirement on 2026-10-10). Retained here as the cheap, small-footprint baseline for MCP hosting comparisons.

context_window_tokens.notes: config.json: max_position_embeddings=1048576 (1M), reached with YaRN RoPE scaling (type=yarn, factor=16, original_max_position_embeddings=65536). The hosted Models & Pricing page independently lists CONTEXT LENGTH 1M for this model.

input_output_shared.notes: One shared 1M pool: context length 1M with MAXIMUM 384K output. Input plus output (including thinking tokens) together consume the window.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived: context window 1048576 minus the 384K (393216) maximum output = 655360. DeepSeek publishes no separate max-input figure; in practice you can prompt closer to 1M if you reserve less output. (Corrects the previous entry, which stated 671744 while its own note derived 655360.)

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default published. The Chat Completions reference says only that input plus generated tokens are bounded by the model's context length and defers the range/default to other docs; the Models & Pricing page publishes only the MAXIMUM (384K).

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Models & Pricing states MAXIMUM: 384K output (384*1024 = 393216), covering thinking and final-answer tokens together. The model card recommends a maximum output length of 384K for the `high` and `max` reasoning-effort levels.

extended_context.notes: 1M is the GA window; no separate beta or extended-context tier is offered, so there is nothing above it to record.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Thinking mode emits `reasoning_content`, which is generated output and shares the 384K output ceiling. `reasoning_effort` takes low / high / max (default high; medium and xhigh are mapped to high). Agentic cost trap: for requests carrying `tools`, reasoning_content must be echoed back on every subsequent request or the API returns 400 — so it is billed as output once and then as input on each following step.

tokenizer_family.notes: config.json: vocab_size=129280 — unchanged across V3/V3.2/V4, so token counts are comparable across DeepSeek generations. The 0813 GA checkpoint keeps the V4 tokenizer unchanged from the preview.

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer + the repo's encoding_dsv4 encoding scripts
tokenizer_access.notes: MIT-licensed weights ship the tokenizer. DeepSeek also publishes an offline tokenizer zip at https://cdn.deepseek.com/api-docs/deepseek_v3_tokenizer.zip, but note it is the V3-era package — for exact V4 counts prefer the model repo's own encoding scripts.

count_tokens_method.value: transformers.AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(<repo>).encode(text); or the repo's encoding scripts; or read usage.prompt_tokens from an API response
count_tokens_method.notes: DeepSeek exposes no count-tokens endpoint; the authoritative count is the `usage` object returned with a completion, or a local run of the model's own tokenizer.

image_token_rule.notes: Text-only model; no image modality documented.

audio_token_rule.notes: No audio modality.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Official rule of thumb re-verified 2026-08-19: 1 English character ~ 0.3 token (= ~3.3 chars/token); 1 Chinese character ~ 0.6 token (~1.7 chars/token). Rough estimate only — JSON tool definitions tokenize denser than prose.

function_calling.notes: OpenAI-compatible function calling on /chat/completions, plus function tools on the native Responses API and Anthropic-format tool blocks on the /anthropic endpoint. Tool use works in both thinking and non-thinking modes.

native_mcp.notes: Not MCP-native. The Responses API compatibility table marks the `mcp` built-in tool "Ignored"; the Anthropic-compatible endpoint marks `mcp_servers` "Ignored" and `mcp_tool_use`/`mcp_tool_result` "Not Supported". An MCP host must flatten MCP tools into `function` definitions before sending them.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Upgraded to explicit documentation: on the Responses API "parallel tool calling is always enabled" and `max_tool_calls` is ignored; on the Anthropic-compatible endpoint `disable_parallel_tool_use` is ignored. The model can emit several tool_calls in one assistant turn.

max_tools_hard.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-pro` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the reference states "A max of 128 functions are supported." SCOPE: AGGREGATE -- it counts every function in the request's `tools` array, i.e. all connected MCP servers plus any built-in/host tools combined, not per MCP server. For self-hosted DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 the binding limits are instead the operator's served context length divided by average tool-definition tokens, the empirical selection cliff (see max_tools_practical) and whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

max_tools_practical.notes: EMPIRICAL, NOT SPEC, and FAMILY-LEVEL, NOT PER-CHECKPOINT (attribution restated 2026-08-19; tier 4, low confidence). What the cited source actually contains: a single undifferentiated leaderboard entry labelled "DeepSeek V4" reporting 89% single-tool accuracy, 81% at 5 tools and 57% at 20+ tools, with the advice to cap practical tool counts at 15-20 and route/tier above that. It does NOT separate DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek-V4-Flash, does not name a checkpoint (-0813 / -0731), and does not state the serving stack, context length or harness used. The same family-level number is therefore recorded identically on both live checkpoints rather than being split into invented per-variant figures (the same correction convention applied to Gemma's variants and Phi's variants in this dataset). Pro is the flagship of the pair, so a family figure that blends Pro and Flash is if anything pessimistic here; it is still not a measurement of this checkpoint. Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in tools. Sits far below the hosted API's 128-function cap, and for a self-hosted deployment it is the accuracy cliff -- not any vendor rule -- that binds first.

tool_definition_shape.notes: {type: 'function', function: {name, description, parameters}} on /chat/completions and on the Responses API. The /anthropic endpoint additionally accepts Anthropic tool blocks (name / description / input_schema fully supported). Shape matters for footprint: the same MCP tool serializes to different token counts in the two shapes.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The serialized `tools` array is part of the prompt and lands in `prompt_tokens`; DeepSeek reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` against that same prompt, so a stable tool-definition prefix is the prime KV-cache candidate. DeepSeek does not state this in one sentence — it follows from the OpenAI-compatible usage object plus the cache guide.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No progressive/deferred tool loading and no server-side tool search. The Responses API supports only function tools, a server-side `web_search`, and the Codex `apply_patch` custom tool; every other built-in (including `mcp`) is ignored. All tool definitions must be resent each request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-pro` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the function name "Must be a-z, A-Z, 0-9, or contain underscores and dashes, with a maximum length of 64." SCOPE: per-tool, and validated by the hosted endpoint's request parser -- the weights themselves reject nothing; a self-hosted deployment inherits whatever its OpenAI-compatible server validates (vLLM/SGLang impose no such name rule by default). It still matters for self-hosting as a PORTABILITY risk: MCP clients namespace tools (server prefix + separator + tool name), so a long server id can push a legal MCP tool name past 64 characters and break the same workload the moment it moves onto the hosted endpoint.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Strict mode is a beta feature: call base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta", set "strict": true on EVERY function, and set "additionalProperties": false on every object. Supported strict-mode JSON Schema types: object, string, number, integer, boolean, array, enum, anyOf. Strings support `pattern` and `format` (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid) but NOT minLength/maxLength. Numbers/integers support const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf. Arrays do NOT support minItems/maxItems. DeepSeek publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling (unlike OpenAI's 100 properties / 5 levels).

max_tool_description_len.notes: No per-request numeric cap documented for the function `description` field. The limits that bind are the 128-function aggregate cap and the 1M context window the serialized descriptions consume as input tokens.

max_request_size.notes: No per-request byte cap documented. The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

max_total_tools.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-pro` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the same "A max of 128 functions are supported." rule as max_tools_hard, recorded here as the AGGREGATE sum-across-servers budget the recommender must allocate, because every connected MCP server plus any host/built-in tools serialize into one `tools` array. For self-hosted weights no vendor aggregate cap exists; the effective ceiling is approximately (served context window - output/reasoning headroom) / average tool-definition tokens, set by the operator's serving config. Host layers cap lower again (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Hosted API (model-API layer): 128 functions per request (aggregate), function names <=64 chars matching a-zA-Z0-9_-, concurrency 500 for deepseek-v4-pro and 2500 for deepseek-v4-flash per account across all keys (HTTP 429 above), `user_id` <=512 chars, and the server closes a connection whose inference has not started within 10 minutes. Agent-loop trap: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` MUST be passed back in full or the API returns 400 — this makes thinking-mode tool loops re-send (and re-pay for) their own chain of thought as input. Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: CHANGED from false: DeepSeek does ship an OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode, in beta (base_url .../beta, `strict: true` on every function, `additionalProperties: false` on every object). It is not identical to OpenAI's: DeepSeek publishes no 100-property / 5-level-depth ceiling, and its unsupported-keyword list is minLength/maxLength/minItems/maxItems (see tool_schema_limits_notes).

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens and are eligible for the disk KV cache. Agentic caveat that dominates real session cost: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` must be passed back in full (400 otherwise), so a thinking-mode tool loop re-submits its own chain of thought as input on every step. Plain multi-turn chat without tools does NOT concatenate previous CoT.

prompt_caching.notes: Disk-based KV cache (context caching), on by default, best-effort. Each request produces cache prefix units at the end of the user input and of the model output, plus units carved at fixed token intervals for long content; entries are cleared when unused, "usually within a few hours to a few days". Usage reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens`. DeepSeek publishes no minimum cacheable prefix size and no explicit statement that tool definitions are separately cacheable — they are cached only as part of a matching prefix. Cache-hit input for deepseek-v4-pro is $0.044/1M peak and $0.022/1M off-peak, against cache-miss input of $1.32/1M peak and $0.66/1M off-peak (peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC; every other hour is off-peak at half rate).

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature in the API.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Cache-MISS input, PEAK rate ($1.32/1M). Off-peak cache-miss input is $0.66/1M. TWO-TIER CLOCK PRICING (this schema has no peak/off-peak dimension, so the recorded value is the PEAK rate — the base list rate the Models & Pricing page publishes, from which it derives the other tier: "Off-peak rates are half of the peak rates"). FULL SCHEDULE for `deepseek-v4-pro`, USD per 1M tokens, peak / off-peak: input cache-miss $1.32 / $0.66; input cache-hit $0.044 / $0.022; output $3.96 / $1.98. PEAK WINDOWS: 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC — 7 of 24 hours. ALL OTHER HOURS ARE OFF-PEAK and bill at exactly half, so a round-the-clock workload pays well below the recorded value; a cross-vendor comparison that reads this value alone overstates DeepSeek by up to 2x for most of the day. Schedule took effect 16:00 UTC on 2026-08-16 (announced in the 2026-08-13 changelog entry: "we will adopt peak/off-peak pricing, with off-peak prices set at half of the peak-hour prices"). Confidence lowered to medium because one number cannot represent a two-tier clock-based rate — not because the figures are in doubt (both tiers re-read on the vendor pricing page 2026-08-19).

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Output, PEAK rate ($3.96/1M). Off-peak output is $1.98/1M. Thinking / `reasoning_content` tokens bill at this same output meter in both tiers. TWO-TIER CLOCK PRICING (this schema has no peak/off-peak dimension, so the recorded value is the PEAK rate — the base list rate the Models & Pricing page publishes, from which it derives the other tier: "Off-peak rates are half of the peak rates"). FULL SCHEDULE for `deepseek-v4-pro`, USD per 1M tokens, peak / off-peak: input cache-miss $1.32 / $0.66; input cache-hit $0.044 / $0.022; output $3.96 / $1.98. PEAK WINDOWS: 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC — 7 of 24 hours. Schedule took effect 16:00 UTC on 2026-08-16 (announced in the 2026-08-13 changelog entry: "we will adopt peak/off-peak pricing, with off-peak prices set at half of the peak-hour prices"). Confidence lowered to medium because one number cannot represent a two-tier clock-based rate — not because the figures are in doubt (both tiers re-read on the vendor pricing page 2026-08-19).

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Disk-KV-cache-HIT input, PEAK rate ($0.044/1M). Off-peak cache-hit input is $0.022/1M. Cache-hit is ~97% cheaper than cache-miss in BOTH tiers (0.044 vs 1.32 peak; 0.022 vs 0.66 off-peak), which is why a stable tool-definition + system-prompt prefix is the single biggest cost lever for MCP sessions. TWO-TIER CLOCK PRICING (this schema has no peak/off-peak dimension, so the recorded value is the PEAK rate — the base list rate the Models & Pricing page publishes, from which it derives the other tier: "Off-peak rates are half of the peak rates"). batch_discount.notes: No batch API and no batch discount is published on the Models & Pricing page (re-read 2026-08-19). The only non-list rate is the clock-based off-peak tier — exactly half the peak rate, applying to every hour outside 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC. That is a time-of-day rate, not a batch mode: you cannot opt into it for a latency trade, you can only schedule work into the off-peak hours.

billing_unit.notes: Hosted API bills per token with separate cache-hit / cache-miss input meters. Self-hosting the same open weights carries compute cost only.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: `reasoning_content` is billed at the output rate ($3.96/1M peak, $1.98/1M off-peak; peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, all other hours off-peak at half) and counts against the 384K output cap. Raising `reasoning_effort` from low to max raises cost on the expensive side of the meter, in both tiers.

release_date.notes: General availability across the DeepSeek app, web ("Expert Mode") and API on 2026-08-13, superseding the 2026-04-24 preview checkpoint. The hosted model id stayed `deepseek-v4-pro`.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not disclosed on the model card, in the GA announcement or in the API docs. Searched the HF card, api-docs changelog and the GA news post; no training cutoff is published.

weights_url.notes: GA checkpoint. The April preview weights remain published separately at https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro.

param_variants.value: 1.7T params total (MoE); FP4 experts + FP8 elsewhere
param_variants.notes: CHANGED from "1.6T total / 49B active": the value now agrees with the model's OWN primary card. The DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 repo header states "1.7T params" (tensor types BF16 / I64 / F32 / F8_E4M3 / I8, license mit); the card prose states no total or activated count. Architecture from the same repo's config.json: 61 hidden layers, hidden_size 7168, 384 routed experts, 6 experts per token, 1 shared expert, moe_intermediate_size 3072, 128 attention heads / 1 KV head, quantization_config fp8 (fmt e4m3, weight_block_size [128,128]) with expert_dtype fp4, num_nextn_predict_layers 1, plus a DSpark config block. CONFLICT (kept, not resolved by us): the sibling DeepSeek-V4-Pro-DSpark card states "DeepSeek-V4-Pro with 1.6T parameters (49B activated)" and describes itself as "not a new model ... the same checkpoint with an additional speculative decoding module attached" (its own repo header also reads 1.7T params); the 2026-04-24 V4 preview announcement likewise states "DeepSeek-V4-Pro: 1.6T total / 49B active params". Reading: 1.6T/49B is the transformer architecture figure and 1.7T is the shipped checkpoint total (it includes the bundled next-token-prediction / DSpark module and embeddings). No card states an activated count for the 0813 checkpoint itself, so for MoE serving math use the sibling/announcement figure of ~49B activated per token. Confidence medium because the two tier-1 DeepSeek surfaces disagree.

native_context_config.notes: config.json max_position_embeddings=1048576 via YaRN (factor=16, original_max_position_embeddings=65536).

max_context_documented.notes: Models & Pricing lists CONTEXT LENGTH 1M for deepseek-v4-pro; config.json agrees.

serving_frameworks.value: vLLM, SGLang, Transformers
serving_frameworks.notes: The GA card ships launch commands for both. DSpark speculative decoding needs no separate draft model — vLLM: --speculative-config '{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":7,"draft_sample_method":"greedy"}' (with --kv-cache-dtype fp8, --enable-expert-parallel); SGLang: --speculative-algorithm DSPARK.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Behind vLLM/SGLang's OpenAI-compatible server, tool calling works with the openai_function shape and a matching --tool-call-parser; none of the hosted-API caps (128 functions, 64-char names) are enforced by the weights themselves. MCP still needs a host/adapter that flattens MCP tools into function definitions. In thinking mode with tools, reasoning_content must be carried forward between turns exactly as on the hosted API.

detail.notes: GA release 2026-08-13 (news260813), replacing the April 2026 preview checkpoint behind the unchanged `deepseek-v4-pro` model id. Adds a native OpenAI Responses API surface (Codex-adapted), three reasoning-effort levels (low/high/max, default high; medium/xhigh map to high) and a bundled DSpark speculative-decoding module. Reported GA benchmarks: HLE 42.7 without tools / 60.0 with tools, Terminal Bench 2.1 87.9, NL2Repo 61.5. For MCP work the two numbers that changed most since the last refresh are the newly documented 128-function aggregate cap and the 2026-08-16 peak/off-peak repricing (roughly 2-3x the preview flat rates at peak).

extended_context.notes: 1M is the GA window; no separate beta or extended-context tier is offered, so there is nothing above it to record.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Thinking mode emits `reasoning_content`, which is generated output and shares the 384K output ceiling. `reasoning_effort` takes low / high / max (default high; medium and xhigh are mapped to high). Agentic cost trap: for requests carrying `tools`, reasoning_content must be echoed back on every subsequent request or the API returns 400 — so it is billed as output once and then as input on each following step.

tokenizer_family.notes: config.json: vocab_size=129280 — unchanged across V3/V3.2/V4, so token counts are comparable across DeepSeek generations. Same tokenizer as DeepSeek-V4-Pro; the repo ships encoding scripts for OpenAI-compatible message encoding.

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer + the repo's encoding_dsv4 encoding scripts
tokenizer_access.notes: MIT-licensed weights ship the tokenizer. DeepSeek also publishes an offline tokenizer zip at https://cdn.deepseek.com/api-docs/deepseek_v3_tokenizer.zip, but note it is the V3-era package — for exact V4 counts prefer the model repo's own encoding scripts.

count_tokens_method.value: transformers.AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(<repo>).encode(text); or the repo's encoding scripts; or read usage.prompt_tokens from an API response
count_tokens_method.notes: DeepSeek exposes no count-tokens endpoint; the authoritative count is the `usage` object returned with a completion, or a local run of the model's own tokenizer.

image_token_rule.notes: Text-only model; no image modality documented.

audio_token_rule.notes: No audio modality.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Official rule of thumb re-verified 2026-08-19: 1 English character ~ 0.3 token (= ~3.3 chars/token); 1 Chinese character ~ 0.6 token (~1.7 chars/token). Rough estimate only — JSON tool definitions tokenize denser than prose.

function_calling.notes: OpenAI-compatible function calling on /chat/completions, plus function tools on the native Responses API and Anthropic-format tool blocks on the /anthropic endpoint. Tool use works in both thinking and non-thinking modes.

native_mcp.notes: Not MCP-native. The Responses API compatibility table marks the `mcp` built-in tool "Ignored"; the Anthropic-compatible endpoint marks `mcp_servers` "Ignored" and `mcp_tool_use`/`mcp_tool_result` "Not Supported". An MCP host must flatten MCP tools into `function` definitions before sending them.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Upgraded to explicit documentation: on the Responses API "parallel tool calling is always enabled" and `max_tool_calls` is ignored; on the Anthropic-compatible endpoint `disable_parallel_tool_use` is ignored. The model can emit several tool_calls in one assistant turn.

max_tools_hard.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-flash` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the reference states "A max of 128 functions are supported." SCOPE: AGGREGATE -- it counts every function in the request's `tools` array, i.e. all connected MCP servers plus any built-in/host tools combined, not per MCP server. For self-hosted DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 the binding limits are instead the operator's served context length divided by average tool-definition tokens, the empirical selection cliff (see max_tools_practical) and whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

max_tools_practical.notes: EMPIRICAL, NOT SPEC, and FAMILY-LEVEL, NOT PER-CHECKPOINT (attribution restated 2026-08-19; tier 4, low confidence). What the cited source actually contains: a single undifferentiated leaderboard entry labelled "DeepSeek V4" reporting 89% single-tool accuracy, 81% at 5 tools and 57% at 20+ tools, with the advice to cap practical tool counts at 15-20 and route/tier above that. It does NOT separate DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek-V4-Flash, does not name a checkpoint (-0813 / -0731), and does not state the serving stack, context length or harness used. The same family-level number is therefore recorded identically on both live checkpoints rather than being split into invented per-variant figures (the same correction convention applied to Gemma's variants and Phi's variants in this dataset). Flash is the smaller, cheaper sibling, so a family figure that blends it with Pro is if anything OPTIMISTIC here -- treat 20 as an upper bound for Flash, not a measured value. The alternative considered was nulling this entry as the weaker attribution of the two; the family figure is kept because the source's leaderboard entry covers the whole V4 generation rather than Pro alone. Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected MCP servers plus built-in tools. Sits far below the hosted API's 128-function cap, and for a self-hosted deployment it is the accuracy cliff -- not any vendor rule -- that binds first.

tool_definition_shape.notes: {type: 'function', function: {name, description, parameters}} on /chat/completions and on the Responses API. The /anthropic endpoint additionally accepts Anthropic tool blocks (name / description / input_schema fully supported). Shape matters for footprint: the same MCP tool serializes to different token counts in the two shapes.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The serialized `tools` array is part of the prompt and lands in `prompt_tokens`; DeepSeek reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` against that same prompt, so a stable tool-definition prefix is the prime KV-cache candidate. DeepSeek does not state this in one sentence — it follows from the OpenAI-compatible usage object plus the cache guide.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No progressive/deferred tool loading and no server-side tool search. The Responses API supports only function tools, a server-side `web_search`, and the Codex `apply_patch` custom tool; every other built-in (including `mcp`) is ignored. All tool definitions must be resent each request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the function name "Must be a-z, A-Z, 0-9, or contain underscores and dashes, with a maximum length of 64." SCOPE: per-tool, and validated by the hosted endpoint's request parser -- the weights themselves reject nothing; a self-hosted deployment inherits whatever its OpenAI-compatible server validates (vLLM/SGLang impose no such name rule by default). It still matters for self-hosting as a PORTABILITY risk: MCP clients namespace tools (server prefix + separator + tool name), so a long server id can push a legal MCP tool name past 64 characters and break the same workload the moment it moves onto the hosted endpoint.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Strict mode is a beta feature: call base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta", set "strict": true on EVERY function, and set "additionalProperties": false on every object. Supported strict-mode JSON Schema types: object, string, number, integer, boolean, array, enum, anyOf. Strings support `pattern` and `format` (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid) but NOT minLength/maxLength. Numbers/integers support const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf. Arrays do NOT support minItems/maxItems. DeepSeek publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling (unlike OpenAI's 100 properties / 5 levels).

max_tool_description_len.notes: No per-request numeric cap documented for the function `description` field. The limits that bind are the 128-function aggregate cap and the 1M context window the serialized descriptions consume as input tokens.

max_request_size.notes: No per-request byte cap documented. The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

max_total_tools.notes: ENFORCEMENT LAYER (restated 2026-08-19): this figure is enforced by DeepSeek's HOSTED API (api.deepseek.com, the model-API layer). It is NOT a property of the open weights this entry is keyed on. The cited Chat Completions reference enumerates only hosted aliases for its `model` parameter -- verbatim "Possible values: [`deepseek-v4-flash`, `deepseek-v4-pro`]" -- and `deepseek-v4-flash` currently resolves to deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731, so the cap does bind anyone calling the hosted endpoint for this checkpoint, and does NOT bind a self-hosted deployment of these weights, where the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang `--tool-call-parser`, `--max-model-len`, KV cache) and the context window consumed by serialized tool definitions set the limits, and an OpenAI-compatible gateway in front of the weights imposes whatever it validates. CONFIDENCE lowered high -> low for exactly that reason: the number is tier-1 accurate for the hosted route but does not bind the open-weight id it is recorded against, so the recommender must not treat it as binding for self-hosting. This matches how the other open-weight files record hosted-API caps (the retired DeepSeek preview ids in this same file; Qwen, whose entries state that the hosted "Maximum 10 MCP servers" Responses-API cap does not cover the open-weight ids; Llama/Gemma/Phi, which record no vendor cap at all because there is no vendor API layer to enforce one). THE CLAIM: the same "A max of 128 functions are supported." rule as max_tools_hard, recorded here as the AGGREGATE sum-across-servers budget the recommender must allocate, because every connected MCP server plus any host/built-in tools serialize into one `tools` array. For self-hosted weights no vendor aggregate cap exists; the effective ceiling is approximately (served context window - output/reasoning headroom) / average tool-definition tokens, set by the operator's serving config. Host layers cap lower again (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Hosted API (model-API layer): 128 functions per request (aggregate), function names <=64 chars matching a-zA-Z0-9_-, concurrency 500 for deepseek-v4-pro and 2500 for deepseek-v4-flash per account across all keys (HTTP 429 above), `user_id` <=512 chars, and the server closes a connection whose inference has not started within 10 minutes. Agent-loop trap: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` MUST be passed back in full or the API returns 400 — this makes thinking-mode tool loops re-send (and re-pay for) their own chain of thought as input. Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: CHANGED from false: DeepSeek does ship an OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode, in beta (base_url .../beta, `strict: true` on every function, `additionalProperties: false` on every object). It is not identical to OpenAI's: DeepSeek publishes no 100-property / 5-level-depth ceiling, and its unsupported-keyword list is minLength/maxLength/minItems/maxItems (see tool_schema_limits_notes).

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens and are eligible for the disk KV cache. Agentic caveat that dominates real session cost: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` must be passed back in full (400 otherwise), so a thinking-mode tool loop re-submits its own chain of thought as input on every step. Plain multi-turn chat without tools does NOT concatenate previous CoT.

prompt_caching.notes: Disk-based KV cache (context caching), on by default, best-effort. Each request produces cache prefix units at the end of the user input and of the model output, plus units carved at fixed token intervals for long content; entries are cleared when unused, "usually within a few hours to a few days". Usage reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens`. DeepSeek publishes no minimum cacheable prefix size and no explicit statement that tool definitions are separately cacheable — they are cached only as part of a matching prefix. Cache-hit input for deepseek-v4-flash is $0.014/1M peak and $0.007/1M off-peak, against cache-miss input of $0.44/1M peak and $0.22/1M off-peak (peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC; every other hour is off-peak at half rate).

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature in the API.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Cache-MISS input, PEAK rate ($0.44/1M). Off-peak cache-miss input is $0.22/1M. TWO-TIER CLOCK PRICING (this schema has no peak/off-peak dimension, so the recorded value is the PEAK rate — the base list rate the Models & Pricing page publishes, from which it derives the other tier: "Off-peak rates are half of the peak rates"). FULL SCHEDULE for `deepseek-v4-flash`, USD per 1M tokens, peak / off-peak: input cache-miss $0.44 / $0.22; input cache-hit $0.014 / $0.007; output $1.32 / $0.66. PEAK WINDOWS: 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC — 7 of 24 hours. ALL OTHER HOURS ARE OFF-PEAK and bill at exactly half, so a round-the-clock workload pays well below the recorded value; a cross-vendor comparison that reads this value alone overstates DeepSeek by up to 2x for most of the day. Schedule took effect 16:00 UTC on 2026-08-16 (announced in the 2026-08-13 changelog entry: "we will adopt peak/off-peak pricing, with off-peak prices set at half of the peak-hour prices"). Confidence lowered to medium because one number cannot represent a two-tier clock-based rate — not because the figures are in doubt (both tiers re-read on the vendor pricing page 2026-08-19).

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Output, PEAK rate ($1.32/1M). Off-peak output is $0.66/1M. Thinking / `reasoning_content` tokens bill at this same output meter in both tiers. cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Disk-KV-cache-HIT input, PEAK rate ($0.014/1M). Off-peak cache-hit input is $0.007/1M. Cache-hit is ~97% cheaper than cache-miss in BOTH tiers (0.014 vs 0.44 peak; 0.007 vs 0.22 off-peak), which is why a stable tool-definition + system-prompt prefix is the single biggest cost lever for MCP sessions. batch_discount.notes: No batch API and no batch discount is published on the Models & Pricing page (re-read 2026-08-19). The only non-list rate is the clock-based off-peak tier — exactly half the peak rate, applying to every hour outside 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC. That is a time-of-day rate, not a batch mode: you cannot opt into it for a latency trade, you can only schedule work into the off-peak hours.

billing_unit.notes: Hosted API bills per token with separate cache-hit / cache-miss input meters. Self-hosting the same open weights carries compute cost only.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: `reasoning_content` is billed at the output rate ($1.32/1M peak, $0.66/1M off-peak; peak = 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, all other hours off-peak at half) and counts against the 384K output cap. Raising `reasoning_effort` from low to max raises cost on the expensive side of the meter, in both tiers.

release_date.notes: Changelog 2026-07-31: "the `deepseek-v4-flash` model has been updated to DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731" — architecture and size unchanged from the preview, re-post-trained for agentic capability. Bloomberg reported the same day as a public-beta API launch; the vendor changelog is the tier-1 record used here.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not disclosed on the model card or in the changelog. Searched the HF card, api-docs changelog and release note.

weights_url.notes: Official (post-preview) checkpoint. Preview weights remain at https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

param_variants.value: 304B params total (MoE); FP4 experts + FP8 elsewhere
param_variants.notes: CHANGED from "284B total / 13B active" (which was cited to the SIBLING DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark card): the value now agrees with the model's OWN primary card. The DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 repo header states "304B params" (tensor types BF16 / I64 / F32 / F8_E4M3 / I8, license MIT); the card prose states no total or activated count, only that the model "outperforms DeepSeek-V4-Pro (Preview) on benchmarks listed below despite its far smaller activated parameter count". Architecture from the same repo's config.json: 43 hidden layers, hidden_size 4096, 256 routed experts, 6 experts per token, 1 shared expert, moe_intermediate_size 2048, quantization_config fp8 (fmt e4m3, weight_block_size [128,128]) with expert_dtype fp4, num_nextn_predict_layers 1, sliding_window 128. CONFLICT (kept, not resolved by us): the sibling DeepSeek-V4-Flash-DSpark card states "DeepSeek-V4-Flash with 284B parameters (13B activated)" and calls itself "not a new model ... the same checkpoint with an additional speculative decoding module attached" (its own repo header reads 165B params — a quantized-checkpoint figure); the 2026-04-24 V4 preview announcement states "DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 284B total / 13B active params", and the 2026-07-31 changelog says "DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 keeps the same model architecture and size as DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Preview, and was only re-post-trained". Reading: 284B/13B is the transformer architecture figure and 304B is the shipped checkpoint total (embeddings plus the bundled next-token-prediction / DSpark module). No card states an activated count for the 0731 checkpoint itself, so for MoE serving math use ~13B activated per token. Confidence medium because the tier-1 DeepSeek surfaces disagree.

native_context_config.notes: config.json max_position_embeddings=1048576 via YaRN (factor=16, original=65536); sliding_window=128.

max_context_documented.notes: Models & Pricing lists CONTEXT LENGTH 1M for deepseek-v4-flash.

serving_frameworks.value: vLLM, SGLang, Transformers
serving_frameworks.notes: Card ships vLLM and SGLang commands with DSpark speculative decoding. At a 304B checkpoint total (~13B activated per token per the sibling/announcement figures — see param_variants) this is the practical self-host target of the V4 family.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Same as V4-Pro: OpenAI-compatible tool calling out of the box behind vLLM/SGLang with a matching --tool-call-parser; the hosted 128-function and 64-char-name caps are API-layer rules, not weight-level ones. MCP requires a host/adapter.

detail.notes: Official release 2026-07-31, replacing the preview behind the unchanged `deepseek-v4-flash` id: same architecture and size, re-post-trained for agentic work, plus native Responses API support, Codex adaptation, low/high/max reasoning effort and a bundled DSpark module. Reported to beat DeepSeek-V4-Pro (Preview) across the published agentic suite (Terminal Bench 2.1 82.7, NL2Repo 54.2, DeepSWE 54.4, Agent Last Exam 25.2) at a fraction of the activated parameters. Cheapest way to run a 1M-context, 128-function tool surface on a first-party endpoint. Legacy aliases `deepseek-chat` / `deepseek-reasoner`, which used to route here, were fully retired after 2026-07-24 15:59 UTC.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. config.json: max_position_embeddings=1048576 via YaRN (factor=16, original_max_position_embeddings=65536).

input_output_shared.notes: One shared window. The hosted 384K output reservation no longer applies to this checkpoint (it is not served by the API); a self-hosted deployment sets its own split.

max_input_tokens.notes: No longer derivable from a hosted output cap: this checkpoint is not offered on the API, so the input/output split is whatever the operator's serving stack configures within the 1M window.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Deployment-configured; nothing published for the self-hosted checkpoint.

tool_definition_shape.notes: {type: 'function', function: {name, description, parameters}} on /chat/completions and on the Responses API. The /anthropic endpoint additionally accepts Anthropic tool blocks (name / description / input_schema fully supported). Shape matters for footprint: the same MCP tool serializes to different token counts in the two shapes.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The serialized `tools` array is part of the prompt and lands in `prompt_tokens`; DeepSeek reports `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` / `prompt_cache_miss_tokens` against that same prompt, so a stable tool-definition prefix is the prime KV-cache candidate. DeepSeek does not state this in one sentence — it follows from the OpenAI-compatible usage object plus the cache guide.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No progressive/deferred tool loading and no server-side tool search. The Responses API supports only function tools, a server-side `web_search`, and the Codex `apply_patch` custom tool; every other built-in (including `mcp`) is ignored. All tool definitions must be resent each request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: The documented 64-character function-name cap is a hosted-API rule and is not enforced by the open weights. A self-hosted deployment inherits whatever its OpenAI-compatible server validates; long MCP-namespaced names remain a portability risk if the workload later moves onto the hosted endpoint.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Strict mode is a beta feature: call base_url="https://api.deepseek.com/beta", set "strict": true on EVERY function, and set "additionalProperties": false on every object. Supported strict-mode JSON Schema types: object, string, number, integer, boolean, array, enum, anyOf. Strings support `pattern` and `format` (email, hostname, ipv4, ipv6, uuid) but NOT minLength/maxLength. Numbers/integers support const, default, minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf. Arrays do NOT support minItems/maxItems. DeepSeek publishes no property-count or nesting-depth ceiling (unlike OpenAI's 100 properties / 5 levels).

max_tool_description_len.notes: No per-request numeric cap documented for the function `description` field. The limits that bind are the 128-function aggregate cap and the 1M context window the serialized descriptions consume as input tokens.

max_request_size.notes: No per-request byte cap documented. The Rate Limit & Isolation page publishes only concurrency limits and a keep-alive rule (the server closes the connection if inference has not started within 10 minutes). Binding limits are the context window and, when self-hosting, the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache).

max_tool_result_size.notes: No per-request numeric cap on a single tool result. Tool results are ordinary message content billed as input tokens, so the binding limit is the 1M context window shared with the 384K output reservation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No per-request numeric cap on how many tool calls one assistant turn may emit; the Responses API explicitly ignores `max_tool_calls` and always enables parallel tool calling. The binding limits are the 128 functions offered and the output-token budget the tool-call JSON consumes.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented server-side cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn. Loop length is set by the agent host/framework; the API-side constraints that bind an agent loop are the concurrency limit and the requirement to echo `reasoning_content` back on every tool-carrying request.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a DeepSeek concept — DeepSeek never sees MCP servers (the `mcp` built-in is ignored), so this is set entirely by the MCP host. Host caps that do bind in practice: Cursor ~40 tools total, Claude Desktop ~100.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor-published per-request numeric cap for self-hosted weights. Effective aggregate ceiling across all connected MCP servers is approximately (context_window - output headroom) / average tool-definition tokens, set by the operator's serving config. Host layers cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Hosted API (model-API layer): 128 functions per request (aggregate), function names <=64 chars matching a-zA-Z0-9_-, concurrency 500 for deepseek-v4-pro and 2500 for deepseek-v4-flash per account across all keys (HTTP 429 above), `user_id` <=512 chars, and the server closes a connection whose inference has not started within 10 minutes. Agent-loop trap: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` MUST be passed back in full or the API returns 400 — this makes thinking-mode tool loops re-send (and re-pay for) their own chain of thought as input. Self-hosted open weights: no model-layer tool-count cap at all; binding limits are the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len, --max-num-batched-tokens, GPU KV cache), a matching --tool-call-parser for the chat template, and the host app. vLLM's common 16K default context silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: Strict function-schema mode is a hosted-API beta feature (base_url https://api.deepseek.com/beta, `strict: true` per function) and the hosted endpoints now serve the GA checkpoints, so no strict-mode guarantee attaches to these preview weights; grammar enforcement on a self-hosted deployment depends on the serving stack. (Previous entry recorded false; corrected to unknown-for-this-checkpoint.)

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension mechanism, no persistent memory, no packaged capability bundles.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System prompts are input tokens and are eligible for the disk KV cache. Agentic caveat that dominates real session cost: for any request carrying `tools`, the previous turn's `reasoning_content` must be passed back in full (400 otherwise), so a thinking-mode tool loop re-submits its own chain of thought as input on every step. Plain multi-turn chat without tools does NOT concatenate previous CoT.

prompt_caching.notes: DeepSeek's disk KV cache is a property of the hosted API, which no longer serves this checkpoint. Self-hosted, prefix caching depends on the serving framework (vLLM/SGLang automatic prefix caching). Recorded true because a cacheable static tool-definition prefix is available on every realistic deployment path, but the >97% hosted cache-hit discount is not available off the hosted API.
