detail.notes: Gemma 4 12B Unified is the newest Gemma 4 variant, shipped 2026-06-03 - three months after the rest of the family - with an encoder-free architecture that runs text, image and audio through a single decoder transformer. Apache 2.0, 256K window, native audio (ASR and translation) which the 31B and 26B A4B do not have. Google positions its quality near the 26B MoE at under half the memory, running on a 16GB-RAM laptop. Refreshed 2026-08-19: still GA, still the most recent Gemma release - the official releases page lists nothing after it. The release date in this entry was corrected from 2026-04-02 to 2026-06-03. For MCP work it is the best fit when the 31B's memory is prohibitive but a large tool footprint plus multimodal input still has to fit one window; budget for image soft tokens and audio tokens sharing that window with the templated tool declarations. MODALITIES CORRECTED 2026-08-19: video was removed; the Gemma 4 model card's per-variant Dense Models table gives the 12B Unified as 'Text, Image, Audio'. Video appears only in family-level prose about processing videos as frame sequences, which is image input, not a listed native modality.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-read config.json 2026-08-19: text_config.max_position_embeddings=131072 (= 128K), vocab_size=262144, sliding_window=512. The Gemma 4 model card and the HF card both state 128K for E4B. The prior pass's note about a suspected metadata bug is resolved - 131072 is correct and equals 128K. Unlike the 256K variants, the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe says E2B/E4B can be served up to the full 131072 default context, so here the architectural window and the practical served window usually match.

input_output_shared.notes: Decoder-only transformer; input, image soft tokens, audio tokens and generated output all share one 128K pool. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived from the context window; no separate max-input cap is published. On a 128K window the templated tool declarations plus system prompt are a materially larger fraction of the budget than on the 256K variants. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not specified in the model card, the HF card or config.json as of 2026-08-19; the default is set by the serving framework (vLLM max_tokens / Transformers max_new_tokens / LiteRT-LM on device).

max_output_tokens_max.notes: No numeric output cap is published; the ceiling is the served window minus input length, chosen by the operator. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

extended_context.notes: No extended, beta or RoPE-scaled context beyond the native 128K is documented for E4B. Re-checked the Gemma 4 model card 2026-08-19.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Re-read the thinking guide 2026-08-19: google/gemma-4-E4B-it is named among the variants supporting thinking, enabled with apply_chat_template(enable_thinking=True) and disabled by removing the <|think|> token. The guide describes the <|channel>thought ... <channel|> delimited form for the larger models; the prior pass's claim that E2B/E4B can disable thinking fully while larger models still emit empty thought blocks was not restated on the page as opened on 2026-08-19, so treat that detail as unconfirmed. Reasoning tokens are generated and occupy the output side of the shared window; self-hosted, so they cost compute. Medium confidence.

tokenizer_family.notes: Re-read config.json 2026-08-19: vocab_size=262144, identical to every other Gemma 4 variant, so text token counts are portable across the family. The Gemma 4 technical report describes a SentencePiece tokenizer with split digits, preserved whitespace and byte-level encodings over a 262k-entry vocabulary. Per-Layer Embeddings make E4B parameter-efficient but do not change text tokenization.

tokenizer_public.notes: Tokenizer files ship with the weights on Hugging Face and Kaggle under Apache 2.0; no licence gate. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoProcessor / AutoTokenizer (latest Transformers; >=5.10.1 required for function calling)
tokenizer_access.notes: Changed 2026-08-19. The HF card no longer pins a floor version - it says Gemma 4 works with the latest Transformers and uses AutoProcessor plus AutoModelForMultimodalLM - while the function-calling guide pins transformers>=5.10.1. The old >=5.5.0 figure is stale for any tool-calling workload.

count_tokens_method.value: HF Transformers AutoProcessor / AutoTokenizer encode()
count_tokens_method.notes: Exact counts locally once the tokenizer is downloaded; no hosted count-tokens endpoint exists for Gemma. To count a tool footprint faithfully, tokenize the output of apply_chat_template(messages, tools=[...]) rather than the raw JSON schemas. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

image_token_rule.value: Variable token budget: 70, 140, 280, 560, or 1120 tokens per image; default 280
image_token_rule.notes: Re-confirmed 2026-08-19 from config.json (vision_soft_tokens_per_image=280) and the Gemma 4 model card (selectable 70, 140, 280, 560, 1120). Same budget mechanism as the larger variants, but on a 128K window a 1120-token image budget is a much bigger bite - prefer 70-280 for on-device agent loops.

audio_token_rule.value: Dedicated audio encoder (12 layers, hidden_size 1024); audio input capped at 30 seconds; no tokens-per-second or samples-per-token figure published
audio_token_rule.notes: Corrected 2026-08-19. Re-reading E4B config.json shows the audio_config has NO audio_samples_per_token key - the prior value named one, which was wrong; that key exists on the 12B Unified (=640), not here. What E4B's config.json does carry is a dedicated audio encoder (num_hidden_layers=12, hidden_size=1024, num_attention_heads=8, attention_chunk_size=12, conv_kernel_size=5), unlike the 12B's encoder-free projection. The 30-second audio cap comes from the Gemma 4 model card. No audio-to-token conversion ratio is published for E4B, so audio context cost cannot be estimated from documentation alone - measure it with the processor.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Estimate, not a vendor-published figure: same 262K-entry SentencePiece tokenizer as the rest of the family, so the same ~4 chars/token English rule of thumb applies. Google publishes no chars-per-token ratio anywhere in the Gemma 4 docs or technical report; Tier 3, derived. Use the HF tokenizer for real counts.

function_calling.notes: Re-read 2026-08-19. Same mechanism as the rest of the family: OpenAI-style JSON function objects passed as apply_chat_template(..., tools=[...]), rewritten by the template into <|tool>declaration:...<tool|>, calls emitted as <|tool_call>call:...<tool_call|>. Requires transformers>=5.10.1. The HF card states native support for structured tool use enabling agentic workflows.

native_mcp.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: no MCP mention in the function-calling guide, the Gemma docs capability index, the E4B HF card or the Gemma 4 technical report. MCP is bridged in the agent host on top of an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; on-device (LiteRT-LM) deployments have no such endpoint by default, so the bridge has to be supplied by the app.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19 from true (medium) to null. The cited tier-1 page was re-opened in this pass and makes NO statement about parallel, simultaneous or multiple-per-turn tool calling -- the previous boolean was inferred from the fact that the guide's `tool_responses` example is a list, which is an inference about response formatting, not a documented model capability. Also re-read 2026-08-19 with the same result: the Gemma 4 prompt-formatting page and the Gemma 4 model card. The only explicit statement found anywhere is tier 4 and empirical -- a practitioner guide (https://lushbinary.com/blog/build-ai-agent-gemma-4-function-calling-mcp-tool-use/, re-opened 2026-08-19) says 'Gemma 4 can generate multiple tool calls in a single turn, but reliability decreases with more than 3 parallel calls' -- which is not a tier-1 source for a capability boolean, so the value stays null rather than being recorded as a vendor-supported feature. In practice the serving parser decides: vLLM ships --tool-call-parser gemma4, which has open issues about control-token leakage in streamed tool_calls. Same tool-calling format across the family, so the same absence of evidence applies; expect the smallest variant to be the least reliable at emitting several well-formed calls at once.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool cap is documented, and no vendor-operated API exists to enforce one. The limits that DO bind on E4B: the 128K aggregate context budget consumed by templated declarations, the served --max-model-len (the vLLM recipe allows E2B/E4B up to the full 131072), the ~10-tool practitioner selection cliff for a model this size, and any host cap. Scope: aggregate; there is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

max_tools_practical.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19 (10 -> 15, and the same value is now used for all three variants). The cited practitioner guide was re-opened in this pass; the ONLY figure it gives is a single family-wide band: 'Keep tool definitions under 10-15 for best accuracy. More tools = more confusion about which to call.' It gives no per-variant numbers, so the previous 15/12/10 ranking across 31B/12B/E4B was invented by interpolation (12 appears nowhere in the source) and has been removed. This entry now carries the top of the band the source actually states; the conservative reading of the same sentence is 10, so treat 10-15 as the usable range and 15 as an optimistic ceiling. EMPIRICAL, NOT SPEC (tier 4, low confidence): Google publishes no tool-count-versus-accuracy benchmark, the Gemma 4 technical report contains no such experiment, the Gemma 4 function-calling guide and prompt-formatting page (both re-read 2026-08-19) state no tool-count limit, and the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard carries no Gemma-4 tool-count curve. Scope: AGGREGATE tools visible in one request, not per MCP server. Variant-specific context: a Tier-4 on-device tool-calling comparison (updated 2026-08-07) reports E4B in the mid-to-high 80s on BFCL v4 composite and evaluates it on a 5-tool customer-support set -- practitioners exercise the smallest variant at single-digit tool counts, so the bottom of the band (10) is the safer planning number here even though the recorded value is the band's top.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Same two-stage shape as the rest of the family: OpenAI-style JSON in, Gemma control tokens (<|tool>declaration:...<tool|>, string values wrapped in <|"|>) after templating. Count tokens on the templated form, not the raw JSON - the difference matters most here, where the window is 128K. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Structural rather than an explicit doc statement: the guide never uses the phrase input tokens, but it shows declarations being written into the prompt string by apply_chat_template, and Gemma offers no side channel for tool schemas, so they are unavoidably prompt tokens. Per-declaration cost scales with name, description and parameter-schema length, measured on the templated form. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

tool_search_deferral.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: the Gemma docs capability index lists no deferred or searchable tool-loading feature. The whole tool set is paid for on every request.

max_tool_name_len.notes: Searched the Gemma 4 function-calling guide, the model card, the HF card and the Gemma 4 technical report on 2026-08-19: no character limit, no token limit and no name-pattern rule for tool names is published. Long MCP-namespaced names are therefore accepted but cost more input tokens, and the guide's own caution applies - the model picks by name and description, so near-identical names hurt selection accuracy. Scope: per-tool.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: no property-count, nesting-depth, enum-size or unsupported-keyword rule is published for any Gemma 4 variant, so nothing rejects a bad schema - errors surface as wrong tool calls. Practical guidance for this variant specifically: keep schemas minimal and descriptions terse, since every declaration is templated into a 128K window and a 4.5B-effective-parameter model is the family's weakest tool selector. Prefer hand-written JSON schemas over auto-generated ones for nested parameters.

max_tool_description_len.notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: the Gemma 4 function-calling guide documents no character or token cap on a tool description. The limits that bind are the context window and the serving stack's --max-model-len; a longer description simply costs more input tokens. Scope: per-tool.

max_request_size.notes: No request-byte cap is published, because there is no vendor-operated Gemma inference API. The ceilings that bind are the serving stack's --max-model-len (the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe says the default context length can be very large and to set --max-model-len to match the workload) and GPU/KV-cache memory. Scope: aggregate - the whole serialized request, including every connected server's tool declarations. Source URL changed from the generic vLLM tool-calling page, which does not cover Gemma, to the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe, which does.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No numeric cap on a single tool result is documented. A result is inserted into the prompt as a tool_responses entry by the chat template, so it is bounded by the served --max-model-len and by the remaining context budget. Scope: per-tool-call, but it consumes the aggregate context budget.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No numeric cap documented. The guide shows tool_responses as a list, so several calls can be answered in one turn; how many the model may emit at once is governed by the chat template and the serving-side parser (vLLM --tool-call-parser gemma4), not by a published limit. Scope: per-turn.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model-level cycle cap is documented; the agent host decides how many tool-call/result cycles to run. Note the thinking guide's constraint that thoughts must NOT be stripped between function calls inside a turn, which makes every extra cycle cost more context. Scope: per-session, host layer.

max_connected_servers.notes: Host-layer concern. Gemma ships no first-party client, so no number exists at the model layer; whatever host wraps the OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint sets it (Cursor ~40 tools aggregate, Claude Desktop ~100). Scope: aggregate across all connected servers.

max_total_tools.notes: No numeric cap is published at any Gemma layer. The binding aggregate ceiling is approximately (served --max-model-len minus output/thinking headroom) divided by average tool-declaration tokens. Important: the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe recommends --max-model-len 8192-32768 for the 31B and 26B A4B variants and up to 131072 for E2B/E4B, so the served window - not the model's native 256K - is usually what binds in practice. Client hosts cap lower again (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). Scope: aggregate (all connected servers plus built-in tools in one request).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open-weight: no per-request numeric tool cap is published at the model layer, because there is no vendor-operated inference API. The limits that DO bind, smallest first: (1) the serving stack - the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe (opened 2026-08-19) requires --tool-call-parser gemma4, --reasoning-parser gemma4 and --chat-template examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja, and recommends --max-model-len 8192-32768 for the 31B/26B A4B variants (up to 131072 for E2B/E4B), so the served window rather than the native 256K is normally the real aggregate ceiling; (2) the aggregate context budget - every tool declaration is serialized into the prompt, so tool defs, system prompt, history and thinking output all compete for one window; (3) the ~10-15-tool practitioner selection cliff for Gemma-class open models (Tier 4, see max_tools_practical); (4) the agent host (Cursor ~40 tools aggregate, Claude Desktop ~100). Serving-side defects to watch: the gemma4 tool parser has open vLLM issues about raw control tokens leaking into streamed tool_calls and pad tokens appearing under concurrency.

strict_function_schema.notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: the Gemma 4 function-calling guide documents no strict-schema mode and no property-count, nesting-depth or unsupported-keyword rules. Tools are authored as OpenAI-style JSON function objects and passed via apply_chat_template(tools=...); the chat template then serializes them into Gemma's <|tool>declaration:...<tool|> control-token form. Schema conformance is therefore a prompting property, not an API-enforced contract - malformed or over-deep schemas degrade silently instead of being rejected.

skills_supported.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 against the Gemma docs capability index: no skills or packaged-capability mechanism exists. Instruction customization is system prompt, retrieval or fine-tuning, all of which are ordinary input tokens.

skills_loading_model.notes: No skills mechanism exists, so there is nothing to load eagerly or progressively. Re-verified 2026-08-19.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: Native system instructions (called out in the Gemma 4 launch post alongside function calling and structured JSON output). System-prompt tokens are ordinary input tokens; no fixed overhead figure is published beyond the chat-template control tokens. Re-checked 2026-08-19. On a 128K window the system prompt plus templated tool declarations are roughly twice the share of the budget they take on the 256K variants, and retained thinking blocks (which must not be stripped between function calls inside a turn) add to that.

prompt_caching.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: no vendor-managed prompt caching. Operator KV/prefix caching via vLLM, Ollama or llama.cpp is the substitute; on a 128K window with an on-device deployment it matters more, because the tool-declaration prefix is a larger fraction of the budget.

memory_feature.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: no memory feature in the Gemma docs capability index. Any persistence is operator-built and costs ordinary input tokens.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Re-checked 2026-08-19: Google publishes no per-token price for Gemma weights and sells no Gemma inference product. Cost is the operator's or the device's compute. E4B specifically targets on-device execution (laptops and high-end phones per the HF card, LiteRT-LM for mobile), where the marginal token cost is battery and latency rather than dollars.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: No vendor output price exists; self-hosted or on-device compute. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input price exists because there is no vendor billing surface. KV/prefix cache reuse cuts prefill work for a repeated tool-declaration prefix but is not metered. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

batch_discount.notes: No vendor batch discount exists. Batching matters little for the single-user on-device deployments this variant targets. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

billing_unit.notes: Billing unit is operator or device compute, not tokens. Re-checked 2026-08-19 against the HF model card, which distributes weights under Apache 2.0 with no pricing attached.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Self-hosted or on-device, so no separate multimodal line item: image soft tokens (default 280, selectable 70/140/280/560/1120) and audio tokens are ordinary input tokens against the 128K window and against prefill compute; audio input is capped at 30 seconds and video at 60 seconds per the model card. The 2.5GB mobile / 4.5GB Q4_0 memory figures are carried over from the prior pass and were not restated on the pages opened 2026-08-19 - treat as indicative.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: No billing category exists for reasoning tokens because there is no vendor billing surface. Thinking blocks are generated tokens: they add decode time and occupy the output side of the shared 128K window - the most visible cost on an edge device. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

release_date.notes: Re-confirmed 2026-08-19: E4B was one of the four variants in the 2026-04-02 Gemma 4 launch post (E2B, E4B, 26B MoE, 31B Dense). Still GA; no successor as of 2026-08-19.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Model card states a training-data cutoff of January 2025; the Gemma 4 technical report gives the same cutoff and confirms audio data was included in E2B, E4B and 12B training.

license.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 on the HF card and the Gemma 4 model card: Apache 2.0, same as every Gemma 4 model. OSI-approved; commercial use and redistribution permitted.

param_variants.value: 4.5B effective / 8B total (with Per-Layer Embeddings); also E2B sibling in family
param_variants.notes: Re-confirmed 2026-08-19 from the Gemma 4 model card: E4B is 4.5B effective / 8B with embeddings; the E2B sibling is 2.3B effective / 5.1B with embeddings. The E prefix denotes Per-Layer Embeddings - large embedding tables used only for lookup, so effective compute parameters are far below the on-disk count. E4B also received a Multi-Token-Prediction drafter in the 2026-04-16 MTP release (alongside E2B, 31B and 26B A4B), a decoding-speed feature that does not change token accounting. The ~4.5GB QAT Q4_0 figure is carried over from the prior pass and was not restated on the pages opened 2026-08-19.

native_context_config.notes: Re-read config.json 2026-08-19: text_config.max_position_embeddings=131072 (= 128K), vocab_size=262144, sliding_window=512, vision_soft_tokens_per_image=280, plus a dedicated audio_config (12 layers, hidden_size 1024). Sliding-window attention of 512 tokens with periodic global layers; the every-6-layers detail is carried over from the prior pass and was not restated on the config as read on 2026-08-19.

max_context_documented.notes: Documented as 128K on the Gemma 4 model card and the HF card; no extended or RoPE-scaled mode beyond it. Re-checked 2026-08-19. Unlike the 256K variants, the vLLM Gemma 4 recipe says E2B/E4B can be served at up to the full 131072, so the documented maximum is realistically attainable here.

serving_frameworks.value: vLLM (with the gemma4 tool/reasoning parsers), HuggingFace Transformers (latest; >=5.10.1 for function calling), llama.cpp (GGUF), Ollama, LM Studio, LiteRT-LM (mobile), MLX, MediaPipe
serving_frameworks.notes: Updated 2026-08-19. The HF card describes E4B as designed for efficient local execution on laptops and mobile devices, including high-end phones; Google also documents Gemma 4 on AI Edge / LiteRT-LM. The vLLM Gemma 4 recipe allows serving E2B/E4B at up to --max-model-len 131072, unlike the 8192-32768 it suggests for the larger variants. The transformers floor moved: the HF card now says use the latest Transformers, while the function-calling guide pins >=5.10.1. The 2.5GB / 2.2GB mobile and ~17.9GB BF16 / ~4.5GB Q4_0 memory figures are carried over from the prior pass and were not restated on the pages opened 2026-08-19 - treat as indicative.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Rechecked 2026-08-19. Same family tool-calling path: serve with vLLM using --tool-call-parser gemma4, --reasoning-parser gemma4 and --chat-template examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja, or tool calls come back as raw control tokens; known open vLLM defects against that parser are control-token leakage into streamed tool_calls and pad tokens under concurrency. Multimodal input needs AutoModelForMultimodalLM plus AutoProcessor. For tool-heavy MCP work prefer the 31B or 12B - E4B targets on-device scenarios where large tool sets are impractical, and on LiteRT-LM there is no OpenAI-compatible endpoint at all, so any MCP bridge must be built into the host app.

detail.notes: Gemma 4 E4B is the smaller of the two edge variants (E2B is smaller still and is not in this roster), launched 2026-04-02 under Apache 2.0. 4.5B effective / 8B with embeddings via Per-Layer Embeddings, 128K window, and 'Text, Image, Audio' as the model card's per-variant input modalities (video only in the sense that frame sequences are image input). Refreshed 2026-08-19: still GA, no successor. For MCP footprint work the 128K window is adequate for small-to-medium servers and is realistically attainable (the vLLM recipe allows serving E2B/E4B at the full 131072, unlike the larger variants), so the binding limit here is tool-selection accuracy, not context. Corrections: an earlier pass added video to modalities - that was a regression and was reverted on 2026-08-19, because the model card's per-variant Dense Models table reads 'Text, Image, Audio' for E4B and video appears only in family-level prose about processing videos as frames; and the audio token rule no longer claims an audio_samples_per_token key - E4B's config.json has none, only a dedicated 12-layer audio encoder, so audio context cost must be measured rather than derived from docs.

models.tokenizer_family: tiktoken BPE (O200K pattern, ~200K base tokens + 2,048 special tokens)
models.tool_definition_shape: llama4_pythonic (Llama 4 chat-template tool syntax); OpenAI function JSON when served behind a vLLM/SGLang OpenAI-compatible endpoint

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified: the Scout model card still states 'Context length: 10M' for the Instruct model (base pretrain 256K). 10,485,760 = 10 x 1024^2, the config.json max_position_embeddings value; config.json itself is behind the gated-repo login (HTTP 401) so the numeric expansion is derived from the card's '10M'. Reality check for the recommender: hosted endpoints cap far lower - Groq serves Scout at 128K and OpenRouter advertises 1,310,720 - so 10M is a self-hosted, multi-node ceiling, not what a caller gets by default.

input_output_shared.notes: Standard transformer: input + output draw from one shared window. The serving stack's max_model_len is the real ceiling.

max_input_tokens.notes: Derived: context_window (10,485,760) minus the 16,384 max_output observed at hosted endpoints. Meta publishes no separate max_input; when self-hosted the operator's --max-model-len is the cap. Previous source (an HF discussion thread) replaced with the model card + OpenRouter cross-check.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No vendor-published default. max_new_tokens is set by the caller or the serving framework config. Deployment-defined.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19: OpenRouter still lists max output 16,384 for Llama 4 Scout. Empirical hosted-endpoint cap, not a Meta spec - self-hosted deployments set their own limit up to max_model_len. Groq's Scout model card (tier 1 for that host) documents a 128K context window and does not publish a completion cap.

extended_context.notes: 10M IS the documented maximum for Scout Instruct; there is no separate extended mode. Reaching it needs multi-node hardware (8xH100 ~1M, 8xH200 ~3.6M in the HF release blog).

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Scout is not a reasoning model - no documented thinking mode or reasoning-token budget. The Llama 4 tokenizer reserves reasoning special tokens that standard inference does not expose.

tokenizer_family.value: tiktoken BPE (O200K pattern, ~200K base tokens + 2,048 special tokens)
tokenizer_family.notes: Re-verified: Llama 4 uses tiktoken with the O200K_PATTERN regex, ~200,000 base tokens plus 2,048 reserved special tokens. Unchanged since the previous pass.

tokenizer_public.notes: Tokenizer ships in the model repo, but the repo is GATED: config.json and tokenizer files return HTTP 401 without an accepted Llama 4 Community License. Re-checked 2026-08-19.

count_tokens_method.value: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('meta-llama/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct'); len(tok.encode(text))
count_tokens_method.notes: HF transformers v4.51.0+ required. Alternatively use the official tokenizer.py from meta-llama/llama-models. Repo is gated; HF account + license acceptance required.

image_token_rule.value: Tile-based: each image split into tiles (~560×560px); each tile encodes to 1+tile_tokens patch tokens (exact count depends on image resolution and tile count). Special tokens <|image_start|>, <|patch|>, <|image_end|>, <|tile_x_separator|>, <|tile_y_separator|> frame the image tokens.
image_token_rule.notes: Exact tokens-per-image depends on resolution and tile count; Meta publishes no tokens-per-image table. The Scout card still states image understanding is tested 'up to 5 input images' (re-verified 2026-08-19).

audio_token_rule.notes: Re-verified: input modalities are 'Multilingual text and image' only; no audio.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: NULLED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous value (3.5) carried no source_url at all and was a tier-3 guess. Meta publishes no characters-per-token figure for Llama 4: the vendor tokenizer implementation (meta-llama/llama-models models/llama4/tokenizer.py) builds a tiktoken.Encoding from a BPE merge file with the O200K_PATTERN regex and num_reserved_special_tokens = 2048, and states no ratio (its only character constants are encoding guards, TIKTOKEN_MAX_ENCODE_CHARS = 400_000 and MAX_NO_WHITESPACES_CHARS = 25_000). Measure with the published tokenizer instead of estimating - it is public, so a footprint number never needs a ratio here.

function_calling.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from vLLM's serving-framework doc (correctly tier 4, not a vendor spec) to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification (meta-llama/llama-models, the vendor's model repo) defines the model's complete tool contract: 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', introduced by 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:' followed by a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects, and the model answers with pythonic calls - [func_name(param1=value1, param2=value2)], e.g. [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - with an alternative <function=function_name>{"param": "value"}</function> form. It states 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively'. Zero-shot function calling is therefore a documented capability of the released weights, not just a serving-stack feature; vLLM's `llama4_pythonic` parser exists to turn that pythonic output back into OpenAI-shaped tool_calls.

native_mcp.notes: RE-SOURCED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous citation was Meta's July-2026 Muse Spark / Meta Model API launch post, which never mentions Llama 4 and whose only MCP sentence is about a different model - an unusable basis for a high-confidence false about this id. Correct tier-1 evidence: Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification (meta-llama/llama-models, the vendor's model repo) defines the model's complete tool contract: 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', introduced by 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:' followed by a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects, and the model answers with pythonic calls - [func_name(param1=value1, param2=value2)], e.g. [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - with an alternative <function=function_name>{"param": "value"}</function> form. It states 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively'. That specification is the whole tool interface Meta publishes for Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct, and it contains no reference to MCP, no MCP client, transport, connector or `mcp` tool type, and no remote-MCP server parameter. The HuggingFace model card for this id likewise does not mention MCP. So the model does not implement the MCP wire protocol: an MCP host must translate `tools/list` into these JSON function definitions and place them in the prompt itself. Scope note: because the bridging happens in the host, every ceiling that applies is aggregate (all servers + built-in tools in one request), never per MCP server.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which states verbatim: 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively', and illustrates it with [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - two calls emitted in one turn. No numeric ceiling on how many calls may appear in one list is published.

max_tools_hard.notes: NULL, and DOWNGRADED from high at the 2026-08-19 remediation, where the citation also moved off vLLM's serving-framework doc (graded tier 4 below) onto Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. That spec describes the JSON function list and the pythonic call format and states no maximum number of tools; no Meta page publishes a per-request tool-count cap for Llama 4. Medium rather than high because this is an absence claim. Scope note - the limits that DO bind: (1) the context window shared by tool definitions, prompt and output, i.e. window / average tool-definition tokens; (2) the empirical ~30-50-tool selection cliff (see max_tools_practical); (3) the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len and KV cache, plus --tool-call-parser llama4_pythonic); (4) whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes. There is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap.

max_tools_practical.notes: Still no Scout-specific published degradation point after searching vendor docs, vLLM docs and aggregator pages on 2026-08-19. Community/Berkeley-FCL-style guidance of roughly 30-50 aggregate tools is the only figure in circulation and is empirical, not spec; we do not record it as a value because no source we opened states it for this model.

tool_definition_shape.value: llama4_pythonic (Llama 4 chat-template tool syntax); OpenAI function JSON when served behind a vLLM/SGLang OpenAI-compatible endpoint
tool_definition_shape.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Definitions go in as OpenAI-style JSON function objects ({name, description, parameters}) inside the system (or user) message under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'; the model REPLIES in the pythonic form [func_name(param=value)], which is why vLLM recommends the `llama4_pythonic` tool parser for Llama 4 models. Footprint note: the input side is ordinary function JSON, so OpenAI-shaped token estimates transfer; the output side is not JSON and is cheaper per call.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from a third-party HuggingFace blog post to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification: function definitions are literally written into the system (or user) message ('All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'). They are therefore ordinary prompt tokens - re-sent and re-counted on every turn of a conversation unless a prefix cache absorbs them - and they compete with the prompt for the same window.

tool_search_deferral.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which places the full catalog up front - 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message' - and documents no runtime tool-search, lazy-loading or deferred-definition mechanism (no Claude ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / defer_loading equivalent). Medium confidence: this is an absence claim over Meta's published spec, not an explicit vendor denial. Any deferral has to be implemented by the MCP host before the request, and every definition it does send is billed as input on every turn.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character-count or character-class cap on function names is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification shows names used verbatim inside the JSON definition and in the pythonic call ([get_weather(city="San Francisco")]) with no length or pattern rule, and there is no OpenAI-style 64-char pattern constraint to inherit because Meta hosts no API for these weights. Consequence for MCP: long client-namespaced tool names cost tokens rather than being rejected, and a name that is awkward inside the pythonic call format is a parser risk, not an API error.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No published per-tool schema size, property-count or nesting-depth limits. The effective limit is context-window consumption: tool JSON is serialized into the prompt and counted as input tokens.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No numeric ceiling on description length is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification includes `description` in each JSON function object with no length rule. The description is serialized into the system message and counts against the shared context window - that budget is the only ceiling.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (open weights, no Meta API layer). Bounded by the serving config (vLLM --max-model-len / --max-num-batched-tokens) and GPU memory. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19: this citation is vLLM's own tool-calling documentation - a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec - so it is tier 4, not tier 2. It documents no numeric ceiling on request payload size. No Meta page publishes one either; for self-hosted weights the real ceiling is the operator's serving config and the context window.

max_tool_result_size.notes: Context-bound: tool results are appended to the prompt and count against max_model_len. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19: this citation is vLLM's own tool-calling documentation - a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec - so it is tier 4, not tier 2. It documents no numeric ceiling on a single tool result. No Meta page publishes one either; for self-hosted weights the real ceiling is the operator's serving config and the context window.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: No numeric ceiling on how many calls may be emitted in one turn is published. Meta's prompt-format specification says only that 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively' and shows a two-call example; the practical bound is the remaining output budget and the tool parser's ability to split the list.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model-level cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn is documented for Llama 4. Meta's own prompt-format specification defines the entire tool contract - the JSON function list in the system or user message and the pythonic [func_name(param=value)] reply - and says nothing about how many call/result cycles a turn may contain, and Meta hosts no API for these weights that could enforce one. Also searched the HuggingFace model card: it states no such number either. This is a host-layer property - the agent framework or MCP host decides when to stop looping - and what actually stops a long loop here is the context window filling with tool results.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model-layer limit and not documented anywhere by Meta. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification - the complete published tool contract for these weights - never mentions MCP at all, and neither does the HuggingFace model card, so there is no vendor cap on connected MCP servers to record. Connected-server caps live in the host application (Claude Desktop, Cursor, an in-house agent) and Llama 4 open weights have no first-party host. What binds instead is the aggregate tool count and token footprint that all connected servers add up to inside the context window.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor cap. Aggregate ceiling ~ (context_window - output headroom) / avg tool-definition tokens, set by the serving config. Host apps cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). RE-GRADED 2026-08-19: this citation is vLLM's own tool-calling documentation - a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec - so it is tier 4, not tier 2. It documents no numeric ceiling on the aggregate tool count. No Meta page publishes one either; for self-hosted weights the real ceiling is the operator's serving config and the context window.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open weights: there is no Meta API layer, so no tool count/name/size cap is enforced at the model API. Binding limits, in the order they usually bite: (1) the host app's aggregate tool budget (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100); (2) the serving stack - vLLM/SGLang max_model_len (default is often 16K, which silently truncates tool calls mid-generation - raise it), max_num_batched_tokens, KV-cache/GPU memory; (3) the hosted endpoint's own context cap (Groq serves Scout at 128K, OpenRouter at 1,310,720 - both far below Meta's documented 10M); (4) the ~30-50-tool aggregate selection cliff; (5) parser mismatch - tool calling requires --tool-call-parser llama4_pythonic and the matching chat template, and vLLM issue #46863 reports Llama-4 tool calls being left in content when a JSON parser is used instead.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (no enforced 100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf contract). Schema fidelity depends entirely on the chat template and the tool-call parser. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19 to tier 4 (vLLM's own serving-framework documentation, not a vendor spec). For completeness: vLLM does expose a `strict` field on tool definitions ('For tool_choice="auto", setting strict: true on at least one tool opts in to structural-tag constraints'), but that is a vLLM feature, not a Llama 4 model contract - Meta publishes no OpenAI-style strict structured-function mode (100-property / 5-level / no-oneOf enforcement) for these weights.

skills_loading_model.notes: No skill loading mechanism exists for Llama 4.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System-prompt tokens count as input against the shared window. Meta ships a recommended system prompt (~170 tokens in the model-card example). There is no platform-injected overhead - the operator controls the entire prompt, including the tool-definition block.

prompt_caching.notes: Prefix/KV caching is a serving-stack capability (vLLM prefix caching, SGLang RadixAttention), not model-native, and carries no billed discount because there is no vendor billing. It does cut recompute for a repeated system prompt + tool-definition prefix, which is the dominant cost for tool-heavy MCP sessions.

detail.notes: Scout is the long-context member of the Llama 4 herd and is still available and undeprecated as of 2026-08-19, but it is now a PREVIOUS-GENERATION model: Meta's 2026 frontier work moved to the Muse family (closed-weight Muse Spark from 2026-04-08, open-weight Muse Glimmer 30B from 2026-08-10), and Meta has shipped no new Llama model since 2025-04-05. The headline 10M window is architectural (iRoPE) and rarely available in practice - Groq serves Scout at 128K and OpenRouter at 1,310,720 - so size an MCP tool budget against the endpoint you actually use, not against 10M. Tool calling via vLLM is production-ready with parallel calls; MCP is bridged by the serving/agent layer, never by the model.

function_calling.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from vLLM's serving-framework doc (correctly tier 4, not a vendor spec) to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification (meta-llama/llama-models, the vendor's model repo) defines the model's complete tool contract: 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', introduced by 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:' followed by a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects, and the model answers with pythonic calls - [func_name(param1=value1, param2=value2)], e.g. [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - with an alternative <function=function_name>{"param": "value"}</function> form. It states 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively'. Zero-shot function calling is therefore a documented capability of the released weights, not just a serving-stack feature; vLLM's `llama4_pythonic` parser exists to turn that pythonic output back into OpenAI-shaped tool_calls.

native_mcp.notes: RE-SOURCED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous citation was Meta's July-2026 Muse Spark / Meta Model API launch post, which never mentions Llama 4 and whose only MCP sentence is about a different model - an unusable basis for a high-confidence false about this id. Correct tier-1 evidence: Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification (meta-llama/llama-models, the vendor's model repo) defines the model's complete tool contract: 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', introduced by 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:' followed by a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects, and the model answers with pythonic calls - [func_name(param1=value1, param2=value2)], e.g. [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - with an alternative <function=function_name>{"param": "value"}</function> form. It states 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively'. That specification is the whole tool interface Meta publishes for Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct, and it contains no reference to MCP, no MCP client, transport, connector or `mcp` tool type, and no remote-MCP server parameter. The HuggingFace model card for this id likewise does not mention MCP. So the model does not implement the MCP wire protocol: an MCP host must translate `tools/list` into these JSON function definitions and place them in the prompt itself. Scope note: because the bridging happens in the host, every ceiling that applies is aggregate (all servers + built-in tools in one request), never per MCP server.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which states verbatim: 'The output supports multiple, and parallel tool calls natively', and illustrates it with [get_weather(city="San Francisco"), get_weather(city="Seattle")] - two calls emitted in one turn. No numeric ceiling on how many calls may appear in one list is published.

max_tools_hard.notes: NULL, and DOWNGRADED from high at the 2026-08-19 remediation, where the citation also moved off vLLM's serving-framework doc (graded tier 4 below) onto Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. That spec describes the JSON function list and the pythonic call format and states no maximum number of tools; no Meta page publishes a per-request tool-count cap for Llama 4. Medium rather than high because this is an absence claim. Scope note - the limits that DO bind: (1) the context window shared by tool definitions, prompt and output, i.e. window / average tool-definition tokens; (2) the empirical ~30-50-tool selection cliff (see max_tools_practical); (3) the serving stack (vLLM/SGLang --max-model-len and KV cache, plus --tool-call-parser llama4_pythonic); (4) whatever aggregate cap the MCP host imposes. There is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap.

tool_definition_shape.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification. Definitions go in as OpenAI-style JSON function objects ({name, description, parameters}) inside the system (or user) message under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'; the model REPLIES in the pythonic form [func_name(param=value)], which is why vLLM recommends the `llama4_pythonic` tool parser for Llama 4 models. Footprint note: the input side is ordinary function JSON, so OpenAI-shaped token estimates transfer; the output side is not JSON and is cheaper per call.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 from a third-party HuggingFace blog post to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification: function definitions are literally written into the system (or user) message ('All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message', under 'Here is a list of functions in JSON format that you can invoke:'). They are therefore ordinary prompt tokens - re-sent and re-counted on every turn of a conversation unless a prefix cache absorbs them - and they compete with the prompt for the same window.

tool_search_deferral.notes: RE-SOURCED 2026-08-19 to Meta's own Llama 4 prompt-format specification, which places the full catalog up front - 'All available functions can be provided either in the system message or in the user message' - and documents no runtime tool-search, lazy-loading or deferred-definition mechanism (no Claude ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH / defer_loading equivalent). Medium confidence: this is an absence claim over Meta's published spec, not an explicit vendor denial. Any deferral has to be implemented by the MCP host before the request, and every definition it does send is billed as input on every turn.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No character-count or character-class cap on function names is published for Llama 4. Meta's prompt-format specification shows names used verbatim inside the JSON definition and in the pythonic call ([get_weather(city="San Francisco")]) with no length or pattern rule, and there is no OpenAI-style 64-char pattern constraint to inherit because Meta hosts no API for these weights. Consequence for MCP: long client-namespaced tool names cost tokens rather than being rejected, and a name that is awkward inside the pythonic call format is a parser risk, not an API error.
