models.tokenizer_family: BPE, 202,048-token vocabulary (200,000 base BPE tokens + 2,048 special tokens)
models.tool_definition_shape: ATEM XML blocks (<atem:function_calls> / <atem:invoke> / <atem:parameter>) inside a channel-scoped chat template; OpenAI function JSON at the wire when served via vLLM with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer

context_window_tokens.notes: config.json (ungated, Apache-2.0 repo) gives text_config.max_position_embeddings = 131072; the model card states 'Context length: 131,072+'. Input and output share this single window. This is a normal-sized window by 2026 standards, so tool-definition footprint matters far more here than it did on Llama 4 Scout's nominal 10M.

input_output_shared.notes: Dense causal transformer with a single positional budget (max_position_embeddings 131072); prompt, tool definitions, reasoning channel and answer all draw from the same pool.

max_input_tokens.notes: Meta documents no separate max_input. The operative cap is the serving stack's --max-model-len, which the official vLLM recipe sets to 131072 (the full trained context) for prompt + completion combined. Cannot be derived because no max_output figure is published.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No vendor default. The model card's generation example uses max_new_tokens=40, which is illustrative only, not a default.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not documented by Meta. Deployment-defined: completion length is bounded by --max-model-len (131072 in the official vLLM recipe) minus the prompt. Note that with a reasoning channel enabled, thinking tokens consume this same budget.

extended_context.notes: Empirical, not spec: Unsloth's model documentation reports the 131,072-token default context is extendable to 262,144 in local runtimes via RoPE extension. Meta documents only '131,072+' and publishes no rope_scaling block in config.json, so treat 256K as an unsupported community extension and expect degradation.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Derived from serving behaviour, not a billing statement (open weights, no vendor billing). Muse Glimmer emits a channel-scoped reasoning stream (`to=self`) that vLLM requires --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer to separate; those are generated tokens occupying the same 131,072-token window, so they consume the output budget and the context budget exactly like answer tokens. Reasoning strength is selected in the system prompt (low / medium / high / xhigh), so an operator can trade reasoning tokens against tool-definition headroom.

tokenizer_family.value: BPE, 202,048-token vocabulary (200,000 base BPE tokens + 2,048 special tokens)
tokenizer_family.notes: config.json gives vocab_size = 202048; the model card describes it as 200,000 BPE tokens plus 2,048 special tokens - the same 200K-class vocabulary size as the Llama 4 family tokenizer. Meta publishes no separate tokenizer reference document for Muse Glimmer; the tokenizer files ship in the (ungated) model repo.

tokenizer_public.notes: Apache-2.0, UNGATED repository - unlike the Llama 4 repos, config.json and tokenizer files are readable anonymously (verified 2026-08-19). The official GGUFs additionally embed the chat template.

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer ('meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B'); chat template also embedded in the official GGUFs (llama.cpp --jinja)
tokenizer_access.notes: Meta ships first-party GGUF K-quants with the chat template embedded, so llama.cpp/Ollama users get correct tool-call framing when run with --jinja.

count_tokens_method.value: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B'); len(tok.encode(text))
count_tokens_method.notes: Standard HF path; no licence gate to accept. For MCP footprint work, tokenize the FULL serialized ATEM tool-definition block, not the bare JSON schema - the channel-scoped template adds framing tokens.

image_token_rule.value: Up to 4,096 visual tokens per image via the ~1.8B ViT-G/14 perception encoder
image_token_rule.notes: The model card states a 4,096 maximum visual-token budget per image. At 131,072 total context, a single max-resolution image consumes ~3.1% of the window - material when budgeting alongside tool definitions. Output is text only.

audio_token_rule.notes: No audio support: input modalities are text + images, output is text only.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: NULLED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous value (3.5) carried no source_url and was an unsourced tier-3 estimate for a '200K-class BPE vocabulary'. The model card publishes no characters-per-token figure. The tokenizer ships in the public, ungated Apache-2.0 repository, so measure it with the real tokenizer - with a 131,072-token window a wrong ratio misprices an MCP tool surface badly, and there is no reason to estimate here.

function_calling.notes: Model card: 'Reliable Tool Use. The model handles a wide range of function calls, invoking tools with precise schemas throughout extended workflows.' Tool use is the model's headline capability - it is explicitly benchmarked on MCP-Atlas, tau3-Bench, DeepSearch QA and SWE-Bench.

native_mcp.notes: RE-SOURCED at the 2026-08-19 remediation. The previous citation was the meta-oss-cookbook agentic-fundamentals README, which documents the ATEM XML tool-block format and contains no MCP content at all. Correct tier-1 evidence is the model's own HuggingFace card, and it is what sets this value: the card reports an MCP-Atlas (Public) score of 75.5 (vs Gemma4-31B 54.2, Qwen3.6-27B 62.5), describes 'reliable tool use' handling 'a wide range of function calls, invoking tools with precise schemas throughout extended workflows', and under Scaffold Compatibility says 'Muse Glimmer works across OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and other agentic orchestration patterns'. That is a benchmark score on tasks whose tools come from MCP servers plus compatibility with external agent scaffolds - NOT an in-model MCP client: the card documents no MCP transport, connector or request parameter, and the model emits ATEM blocks (<atem:function_calls> / <atem:invoke> / <atem:parameter>), not MCP messages. Medium confidence because the card never explicitly denies MCP; it simply never documents one. Practical reading: this model is unusually good at MCP-sourced tool tasks, but the MCP client always lives in the host, so every ceiling is aggregate and the ATEM shape - not MCP JSON - is what the tokens are spent on.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Meta's own OSS cookbook shows multiple <atem:invoke> elements inside a single <atem:function_calls> block, and warns that stopping generation on <|eom|> instead of the correct stop set [<|eot|>, <|end_of_text|>] 'collapses' multi-tool turns - i.e. parallel calls are the intended behaviour.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool cap is documented, and for open weights there is no vendor API layer that could enforce one. Meta's cookbook explicitly provides 'no explicit guidance on token counting for tool definitions, maximum tool count, or schema size limits'. The limits that DO bind are all AGGREGATE across every connected server plus built-in tools: (1) the 131,072-token shared window, which tool definitions, the reasoning channel and the answer all draw from - roughly 8x tighter than Llama 4 Maverick's nominal 1M; (2) the serving stack's --max-model-len; (3) the host app's own tool budget (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100); (4) the empirical tool-selection cliff. There is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap.

max_tools_practical.notes: No Muse-Glimmer-specific degradation point has been published. Searched the model card, Meta's OSS cookbook, developer.meta.com, the vLLM recipe and enablement PR, and launch coverage on 2026-08-19: none state a tool-count cliff. The commonly cited ~30-50-tool aggregate figure is generic practitioner folklore and is not recorded as a value here. Empirical guidance, if you need one, must come from your own eval.

tool_definition_shape.value: ATEM XML blocks (<atem:function_calls> / <atem:invoke> / <atem:parameter>) inside a channel-scoped chat template; OpenAI function JSON at the wire when served via vLLM with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer
tool_definition_shape.notes: Meta's cookbook documents the format: '<atem:function_calls><atem:invoke name="get_weather"><atem:parameter name="city">Paris</atem:parameter></atem:invoke></atem:function_calls>', where scalars and strings are written as-is and lists/objects are JSON. Critically, an <atem:invoke> echoed inside a to=self reasoning block or a to=user answer is NOT a real call - the parser strips non-routed spans. Shape matters for footprint: ATEM XML framing is a different token cost from OpenAI function JSON for the same MCP tool.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tool definitions are rendered into the prompt by the chat template and are consumed as input tokens from the 131,072-token window. Meta gives no token-accounting guidance for them, so measure with the public tokenizer.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No deferred / lazy tool-definition loading in the model, the chat template or the documented serving path. Any progressive disclosure is the agent harness's job.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No documented character or token limit on tool names. Names appear as the ATEM invoke `name` attribute; MCP clients that namespace names simply spend more input tokens rather than hitting a cap.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No published per-tool schema size, property-count or nesting-depth limits - Meta's cookbook states there is no explicit guidance on schema size limits. Note one real constraint from the vLLM enablement PR: the muse_glimmer parser sets supports_required_and_named = False, so tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are NOT supported and JSON guided decoding is deliberately not applied to tool arguments. Argument fidelity therefore rests on the model, not on constrained decoding.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No vendor cap. Descriptions are prompt text and count against the 131,072-token window.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (open weights). Bounded by the serving config - the official vLLM recipe uses --max-model-len 131072 with --max-num-seqs 64 - and by KV-cache/GPU memory. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19 to tier 4: the vLLM recipe is a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec. It documents serving this model at --max-model-len 131072 with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer and --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer, and documents no numeric ceiling on request payload size; its only size warning is that 'a tight budget can truncate before the final channel closes, returning empty content with finish_reason: stop'.

max_tool_result_size.notes: Context-bound: tool results are appended to the prompt and count against --max-model-len. With a 131,072-token window this is a real constraint - one chatty MCP tool result can crowd out the tool catalogue. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19 to tier 4: the vLLM recipe is a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec. It documents serving this model at --max-model-len 131072 with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer and --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer, and documents no numeric ceiling on a single tool result; its only size warning is that 'a tight budget can truncate before the final channel closes, returning empty content with finish_reason: stop'.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Multiple invokes per ATEM block are supported but no numeric ceiling is documented.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No model- or serving-level cap on tool-call/result cycles; the agent harness decides when to force an answer.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model property - set by the MCP host. Meta ships no first-party MCP client for Muse Glimmer. SOURCED 2026-08-19 to the model card, which mentions MCP only as the MCP-Atlas benchmark and names external scaffolds (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent) rather than a first-party host - so no connected-server cap exists at the model layer; it is a host-application property.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor cap. Aggregate ceiling ~ (131,072 - reasoning and answer headroom) / avg ATEM tool-definition tokens, set by the serving config. Host apps cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). RE-GRADED 2026-08-19 to tier 4: the vLLM recipe is a serving-framework doc, not a model-vendor spec. It documents serving this model at --max-model-len 131072 with --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer and --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer, and documents no numeric ceiling on the aggregate tool count; its only size warning is that 'a tight budget can truncate before the final channel closes, returning empty content with finish_reason: stop'.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open weights: no Meta API layer, so no tool count/name/size caps are enforced at the model API. Binding limits, in practice: (1) the 131,072-token aggregate window shared by tool definitions, reasoning channel and answer - much tighter than the Llama 4 pair, so tool footprint is a first-order concern again; (2) serving config - the official vLLM recipe requires vLLM 0.27.0+ and BOTH --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer AND --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer, because the model emits neither JSON tool calls nor tag-wrapped reasoning; omitting either leaves tool calls unparsed in content; (3) tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are unsupported (supports_required_and_named = False), so you cannot force a specific tool; (4) the stop set must be [<|eot|>, <|end_of_text|>] - stopping on <|eom|> collapses multi-tool turns; (5) as of 2026-08-19 the muse_glimmer parser is not yet listed in vLLM's tool_calling doc on main (enablement PR #51655 was still open), so pin a build that contains it; (6) host-app aggregate tool budgets (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

strict_function_schema.notes: The vLLM enablement PR sets supports_required_and_named = False for the muse_glimmer parser specifically to prevent JSON guided decoding being applied. There is no OpenAI-style strict schema contract (no enforced property/depth/oneOf rules) and no constrained decoding of tool arguments. RE-GRADED 2026-08-19: a vLLM pull request is tier 4 (third-party serving-framework repo), not tier 2, even though it is the enablement PR for this model.

skills_supported.notes: No skills concept for the open-weight model. Meta's only first-party skills surface is the Muse Code terminal agent's bundled skills (/plan, /grill, /goal), which is a harness feature tied to the hosted Muse Spark 1.2 model, not a Muse Glimmer capability and not a published package format.

skills_loading_model.notes: No skill loading mechanism. External frameworks that inject instruction bundles do so as ordinary prompt text.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: No native skills. Anything a framework injects (skill instructions, tool catalogues, retrieved context) is plain input tokens against the 131,072-token window, competing directly with the ATEM tool-definition block and the reasoning channel.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: System-prompt tokens count as input. Muse Glimmer takes a functional directive in the system prompt - 'Reasoning strength: <low|medium|high|xhigh>' - so the system prompt is also the reasoning-budget control: raising reasoning strength spends output/context tokens that are then unavailable to tool definitions. No platform-injected overhead; the operator owns the whole prompt.

prompt_caching.notes: Serving-stack capability, not model-native, and with no billed discount (open weights). The official vLLM recipe is a standard prefix-caching-capable deployment (it reports a 26.8M-token KV pool at 4-way tensor parallelism on GB300), so a stable system-prompt + tool-definition prefix can be reused across turns. Verify prefix caching is enabled in your own build.

memory_feature.notes: No built-in persistent memory. Long-horizon state is the harness's responsibility; the model card positions the 131,072-token window plus failure recovery as the mechanism for 'long tasks'.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Open weights under Apache-2.0 - Meta charges nothing, so no tier-1 per-token price exists. Cost is self-hosted compute. No hosted per-token price for Muse Glimmer was found on any source opened 2026-08-19.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Open weights - no vendor price. Cost is self-hosted GPU (or CPU/NPU) compute.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No vendor caching price. Serving-stack prefix caching reduces recompute but there is no billed discount.

batch_discount.notes: No vendor batch pricing. Continuous batching improves GPU utilization without any token-price concept.

billing_unit.notes: Apache-2.0 open weights - the unit of cost is self-hosted compute. Meta's own positioning is on-device/local: ~55 GB native footprint, under ~20 GB after 4-bit quantization, single consumer GPU.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Open weights / self-hosted compute. Images consume up to 4,096 visual tokens each from the same 131,072-token context window; there is no separate per-image charge.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: N/A - open weights, no vendor billing. Operationally, reasoning-channel tokens are generated tokens and consume the same window and the same generation time as answer tokens (see reasoning_tokens_count_as_output).

release_date.notes: NEW ENTRY. The official model card states only 'Model Release Date: August 2026' (tier 1). The exact day is fixed by three independent same-day sources opened 2026-08-19: the SiliconANGLE launch report dated 2026-08-10, the vLLM enablement PR #51655 dated 2026-08-10, and the Intel day-0 enablement blog on HuggingFace dated 2026-08-10.

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Official model card states a knowledge cutoff of January 4, 2026; the official GGUF repo repeats it.

weights_url.notes: UNGATED (unlike every Llama repo): no licence click-through, config.json readable anonymously. Official sibling repos: -GGUF (K-quants, chat template embedded), -assistant (DFlash speculative-decoding draft head), -ExecuTorch-PTE (on-device build).

license.notes: Confirmed on Meta's own model page and on the HuggingFace card and GGUF repo. This is a real licensing change of direction: every Llama model ships under the bespoke Llama Community License with a 700M-MAU carve-out, while Muse Glimmer is plain Apache-2.0.

param_variants.value: ~29.6B dense text decoder (52 layers, hidden 6656, GQA 32/2 heads, local/global attention with 2048 sliding window) + ~1.8B ViT-G/14 perception encoder; BF16 (~59.6 GB), FP8 block-scaled (~32.8 GB), NVFP4 W4A4 (~25.4 GB), and official GGUF K-quants (~16.8-19.7 GB)
param_variants.notes: Architecture from the model card and config.json (model_type 'muse_glimmer', architectures ['MuseGlimmerForConditionalGeneration'], 52 text layers at hidden 6656, 50-layer vision tower at hidden 1536, 4096-wide projector, bfloat16, no MoE experts). Quantized footprints from the vLLM recipe and the official GGUF repo. Distilled from the proprietary Muse Spark family.

native_context_config.notes: text_config.max_position_embeddings = 131072, read directly from the ungated config.json. No rope_scaling block is present.

max_context_documented.notes: Model card states 'Context length: 131,072+'; the official vLLM recipe calls 131072 'the full 128K trained context'. Community RoPE extension to 262,144 is reported by Unsloth but is not vendor-documented.

serving_frameworks.value: vLLM 0.27.0+ (day-0, incl. Intel GPU/Xeon), SGLang, llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio, Docker Model Runner, HF Transformers, ExecuTorch
serving_frameworks.notes: Meta's own OSS cookbook ships inference-server recipes for vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio, SGLang and llama.cpp; the vLLM recipe requires 0.27.0+; Intel published day-0 vLLM/Transformers enablement for Xe GPUs and Xeon CPUs; AMD published a Ryzen AI Max / Radeon guide. ExecuTorch PTE weights are released for on-device.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: vLLM (official recipe): `vllm serve <model> --served-model-name muse-glimmer --tensor-parallel-size 4 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 --max-model-len 131072 --max-num-seqs 64 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer --generation-config auto`. BOTH parsers are mandatory: the model emits neither JSON tool calls nor tag-wrapped reasoning, so a JSON parser leaves ATEM tool calls sitting in `content`. The parser also strips <atem:invoke> spans echoed inside to=self reasoning or to=user answers so they are not mis-executed. tool_choice='required' and named tool choice are unsupported. llama.cpp/Ollama: run the official GGUFs with --jinja so the embedded chat template frames tool calls correctly. Behind vLLM's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, MCP tool definitions serialized as OpenAI functions are translated into the ATEM block by the chat template - the model itself never sees MCP.

detail.notes: NEW 2026-08-19. Muse Glimmer 30B (released 2026-08-10) is Meta's first open-weight model since Llama 4 in April 2025, the first open-weight release from Meta Superintelligence Labs, and the first Meta model under a plain Apache-2.0 licence with an UNGATED repository - a genuine break from the Llama Community License era. It is distilled from the proprietary Muse Spark family and explicitly built for agentic tool use (benchmarked on MCP-Atlas, tau3-Bench, DeepSearch QA, SWE-Bench) while fitting on a single consumer GPU (~20 GB at 4-bit). For MCP footprint work it inverts the Llama 4 story: the window is 131,072 tokens, not 1M-10M, so tool-definition footprint, tool-result size and the reasoning channel all compete for a normal-sized budget, and the ATEM XML tool shape has a different token cost than the OpenAI function JSON most footprint tooling assumes. Two operational traps: both --tool-call-parser muse_glimmer and --reasoning-parser muse_glimmer are required, and tool_choice='required'/named tool choice are not supported.

models.tool_definition_shape: OpenAI function JSON (Meta Model API is OpenAI-SDK compatible; base URL https://api.meta.ai/v1)

context_window_tokens.notes: Meta's own Muse Spark 1.2 model page states a 1M-token context window; OpenRouter independently lists 1,048,576 (= 2^20). Meta does not publish whether input and output are separate pools, so treat 1M as the shared aggregate budget that prompt, tool definitions and completion all draw from.

input_output_shared.notes: Not documented. Meta publishes no model card for Muse Spark and no statement about whether the completion budget sits inside or outside the 1M window. Recorded null rather than assumed.

max_input_tokens.notes: Not documented separately, and cannot be derived because no max_output figure is published.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: Not documented in any source opened 2026-08-19.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Not documented. Meta publishes no completion cap and OpenRouter's Muse Spark 1.2 page lists no max-output value. This is the single most consequential gap for session sizing on this model.

extended_context.notes: No extended/beta context mode is documented beyond the 1M window.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Muse Spark 1.2 exposes configurable reasoning effort (a 'Thinking' mode is also surfaced in the Meta AI app), but Meta publishes no statement on whether reasoning tokens are billed or counted as output. Recorded null; assume they are billable output until Meta documents otherwise.

tokenizer_family.notes: Closed model - Meta publishes no tokenizer, no vocabulary size and no tokenizer documentation for the Muse Spark line. The distilled open-weight sibling Muse Glimmer 30B uses a 202,048-token BPE vocabulary (200,000 base + 2,048 special), which is suggestive of the family design but is NOT evidence for Muse Spark's tokenizer.

tokenizer_public.notes: No public tokenizer for any Muse Spark version; weights and tokenizer are proprietary.

tokenizer_access.notes: No public access and no documented count-tokens endpoint.

count_tokens_method.notes: No count-tokens API is documented in Meta's own Model API cookbook. Practical options: read the usage object returned by the OpenAI-compatible response after the fact, or approximate locally with the public Muse Glimmer 30B tokenizer (same vendor family, no guarantee of identical merges).

image_token_rule.notes: Images are an accepted input modality but Meta publishes no image-to-token conversion rule or per-image token table.

audio_token_rule.notes: Audio is an accepted input modality (OpenRouter lists text, images, video, audio and PDF inputs) but no tokens-per-second rule is documented.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: No published figure and no public tokenizer to measure against.

function_calling.notes: Meta's Model API launch post states the model 'zero-shot generalizes to new native tools, MCP servers, and custom skills' and supports parallel tool calling; Meta's own Model API cookbook ships a tool/function-calling recipe with an execute-and-feed-back loop. Function calling is the model's headline positioning ('built for agentic tasks').

native_mcp.notes: Deliberately recorded false. Meta's tier-1 wording - the model 'zero-shot generalizes to new native tools, MCP servers, and custom skills' - is a claim about generalizing to tools SOURCED FROM MCP servers, not about the API accepting an MCP server reference. No documented `mcp` tool type, remote-MCP connector or server-URL parameter appears in Meta's Model API cookbook or on any page opened 2026-08-19; the API is OpenAI-SDK compatible, so an MCP host still translates tools/list into function JSON. A tier-4 developer guide asserts MCP servers work 'out of the box', which is consistent with client-side bridging rather than protocol support. Confidence medium because Meta's own docs body is JavaScript-rendered and could not be read; if a request-level MCP connector is later documented, this flips to true.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Meta's Muse Spark 1.1 announcement explicitly lists parallel tool calling; OpenRouter lists 'parallel function calling' for 1.2 and a tier-4 developer guide reports a parallel_tool_calls parameter on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool cap is published. Meta's own Model API cookbook records no tool-count ceiling, and no such ceiling appears on any page opened 2026-08-19 (caveat: developer.meta.com and dev.meta.ai render their doc bodies client-side and could not be machine-read, so an undiscovered cap in the rendered docs cannot be ruled out - hence medium, not high). The limits that DO bind are AGGREGATE across all connected servers plus built-in tools: the 1,048,576-token window shared by tool definitions, reasoning and completion; whatever request-size and rate limits the preview enforces undocumented; and the host app's own tool budget. There is no documented per-MCP-server cap. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

max_tools_practical.notes: No published degradation point for Muse Spark. Nothing model-specific was found on 2026-08-19; the generic ~30-50-tool aggregate figure is practitioner folklore and is not recorded as a value.

tool_definition_shape.value: OpenAI function JSON (Meta Model API is OpenAI-SDK compatible; base URL https://api.meta.ai/v1)
tool_definition_shape.notes: Meta's own Model API cookbook states the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK' against https://api.meta.ai/v1, so MCP tool definitions serialized as OpenAI functions are the wire shape. Note this differs from the open-weight sibling Muse Glimmer, which uses ATEM XML - the same MCP server therefore has a different token footprint on the two models. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Not stated explicitly by Meta, but the API is OpenAI-compatible and tool definitions are part of the request body, so they are consumed as input tokens from the 1M window and billed at the input rate. Recorded medium because Meta publishes no token-accounting statement. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No tool-search / deferred tool-definition loading feature is documented for the Meta Model API. With a 1M window the pressure to defer is lower, but the input-token cost of a large catalogue is still paid on every request. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No documented tool-name length or pattern constraint.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No documented JSON-Schema constraints (property count, nesting depth, oneOf/anyOf/$ref support). OpenRouter reports structured output support for 1.2, but Meta publishes no strict-schema contract. Meta's own docs body could not be read (client-side rendered), so treat this as unverified rather than as an absence of rules.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No documented cap; descriptions are input tokens billed at the input rate.

max_request_size.notes: No documented byte cap for the Meta Model API. Multimodal inputs (video, audio, PDF) make this a real unknown for large requests. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No documented cap. Tool results are appended to the conversation and consume the 1M window and input billing. Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Parallel tool calling is supported but no numeric ceiling on simultaneous calls is documented.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: No documented cap on tool-call/result cycles per turn; in practice the agent harness decides.

max_connected_servers.notes: Not a model property. Meta's Muse Code harness connects tools/skills but publishes no server-count limit.

max_total_tools.notes: No published aggregate cap. Effective ceiling ~ (1,048,576 - reasoning and completion headroom) / avg tool-definition tokens, and in a host app whatever that app's tool budget is (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). Coverage caveat added 2026-08-19: the meta-model-cookbook repository documents muse-spark-1.1 (it states the '1,048,576-token context window; the preview is free' and that the API is 'drop-in compatible with the OpenAI SDK') and names no 1.2-specific tool limits, so this records the Meta Model API contract generally rather than a statement about this id.

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Meta Model API is a PUBLIC PREVIEW: the 1.1 launch was US-developer-only with $20 of free credits, and rate limits are not documented anywhere. Documentation quality is the dominant caveat for this entry - developer.meta.com and dev.meta.ai render their documentation bodies client-side, so the tool-calling reference page could not be machine-read; independent guides also observe the API is 'documented sparsely, with no detailed model card and no official, precise confirmation of some core specs'. Everything recorded here comes from Meta's blog posts, Meta's own GitHub cookbook, and clearly-labelled tier-3/4 cross-checks.

strict_function_schema.notes: OpenRouter reports structured-output support for Muse Spark 1.2, but no OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (enforced property/depth/oneOf rules) is documented by Meta. Recorded null rather than false because the docs could not be read.

skills_supported.notes: Qualified yes, at the HARNESS layer only. Meta's Muse Code terminal agent (powered by Muse Spark 1.2) ships 'bundled skills' - /plan for task decomposition, /grill for stress-testing plans, /goal for objective completion - and the Muse Spark 1.1 post says the model zero-shot generalizes to 'custom skills'. There is no published skill package format, no skill manifest spec, and no skills parameter on the Model API, so this is not a platform capability a third-party caller can invoke. Confidence low precisely because the mechanism is undocumented.

skills_loading_model.notes: Undocumented. Whether Muse Code's bundled skills are always-on system-prompt text or progressively disclosed is not published, so their context cost cannot be characterized.

skills_context.skills_context_cost_notes: Unquantifiable from public sources. Any skill instructions the Muse Code harness injects are ordinary input tokens billed at the input rate against the 1M window, but Meta publishes neither the skill payloads nor a token accounting for them.
skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: No documented platform-injected system-prompt overhead on the raw Model API; the caller owns the prompt. Inside the Muse Code harness the picture differs (bundled skills, an event-log runtime, background agents), and none of that overhead is published.

prompt_caching.notes: OpenRouter publishes a separate cache-read rate for Muse Spark 1.2 ($0.15/M vs $1.25/M standard input), which only exists if the endpoint supports prompt caching. Meta's own pricing/caching documentation could not be read (client-side rendered), so this is a tier-3 inference about a real feature rather than a tier-1 confirmation. For MCP sessions this matters a lot: a cached tool-definition prefix would cost roughly 12% of the uncached rate.

memory_feature.notes: Not documented for the Model API. The consumer Meta AI app has its own memory behaviour, but nothing is published about a developer-facing persistent memory feature.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: NULL BY POLICY, not by ignorance: pricing is a tier-1-required field and Meta's own pricing page renders client-side and could not be read on 2026-08-19. Consistent tier-3/4 figure across OpenRouter, LLMReference and two independent developer guides: $1.25 per 1M input tokens. Treat as the working number but do not present it as vendor-confirmed.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: NULL BY POLICY (tier-1 pricing source unreadable). Consistent tier-3/4 figure: $4.25 per 1M output tokens - a 3.4x input-to-output ratio, so completion length and reasoning effort dominate session cost.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: NULL BY POLICY (tier-1 pricing source unreadable). OpenRouter lists a cache-read rate of $0.15 per 1M tokens, i.e. ~88% off standard input - materially relevant to repeated MCP tool-definition prefixes.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-pricing tier is documented for the Meta Model API.

billing_unit.notes: Hosted, paid, closed-weight API - billing is per token, unlike every other entry in this file. Meta launched the Model API as a public preview with free credits and per-token rates thereafter.

cost.multimodal_billing_notes: Images, video, audio and PDF are accepted inputs but Meta publishes no conversion rule or per-modality rate, so multimodal session cost cannot be estimated from public sources.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Reasoning effort is configurable, but Meta does not document whether reasoning tokens are billed as output. Assume yes for budgeting until documented.

release_date.notes: NEW ENTRY. Meta AI Research announced Muse Spark 1.2 together with the Muse Code terminal agent on 2026-08-05; OpenRouter lists the same release date. Lineage: Muse Spark (2026-04-08, Meta Superintelligence Labs' first proprietary frontier model) -> Muse Spark 1.1 on the Meta Model API public preview (2026-07-09) -> Muse Spark 1.2 (2026-08-05).

knowledge_cutoff.notes: Not documented. Meta's launch posts, its model page and its own cookbook all omit a knowledge cutoff for the Muse Spark line, and independent guides note the API is documented sparsely with no detailed model card. For reference, the distilled open-weight sibling Muse Glimmer 30B carries a 2026-01-04 cutoff, but that is not evidence for Muse Spark.

weights_url.notes: CLOSED WEIGHTS. Muse Spark is Meta Superintelligence Labs' proprietary frontier line, launched 2026-04-08 as an API/product model with a private API preview; no weights have been published for any 1.x version. A tier-3 2026 retrospective reports Meta has signalled an intent to open-source Muse Spark 1.2 weights in future - unconfirmed by Meta and not treated as fact here. The distilled open-weight sibling is Muse Glimmer 30B.

license.notes: Access is via the paid Meta Model API; no weights licence exists. Contrast Muse Glimmer 30B (Apache-2.0) and Llama 4 (Llama 4 Community License).

param_variants.notes: Parameter count and architecture are not disclosed. Meta reports only that Muse Spark needs 'over an order of magnitude less compute' than Llama 4 Maverick for its results.

native_context_config.notes: Not applicable - no weights, no config.json.

max_context_documented.notes: 1M tokens per Meta's own Muse Spark 1.2 model page; 1,048,576 confirmed by OpenRouter.

serving_frameworks.notes: Not self-hostable. Hosted only, via https://api.meta.ai/v1 (OpenAI-SDK compatible) and resellers such as OpenRouter. API keys take the form LLM|{numeric_id}|{secret} per Meta's own cookbook.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Hosted OpenAI-compatible function calling at https://api.meta.ai/v1 - point an existing OpenAI SDK client at that base URL with model 'muse-spark-1.2'. MCP servers are consumed by translating tools/list into OpenAI function JSON on the client side; there is no documented request-level MCP connector. Meta's own meta-model-cookbook repository ships agentic-workflow and multi-agent recipes including a tool/function-calling execute-and-feed-back loop.

detail.notes: NEW 2026-08-19, and a deliberate scope note: this is a CLOSED-WEIGHT, hosted, paid model in a file whose provider group is 'open_weight'. It is recorded here because the dataset has no data/saas/meta.json, and omitting it would leave Meta's actual current-generation flagship - and the only Meta model with first-party MCP wording - invisible to the recommender. Consumers that filter this file by group should exclude id 'muse-spark-1.2'. Lineage: Muse Spark (2026-04-08) -> 1.1 on the Model API public preview (2026-07-09) -> 1.2 (2026-08-05, coding-optimized, powers the Muse Code terminal agent). 1M context, multimodal in (text/image/video/audio/PDF), text out, parallel function calling, configurable reasoning effort. The dominant caveat is documentation: Meta's developer docs render client-side and could not be machine-read, so max_output, knowledge cutoff, tokenizer, rate limits, request-size caps and every tool-shape limit are null, and pricing is null-by-policy with the tier-3 consensus ($1.25 in / $4.25 out / $0.15 cached per 1M) recorded in notes only. STATUS CORRECTED 2026-08-19: previously 'preview'. Neither cited Meta page calls Muse Spark 1.2 a preview - the 2026-08-05 Meta AI Research announcement states verbatim 'Muse Spark 1.2 is available today in Muse Code and in Meta Model API with expanded global access', so the model is recorded as GA. What is preview/beta is the surrounding platform, not this model: the same post calls the terminal agent 'Muse Code (beta)', and the earlier Muse Spark 1.1 launch post describes the Meta Model API itself as being 'in public preview'.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. config.json: max_position_embeddings=16384, original_max_position_embeddings=16384, rope_scaling=null, rope_theta=250000. tokenizer_config.json model_max_length=16384. Tech report: pretraining context 4,096, 'later extended to a 16K context length during midtraining'. Foundry lists input 16,384 / output 16,384.

input_output_shared.notes: Foundry (page updated 2026-07-24) shows Phi-4 input 16,384 and output 16,384 — the two numbers are the same ceiling, not two pools: prompt + completion must together fit in the 16,384-token window. Self-hosted, the serving stack enforces it via --max-model-len.

max_input_tokens.notes: Foundry documents 16,384 input tokens (unchanged 2026-08-19). Self-hosted: max_position_embeddings=16384 is the hard ceiling.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default published. The Foundry table gives only a maximum (16,384); the HF card gives none. Self-hosted via vLLM/Ollama/Transformers the operator sets max_new_tokens per request.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Foundry documents output up to 16,384 tokens (re-checked 2026-08-19). Self-hosted the ceiling is the 16K window shared with the prompt.

extended_context.notes: No extended/beta context mode documented. rope_scaling is null in config.json — no RoPE-scaling path to a longer window. The native ceiling is 16K.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Phi-4 is not a reasoning model — it emits no <think> trace and has no separate thinking-token accounting, so there is no reasoning-vs-output split to record; left null. Phi-4-reasoning and Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B are separate models where the question is live.

tokenizer_family.notes: CORRECTED 2026-08-19 (was recorded as o200k_base-derived — that was wrong). tokenizer_config.json's added_tokens_decoder places <|endoftext|>=100257, <|fim_prefix|>=100258, <|fim_middle|>=100259, <|fim_suffix|>=100260, <|endofprompt|>=100276 — exactly tiktoken's cl100k_base special-token IDs (o200k_base puts <|endoftext|> at 199999). Base vocab therefore occupies 0–100255 = cl100k_base, plus 96 Microsoft special tokens at 100256–100351 (<|im_start|>/<|im_end|>/<|im_sep|> + <|dummy_*|> padding); config.json vocab_size=100352. Tech report: 'we now use the tiktoken tokenizer … with a padded vocabulary size of 100,352'. NOTE: Phi-4-mini and Phi-4-multimodal use a DIFFERENT tokenizer (o200k_base, vocab 200,064) — do not share counts between them. For this app, the generic_cl100k profile is the right one for Phi-4.

tokenizer_public.notes: Weights and tokenizer files are public on the MIT-licensed HF repo (re-checked 2026-08-19).

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer (microsoft/phi-4) — or tiktoken cl100k_base for the base vocab, with the 96 Phi-4 special tokens (100256-100351) added on top
tokenizer_access.notes: Corrected alongside tokenizer_family: the tiktoken-side equivalent is cl100k_base, not o200k_base.

count_tokens_method.value: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('microsoft/phi-4'); len(tok.encode(text))

image_token_rule.notes: Phi-4 is text-only (model card 'Input: Text'); no image token rule.

audio_token_rule.notes: Phi-4 is text-only; no audio token rule.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Rule of thumb only: ~4 characters per token for English. Phi-4 and Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B use tiktoken cl100k_base as their base vocabulary, so OpenAI's published ~4-chars/token English heuristic applies directly. Use the HF AutoTokenizer for exact counts — never this estimate for a hard budget. (Previously recorded as 3.5 with no source; replaced with the sourced ~4 figure.)

function_calling.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. Foundry (updated 2026-07-24) still lists 'Tool calling: No' for Phi-4. The HF model card documents no function-calling format, and tokenizer_config.json contains no tool special tokens — unlike Phi-4-mini, whose vocabulary carries <|tool|>/<|tool_call|>/<|tool_response|>. Confidence stays 'medium' because this is an absence-of-documentation finding: the weights can still be prompted into emitting JSON, just without trained tool-calling behaviour.

native_mcp.notes: No MCP at the model level; MCP must be bridged by the host/serving stack (re-checked 2026-08-19).

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Undocumented, and moot: Phi-4 has no trained function-calling format at all, so there is nothing to emit in parallel.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool-count cap is documented at the model API layer — open weights have no API layer to enforce one. The limits that DO bind, in order: (1) the 16,384-token context window shared by prompt and completion — the tightest window in this roster; (2) the ~30–50-tool selection cliff reported empirically (and lower for a 14B model); (3) the host's aggregate catalog cap (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100). Scope: any cap that applies is AGGREGATE across all connected servers plus built-in tools; there is no documented per-MCP-server tool cap.

max_tools_practical.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: 5 -> null. The previous value was an interpolation. It was cited to a dev.to tool-overload post (2026-03-06) that was re-opened in this pass: its single measurement ('accuracy on correct tool selection dropped from ~95% with a focused toolset to ~71% with the full GitHub MCP server loaded', ~4 tools / ~1,200 tokens vs ~46 tools / ~42,000 tokens) was run with model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", and the post never mentions Phi. Attributing a per-Phi-variant number to a measurement of another vendor's model is not admissible, and the four Phi variants were merely ranked against each other by judgement. SEARCHED 2026-08-19 for a Phi-specific figure and found none: the four Hugging Face model cards (tier 1), the Phi-4 / Phi-4-mini technical reports, Microsoft's PhiCookBook function-calling sample (its example declares exactly one tool and gives no guidance), an on-device tool-calling comparison covering Phi-4-mini (ertas.ai, updated 2026-08-07 -- BFCL v4 composite scores and a 5-tool customer-support evaluation set, but no tool-count-vs-accuracy curve), a 2026 tool-calling benchmark round-up (presenc.ai) and a catalog-scaling study (nerdleveltech), neither of which mentions Phi. No Azure AI Foundry page states a tool count either. WHAT ACTUALLY BINDS on this variant: the 16,384-token context window (model card, tier 1: 'Context length: 16K tokens') divided by the ~200-400 tokens a typical MCP tool definition costs, minus conversation and output headroom -- the smallest budget in the open-weight roster, and the ~42,000-token GitHub MCP surface in the cited measurement does not fit in it at all. Compounding this, the phi-4 model card does not mention function calling or tool use anywhere, so there is no trained tool-calling format to rely on. Scope when a number is eventually recorded: AGGREGATE (all connected servers plus built-in tools in one request), not per server.

tool_definition_shape.notes: No native tool format exists in the Phi-4 chat template, so the shape is whatever the serving stack injects — in practice OpenAI function-call JSON via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Re-checked 2026-08-19: vLLM's supported --tool-call-parser list contains no Phi entry, so even that path needs a custom parser or client-side extraction.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: Tool definitions are serialized into the prompt, so they are ordinary input tokens counted against max_position_embeddings=16384. At a 16K window this is the dominant footprint risk in this dataset.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No deferred/lazy tool loading at the model level — no equivalent of Claude Code's tool-search / defer_loading. Any deferral must be built by the host.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No tool-name length or pattern rule is documented (there is no tool API to enforce one). Whatever the serving stack / client imposes is the operative limit.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: No documented schema-size limits — the binding constraint is the 16,384-token window that prompt, tool definitions and completion all share. A single mid-size MCP server (50 tools at ~200 tok/def = ~10K tokens) consumes ~60% of the window before the first user message, and a large one (the ~42K-token GitHub server measured in the cited tool-overload report) cannot be loaded at all. Scope: aggregate across all connected servers; there is no per-server cap to check against.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No vendor cap documented; description text simply counts against the 16K context window.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (no vendor-run API). Bounded by the serving config (vLLM --max-model-len / --max-num-batched-tokens), any reverse proxy body limit, and GPU memory.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No documented cap on a single tool result; results are context-bound and count against max_model_len — at 16K a chatty tool result can evict the whole conversation.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Not documented; would be set by the chat-template tool-call parser, and vLLM ships none for Phi. See parallel_tool_calls.

tool_use_per_turn_limit.notes: Not a model property — the agent host/framework decides how many tool-call/result cycles a turn may run.

max_connected_servers.notes: Client/agent-framework-defined (e.g. Cursor caps ~40 tools total across servers); nothing at the model or serving layer counts servers.

max_total_tools.notes: No vendor cap. The effective AGGREGATE ceiling is approximately (context_window − output headroom) ÷ average tool-definition tokens, set by the serving config; for Phi-4's 16,384-token window that is roughly 30–50 small definitions with nothing left for history. Host apps cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

tools_mcp.other_limits_notes: Open-weight: the model API layer imposes NO tool count/size caps. Binding limits come from (1) the serving stack — vLLM/SGLang max_model_len, max_num_batched_tokens, GPU KV-cache; (2) the model chat-template tool-call parser — re-checked 2026-08-19, vLLM's supported --tool-call-parser list (Hermes, Mistral, Llama, Granite, InternLM, Jamba, xLAM, Qwen, DeepSeek, OpenAI OSS, Kimi-K2, Hunyuan, Cohere, GLM, FunctionGemma, Olmo 3, Apertus, pythonic, …) contains NO Phi entry, so OpenAI-shaped tool calling over vLLM needs a custom parser or client-side parsing of the model's own template; (3) the agent host (Cursor ~40-tool cap, Claude Desktop ~100). vLLM's default context is often 16K which silently truncates tool calls — raise --max-model-len.

strict_function_schema.notes: No OpenAI-style strict function-schema mode (100-prop / 5-level-depth / no-oneOf enforcement) is documented for any Phi model — neither the HF model cards nor the Foundry model pages define schema validation rules. Schema constraints are whatever the serving stack's guided-decoding backend enforces, not a model/API rule.

skills_supported.notes: No skills/extension concept for self-hosted Phi weights (re-checked 2026-08-19).

skills_loading_model.notes: No skills mechanism exists, so there is nothing to load eagerly or progressively.

skills_context.system_prompt_overhead_notes: No fixed system-prompt overhead is documented. The chat template adds only a few special tokens per turn (<|im_start|>, <|im_sep|>, <|im_end|>, IDs 100264-100266). The system prompt itself counts as ordinary input tokens against the shared 16,384-token pool.

prompt_caching.notes: No vendor-level prompt caching exists for self-hosted open weights (there is no per-token bill to discount). Serving stacks can reuse the KV-cache prefix — vLLM --enable-prefix-caching, SGLang RadixAttention — which cuts recompute for a static system prompt + tool block, but it is operator-configured, not model-native.

memory_feature.notes: No persistent memory feature at the model level; memory is entirely the host's job.

input_per_mtok_usd.notes: Open weights — no per-token list price to record. Re-checked 2026-08-19: the Microsoft Foundry pricing page still shows '$-' for every Phi row (Phi-4, Phi-4-mini, Phi-4-multimodal text+image, Phi-4-multimodal audio, Phi-4-mini-reasoning, Phi-4-reasoning, Phi-4-reasoning-plus). Self-hosting means the operator pays GPU/cloud cost.

output_per_mtok_usd.notes: Same as input: no published per-token price; self-hosted compute only.

cached_input_per_mtok_usd.notes: No cached-input price exists for self-hosted weights; vLLM/SGLang prefix caching saves GPU time, not a billed token rate.

batch_discount.notes: No batch-discount tier is published for Phi; batching is a throughput setting of the operator's serving stack.

billing_unit.notes: Self-hosted compute (GPU hours / cloud instance cost); the Foundry pricing page publishes no token rate for Phi.

reasoning_billed_as_output.notes: Phi-4 emits no reasoning trace, and self-hosted weights carry no per-token billing at all, so there is no reasoning-billing rule to record; left null. Cost is GPU time.

self_host.framework_tool_calling_notes: Phi-4 has no function-calling post-training and no tool tokens in its vocabulary. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint you can still pass a tools array, but the model was never trained to honour it, and as of 2026-08-19 vLLM ships no Phi --tool-call-parser, so tool calls must be parsed client-side out of free text. For tool/MCP work inside this family use Phi-4-mini-instruct or Phi-4-multimodal-instruct, whose chat templates take a tools argument natively.

detail.notes: Phi-4 (14B, Dec 2024) is the largest plain text model in the Phi-4 family and remains GA on Microsoft Foundry (lifecycle page checked 2026-08-17: GA, no retirement date). Its 16,384-token window is the smallest in this open-weight roster, which makes it the highest-risk model here for MCP footprints: a 50-tool server at ~200 tokens per definition eats ~60% of the window, and the ~42K-token GitHub MCP surface cannot be loaded at all. Function calling is not supported (Foundry: 'Tool calling: No'; no tool tokens in the tokenizer). 2026-08-19 correction: its tokenizer is tiktoken cl100k_base-derived (padded vocab 100,352), NOT o200k_base — count Phi-4 with the generic_cl100k profile and Phi-4-mini/multimodal with generic_o200k.

context_window_tokens.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19. config.json max_position_embeddings=131072 (original_max_position_embeddings=4096, rope_scaling.type=longrope); tokenizer_config.json model_max_length=131072; model card 'Context length: 128K tokens'; tech report 'support 128K context length based on LongRoPE'. Foundry lists 131,072 input.

input_output_shared.notes: Foundry (updated 2026-07-24) documents input 131,072 / output 4,096 for the hosted endpoint. These are caps inside one 131,072-token attention window, not two independent pools — the completion is drawn from the same budget the prompt consumes. Self-hosted, --max-model-len is the single ceiling.

max_input_tokens.notes: Foundry documents 131,072 input tokens (unchanged 2026-08-19); matches config.json max_position_embeddings.

max_output_tokens_default.notes: No default published. Foundry publishes only the 4,096 maximum; the HF card's examples pass max_new_tokens explicitly (values 40–500). Self-hosted the operator sets it per request.

max_output_tokens_max.notes: Foundry documents output up to 4,096 tokens (re-checked 2026-08-19). Self-hosted this is not enforced — the serving stack can generate up to the 131,072-token window.

extended_context.notes: 128K (131,072) via LongRoPE is the native documented maximum; no additional beta/extended window is published.

reasoning_tokens_count_as_output.notes: Phi-4-mini-instruct is not a reasoning model and emits no thinking trace, so there is no reasoning-vs-output split to record; left null. Phi-4-mini-reasoning is a separate model.

tokenizer_family.notes: Upgraded to a tier-1 statement 2026-08-19: the Phi-4-Mini tech report says the model uses the 'o200k_base tiktoken' tokenizer with a 'vocabulary size of 200,064'. Corroborated by config.json auto_map AutoTokenizer='Xenova/gpt-4o' and tokenizer_config.json tokenizer_class=GPT2Tokenizer. On top of the o200k_base base vocab sit Phi-4-mini's tool special tokens: <|tool|>=200023, <|/tool|>=200024, <|tool_call|>=200025, <|/tool_call|>=200026, <|tool_response|>=200027. This is a DIFFERENT tokenizer from Phi-4 / Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B (cl100k_base, vocab 100,352) — use generic_o200k for this model.

tokenizer_public.notes: Tokenizer files ship in the MIT-licensed HF repo (re-checked 2026-08-19).

tokenizer_access.value: HF AutoTokenizer (microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct, trust_remote_code=True) — or tiktoken o200k_base for the base vocab plus the Phi-4-mini special tokens

count_tokens_method.value: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct', trust_remote_code=True); len(tok.encode(text))
count_tokens_method.notes: For a tool-loaded prompt use tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=[...]) so the <|tool|> wrapper and the serialized tool JSON are counted the way the model will actually see them.

image_token_rule.notes: Phi-4-mini-instruct is text-only; images require Phi-4-multimodal-instruct or Phi-4-reasoning-vision-15B.

audio_token_rule.notes: Phi-4-mini-instruct is text-only; audio requires Phi-4-multimodal-instruct.

chars_per_token_estimate.notes: Rule of thumb only: ~4 characters per token for English. Phi-4-mini / Phi-4-multimodal use tiktoken o200k_base (vocab 200,064) per the Phi-4-Mini tech report, so OpenAI's published ~4-chars/token English heuristic applies directly. Use the HF AutoTokenizer for exact counts — never this estimate for a hard budget. (Previously recorded as 3.5 with no source; replaced with the sourced ~4 figure.)

function_calling.notes: Re-verified 2026-08-19 at the tokenizer level, which is stronger than the prose: tokenizer_config.json reserves <|tool|>=200023, <|/tool|>=200024, <|tool_call|>=200025, <|/tool_call|>=200026, <|tool_response|>=200027, and the bundled chat_template branches on "message['role'] == 'system' and 'tools' in message" to emit <|tool|>[…]<|/tool|>. The model card documents the same 'tool-enabled function-calling format' and lists function calling as an intended use; the tech report notes Phi-4-Mini was trained on 'a significantly larger and more diverse set of function calling' data. NOTE the split: the WEIGHTS support tool calling, while the Foundry-hosted endpoint still advertises 'Tool calling: No'.

native_mcp.notes: No MCP protocol at the model level — tools arrive as a JSON array inside the system message, and an MCP host must translate tools/list into that array. Foundry lists 'Tool calling: No' for the hosted endpoint (page updated 2026-07-24), so MCP over Foundry is not available either; MCP use means self-hosting.

parallel_tool_calls.notes: Still undocumented as of 2026-08-19. The chat template accepts an arbitrary tools array and wraps model output in a single <|tool_call|>…<|/tool_call|> span; neither the model card nor the tech report states whether multiple simultaneous calls per turn were trained. Treat multi-call turns as unverified.

max_tools_hard.notes: No per-request numeric tool-count cap is documented — open weights have no API layer to enforce one. What binds instead: the 131,072-token window shared with the prompt, the empirical tool-selection cliff (lower than the usual 30–50 for a 3.8B model), and the host's aggregate catalog cap. Scope: AGGREGATE across all connected servers plus built-in tools; no per-MCP-server cap is documented anywhere.

max_tools_practical.notes: CHANGED 2026-08-19: 20 -> null. The previous value was an interpolation. It was cited to a dev.to tool-overload post (2026-03-06) that was re-opened in this pass: its single measurement ('accuracy on correct tool selection dropped from ~95% with a focused toolset to ~71% with the full GitHub MCP server loaded', ~4 tools / ~1,200 tokens vs ~46 tools / ~42,000 tokens) was run with model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", and the post never mentions Phi. Attributing a per-Phi-variant number to a measurement of another vendor's model is not admissible, and the four Phi variants were merely ranked against each other by judgement. SEARCHED 2026-08-19 for a Phi-specific figure and found none: the four Hugging Face model cards (tier 1), the Phi-4 / Phi-4-mini technical reports, Microsoft's PhiCookBook function-calling sample (its example declares exactly one tool and gives no guidance), an on-device tool-calling comparison covering Phi-4-mini (ertas.ai, updated 2026-08-07 -- BFCL v4 composite scores and a 5-tool customer-support evaluation set, but no tool-count-vs-accuracy curve), a 2026 tool-calling benchmark round-up (presenc.ai) and a catalog-scaling study (nerdleveltech), neither of which mentions Phi. No Azure AI Foundry page states a tool count either. WHAT ACTUALLY BINDS on this variant: model capacity rather than the window -- 3.8B parameters with a 128K context length (model card, tier 1). The model card documents a tool-enabled function-calling format (tools passed in the system prompt between <|tool|> and <|/tool|>) but gives no guidance whatsoever on tool quantity, and its red-team section reports that 'With function calling scenarios, the model could sometimes hallucinate function names or URL's.' Treat tool-selection reliability as degrading earlier than the ~30-50 range reported for frontier models, but the dataset now records no number because none has been measured on this model. Scope when a number is eventually recorded: AGGREGATE, not per server.

tool_definition_shape.notes: Native shape: a JSON array of {name, description, parameters} objects placed in the SYSTEM message and wrapped by the <|tool|> / <|/tool|> special tokens — structurally close to OpenAI function JSON but injected as prompt text rather than a separate API field. Re-checked 2026-08-19: vLLM's supported --tool-call-parser list still has no Phi entry, so an OpenAI-compatible server will not translate or parse this shape for you; use tok.apply_chat_template(..., tools=[...]) and parse <|tool_call|> spans client-side.

tool_defs_count_as_input.notes: The tool JSON is literally part of the system message, so it is ordinary input tokens against the 131,072-token window — plus ~5 special tokens of wrapper overhead. The 128K window gives far more headroom than Phi-4's 16K, but a 3.8B model's selection accuracy degrades well before the window fills.

tool_search_deferral.notes: No deferred/lazy tool loading at the model level; the whole tool array is materialized in the system message every turn. Any progressive disclosure must be built by the host.

max_tool_name_len.notes: No name-length or character-pattern rule is documented; names are free-form JSON strings inside the system message. The operative limit is whatever the MCP host imposes after namespacing.

tools_mcp.tool_schema_limits_notes: Tools are injected as a JSON array in the system message between <|tool|> (200023) and <|/tool|> (200024); model tool calls come back between <|tool_call|> (200025) and <|/tool_call|> (200026), and results are fed back after <|tool_response|> (200027). No schema-size, nesting-depth or keyword restriction is documented — the definitions are plain prompt text counted against the 131,072-token window. Practical caution from the model card's red-team section: the model 'could sometimes hallucinate function names or URLs' in function-calling scenarios, so validate the emitted name against the registered tool set before dispatching.

max_tool_description_len.notes: No vendor cap documented; description text counts against the 128K context window like any other prompt text.

max_request_size.notes: No vendor byte cap (no vendor-run API). Bounded by the serving config (vLLM --max-model-len / --max-num-batched-tokens), proxy body limits, and GPU memory.

max_tool_result_size.notes: No documented cap on a single tool result; results arrive after <|tool_response|> as ordinary tokens and count against max_model_len.

max_parallel_tool_calls_count.notes: Not documented; would be governed by the chat-template tool-call parser, and vLLM ships none for Phi. See parallel_tool_calls.

Host apps cap lower (Cursor ~40, Claude Desktop ~100).

detail.notes: Phi-4-mini-instruct (3.8B, Feb 2025) is the Phi model to reach for when tool/MCP use matters: it is the only Phi-4-family model whose vocabulary and chat template natively encode tool calling (<|tool|> 200023 … <|tool_response|> 200027), and its 128K LongRoPE window leaves room for a real tool surface — unlike Phi-4's 16K. Two caveats that have not changed as of 2026-08-19: (1) the Foundry-hosted endpoint still advertises 'Tool calling: No', so MCP use means self-hosting the weights; (2) at 3.8B parameters, selection accuracy degrades long before the window fills, and the model card's own red-teaming reports hallucinated function names. Still GA on Foundry (lifecycle page checked 2026-08-17: GA, no retirement date). Fits in ~8GB VRAM quantized.
